# Engineering law
The discipline shared by the public Vidoxlabs repositories, kept here in one page and linked from the family.

- License: MIT, exact text, one copy per repository, no riders.
- Dependencies: zero at runtime. A dependency proposal is an architecture decision before it is a package.
- Runtime: Node 22.13 or newer. `npm test` stays green on every commit.
- Claims: every capability carries `implemented`, `specified`, `planned`, or `observed`, and the label must be true.
- Unknowns fail closed: a missing head, a failed fetch, or an unreadable source stops the work. Nothing is guessed, filled in, or reported as empty when it is unknown.
- Public safety: no credentials, tokens, account names, personal handles, hostnames, IP addresses, port numbers, container names, cluster names, or network topologies in any committed file.
- Text only: documentation pages and synced sources stay text. No binaries enter this hub.
- Prose: short plain sentences, noun-led lines, no invented product names, no em-dashes anywhere.

# The family and this hub
The public products grow from botany: seed, capillary, myosotis, aestivation, drosera, and bloom, with trellis standing outside the call path to probe them. The naming law, the stack, and the reason the line is botanic live in [capillary's docs/family.md](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary/blob/main/docs/family.md).

This repository is plain-named by owner decision, as `videsign` is: infrastructure carries plain words, and the botanic line stays for products. The hub serves the whole family. It writes the shared pages once, and it carries each member's own documentation verbatim, with digests and heads, so a reader or a site can trust exactly what landed and when.

Per-source documentation lands under `sources/<name>/` as written upstream. The hub formats nothing, edits nothing, and resolves no conflicts between sources: a disagreement between two repositories' pages stays visible until the owner settles it upstream.

# Family glossary
This glossary establishes shared terminology for public timeline specifications, contracts, and capability ledgers. For naming rules across the botanic product family, see [seed's docs/lexicon.md](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed/blob/main/docs/lexicon.md) and [capillary's docs/family.md](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary/blob/main/docs/family.md).

Generalized family and role terms
Public repositories use only two naming forms: proper nouns for the public repositories (`seed`, `capillary`, `myosotis`, `aestivation`, `drosera`, `trellis`, `bloom`, `docs`, `videsign`) and generalized role terms for concepts and roles:

| Generalized term | Public product | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `native client` | none (private surface) | The desktop application a person works from. |
| `intelligence backend` | none (private service) | The private backend service behind client applications. |
| `coding workspace` | none (private session) | A direct session in which an agent edits a real work tree. |
| `step admission and scaling` | none | Planning which worker, timeout, and context a chain step receives. |
| `documentation base` | `docs` (hub) | The governed documentation repository and synced knowledge surface. |
| `design system` | `videsign` | The shared visual design tokens and canon. |
| `tooling fabric` | `drosera` | Declarative tool faces, skills, hooks, and cookbooks. |
| `local cluster` | none | Private local infrastructure; never described further in public repositories. |
| `memory fabric` | `myosotis` | Governed memory with explicit consent, correction, and forget epochs. |
| `storage triangle` | none | Record authority, cache projection, and graph projection. |
| `admission and ratification loop` | `aestivation` | Plan proposal, independent review verdicts, and the assembly gate. |
| `context retrieval system` | `capi

Timeline and harness terms
- **`capability`**: A tracked unit of family behavior (`CAP-01` to `CAP-19`) with one lead repository, optional touched repositories, an acceptance specification, and ordered slices.
- **`ledger`**: The capability status table in [docs/timeline/ledger.md](timeline/ledger.md) backed by [docs/timeline/capabilities.json](timeline/capabilities.json) and each repository's `docs/capabilities/index.json`.
- **`milestone`**: A numbered delivery checkpoint (`M0` to `M9`) grouping capabilities that ship together when their tests land.
- **`horizon`**: Planning bucket for milestones and capabilities: `now` (`M0` to `M2`), `next` (`M3` to `M6`), or `later` (`M7` to `M9`).
- **`slice`**: The smallest independently testable, shippable increment of a capability (`CAP-NN.k`), delivered with its ledger and changelog updates in one PR.
- **`proposal`**: An intake document (`docs/proposals/P-YYYYMMDD-<slug>.md`) proposing a new capability or cross-repository change prior to owner decision.
- **`ADR`**: Architecture Decision Record (`docs/adr/NNNN-<slug>.md`) recording context, decision, consequences, and alternatives; moves from `Proposed` to `Accepted` only by owner decision.
- **`owner gate`**: A runtime pause requiring a digest-bound owner decision record (`seed`) before an effect, scope expansion, plan approval, or third-party egress action may proceed.
- **`plan gate`**: Deterministic assembly gate (`aestivation` `assemblyGate`) checking plan validation, verdict

Memory that keeps only what you allow # myosotis Governed memory for agents: consent to keep, structural forget. Myosotis is the memory member of the bloom agent family. It holds the contracts and reference modules for agent memory where two promises sit on the face of the thing: memory is only kept under proper consent, and a real forget is structural. A forget invalidates every projection built before it and withholds forgotten content from later reads. A stale projection fails closed; it never resurrects.

Status
Version 1.2.0. The record, consent, forget, bounded recall, and in-process continuity rules are `implemented` as a tested reference library. A durable store, projection adapters, and service interfaces remain `specified` or `planned`.

Install
```bash
npm install @vidoxlabs/myosotis
```

Requires Node >= 22.13. Zero runtime dependencies.

Modules
| Module | What it holds | Label |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `records.mjs` | Memory record shape and the closed set of memory classes: organizational, personal-consented, active-thread, unconfirmed. | `implemented` |
| `consent.mjs` | Consent grants and revocations, ordered by an optional sequence so a later grant is re-consent, and the state that answers whether a scope currently has consent. | `implemented` |
| `forget.mjs` | The memory store state machine: admission and supersede, the confirmed and keyed forget that tombstones a whole supersede chain, the epoch, and stamped projections of identifiers and digests that are refused once stale and rebuilt before they serve. | `implemented` |
| `recall.mjs` | Bounded selection from caller-held records, with sensitivity checks and candidate, eligible, and selected counts. | `implemented` |
| `continuity.mjs` | One active continuity per subject, held in the process. Lookup never opens one, attach refuses any id that is not this subject's active id without saying why, and isolate opens a new active id. | `implemented` |

Why the classes stay distinguishable
The four memory classes never collapse into one bucket:

- **organizational**: knowledge that belongs to a scope, like a team's working notes. Kept without personal consent because it is not about a person.
- **personal-consented** requires a live grant for its scope, an admissible sensitivity, and provenance of the principal's explicit confirmation.
- **active-thread**: working context for the conversation happening now. Ephemeral by nature, never promoted to durable silently.
- **unconfirmed**: an observation that has not been established. Stays marked. Never presented as known.

Conflating them is the failure mode this fabric exists to prevent.

Why forget is an epoch
A forget that only deletes a row leaves every cached copy of that row alive. Myosotis models forget as an epoch bump: every projection (a cache, an index, a summary) carries the epoch it was built at, and any projection whose stamp no longer matches fails closed. Reading it is refused until it is rebuilt from the store. Bypass and rebuild, never resurrect.

The family
The family follows one design law: ordinary botanical words for public products.

| Name | Province |
| :--- | :--- |
| [`seed`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed) | Harness foundation: runs, tools, providers |
| [`capillary`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary) | Context retrieval and relations, provenance-first |
| `myosotis` (this repo) | Memory with consent and structural forget |
| [`aestivation`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/aestivation) | Plans, verdicts, and the gate before assembly |
| [`drosera`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/drosera) | Tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks |
| [`trellis`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/trellis) | Multi-point testing with dated evidence |
| [`bloom`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) | The team workspace harness |
| [`docs`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs) | Family documentation, synced from every public repository |

Documentation
- `AGENTS.md`: start here before editing. Stay in this repository's province.
- `docs/charter.md`: mission, principles, non-goals.
- `docs/architecture.md`: the parts and how they compose.
- `docs/contracts/`: the record, consent, and forget contracts.
- `docs/interop.md`: how bloom consumes memory, and where capillary ends and myosotis begins.

Development
```bash
npm test
```

Tests use the Node built-in runner. Adding a rule means adding the test that holds it.

License
MIT

The Vidoxlabs name and mark are trademarks of Vidoxlabs LLC. They are not covered by this repository's MIT license.

# Architecture Decision Records
Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for `myosotis` live in this directory, numbered sequentially from `0001` (`NNNN-<slug>.md`).

- Format, lifecycle (`Proposed`, `Accepted`, `Superseded by NNNN`, `Deferred`), and review rules follow the hub ADR convention in [Vidoxlabs/docs](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs/blob/main/docs/adr/README.md).
- Agents write `Proposed` ADRs; only an explicit owner decision moves an ADR to `Accepted`.
- Any runtime dependency proposal requires an ADR before adding a package.
- Record every added or updated ADR in `docs/capabilities/index.json` in the same pull request.

# Myosotis architecture
Four parts, one hard rule each.

```
memory record ──► consent check ──► store (epoch N) ──► projections (cache, index, summary)
                        │                  │                    │
                   refusal on          forget(id)          stamp = epoch at build
                   missing grant            │                    │
                                           ▼                    ▼
                                    epoch N+1          stale stamp fails closed
```

The memory record
Every record has `{ id, text, kind, scope }`. The `kind` is one of `organizational`, `personal-consented`, `active-thread`, or `unconfirmed`. The `scope` names who the memory belongs to, such as a team, a channel, or a person's space. A personal record also carries its sensitivity and explicit confirmation provenance.

The consent registry
Grants and revocations over scopes. In this edition, consent is personal: the subject of the memory grants it. A grant says "personal memory in this scope is permitted." A revocation kills the grant. A later grant, ordered on the record by its sequence, is re-consent. The check is plain: a `personal-consented` record is admissible only while a live grant for its scope exists. Every other class is admitted without personal consent because none of them are personal memory — but scope is still required.

The store and the epoch
The store is the ordered pair `{ epoch, records }`. The epoch is a monotonic counter that only moves when memory is forgotten.

- **Admission** validates the record, checks consent when the class is personal, stamps the record with the epoch it entered at, and appends. Refusals carry the reason.
- **Forget** is confirmed and keyed. It removes the record with that id and every record it superseded, leaves a digest-only tombstone for each, and bumps the epoch once. A repeated key replays without a second bump. Otherwise it or reports `unknown` with no state change. That asymmetry is deliberate: forgotten-with-bump on a hit, declared-unknown on a miss. A miss that bumped the epoch would poison every projection for nothing, and a hit that did not bump would leave stale projections serving dead content.

Projections
Anything derived from the store — a cache, an index, a recall list, a summary — is a projection carrying the stamp of the epoch it was built at. A projection is current only while its stamp equals the store's epoch. The moment the epoch moves, every prior projection is stale, and stale means refused: rebuild from the store, never serve from the stale copy. This is the discipline that makes forget-correctness structural rather than a matter of hoping every consumer cleaned up its cache. In `src/`, `readProjection` refuses a stale or unverifiable projection and serves no records with the refusal, and `recallCurrent` rebuilds from the store before serving, so a consumer that reads through them cannot serve forgotten content. A projection holds identifiers and digests, not text; `recallCurrent` resolves text from the store and rebuilds when an entry no longer resolves.

Continuity
A continuity is the one thread of memory a subject is working in. The ledger is a frozen value the caller holds in the process, keyed by the same subject string consent uses. Lookup only reads. Attach resumes the active continuity, or opens one when the subject has none, and refuses any id that is not that subject's active id with one answer that does not say why. Isolate retires the active id and opens a new one. The ledger touches neither the store nor its epoch.

What this edition is
`src/` implements these four parts as pure state machines over explicit state objects: validation, consent state, admission, forget, and the epoch stamping, with continuity kept apart in its own ledger. No I/O, no store backend, no concurrency. A durable store behind this state machine is `specified` in the contracts; the mapping onto any particular database is deliberately out of scope here.

# CAP-11: Memory integration
- ID: `CAP-11`
- Title: Memory integration
- Lead: `myosotis`
- Touches: `bloom`, `capillary`
- Horizon: `next`
- Milestone: `M3`
- CLI phase: `P3`
- Status: `proposed`
- Claim: `planned`
- Depends on: `CAP-05`

Why
Context retrieval and agent execution must integrate with governed memory without collapsing retrieval into durable memory, serving stale projections after a forget, leaking personal records without consent, or letting agent-written artifacts impersonate owner decisions.

What it does
- **Typed memory kinds with provenance in context packets**: recalled memory enters the context packet built by `capillary` (`CAP-05`) carrying its closed `myosotis` kind (`organizational`, `personal-consented`, `active-thread`, `unconfirmed`) and explicit provenance metadata through `capillary`'s epoch-guarded packet builder (`buildEpochGuardedPacket`).
- **Consent before admission**: `personal-consented` records enter only when a live subject-granted consent grant covers the scope, sensitivity is in `{ public, internal, restricted }`, and provenance is `explicit-user`. Ambient conversation text never creates personal memory.
- **Structural forget across projections**: confirmed and keyed `forgetMemory` removes the record and its supersede chain, records digest-only tombstones, and bumps the store epoch once. Stale projections fail closed (`readProjection` refuses prior stamps; `recallCurrent` rebuilds before serving; `recallBounded` enforces character budgets).
- **Per-thread continuity**: `openContinuity`, `lookupContinuity`, `attachContinuity`, and `isolateContinuity` maintain at most one active continuity per thread/subject. Lookup never opens a continuity, and attach refuses unknown, isolated, or other-subject IDs with a single uniform error that reveals nothing.
- **Experience receipts (`CAP-11.1`, `D11`)**: agents may write experience receipts recording what ran, on which content digest, and with what result. Record validation enforces that experience rec

Contract touchpoints
- `myosotis/docs/contracts/records.md`: closed four memory kinds, personal sensitivity and `explicit-user` provenance, plus experience receipt record shape and non-authority constraints (`CAP-11.1`).
- `myosotis/docs/contracts/consent.md`: subject-granted scope consent preceding personal admission and sequence-ordered revocation/re-consent.
- `myosotis/docs/contracts/forget.md`: confirmed and keyed forget, supersede chain tombstones, monotonic epoch bump, fail-closed stale projections, and bounded recall.
- `myosotis/docs/contracts/continuity.md`: one active continuity per subject/thread and uniform attach refusal.
- `capillary/docs/contracts/retrieval.md`: `buildEpochGuardedPacket`, typed memory provenance in context packets, and `deletion-epoch-changed` / `deletion-epoch-unavailable` refusals (`CAP-11.2`).
- `bloom/docs/architecture.md`: per-thread continuity wiring, consent enforcement on writes, strict fail-closed turn stop on memory read failure, and digest-only trace logging (`CAP-11.3`).

Tool IDs and events
### Tool IDs

No new tool IDs are introduced by `CAP-11` (existing memory domain faces are documented in `docs/interop.md`).

| Tool ID | Effect class | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

### Events

No standalone events are introduced by `CAP-11`; context packet assembly emits `context.packet` (`CAP-05`), and trace records (`CAP-10`) log memory identity as digests only.

| Event | Source | Payload summary |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

Acceptance tests
- `experience-receipt-distinct-from-owner-decision`: an agent-written experience receipt records what ran, on which digest, and with what result, and is refused if shaped as or promoted to an owner decision, consent grant, or ratified rule (`D11`).
- `consent-precedes-personal-keep`: admitting a `personal-consented` record without a live subject-granted consent grant for the scope or without `explicit-user` provenance is refused.
- `forget-bumps-epoch-and-fails-stale-projection`: a confirmed keyed forget bumps the epoch, refuses projections carrying an earlier stamp, and rebuilds current recall without forgotten content.
- `epoch-guard-refuses-mid-read-forget`: `capillary` `buildEpochGuardedPacket` refuses packet assembly with `deletion-epoch-changed` when the epoch moves during a read, or `deletion-epoch-unavailable` when unreadable.
- `strict-recall-failure-stops-turn`: a failed memory read or epoch refusal under strict recall policy stops the turn rather than continuing with empty or stale memory.
- `trace-records-memory-digest-not-text`: trace entries emitted for recall and forget record memory identity as a SHA-256 digest and never emit raw memory text.
- `continuity-isolated-per-thread`: continuity lookup, attach, and isolate keep one active continuity per thread/subject and refuse unknown, isolated, or cross-subject IDs uniformly.

Slices
- `CAP-11.1` (`myosotis`, `M3`, `proposed`): Experience receipt record rules and fail-closed strict recall policy.
- `CAP-11.2` (`capillary`, `M3`, `proposed`): Epoch-guarded packet integration with typed memory kinds and provenance.
- `CAP-11.3` (`bloom`, `M3`, `proposed`): Thread continuity, consent enforcement, and digest-only trace logging.

Non-goals
- Implicit or ambient memory creation from conversation messages, tool outputs, or evidence reads without an explicit keep or receipt act.
- Silent promotion of `unconfirmed` or `active-thread` records or experience receipts into `personal-consented` memory or owner decisions.
- Semantic embedding indexes or external database services inside `myosotis`.
- Allowing any projection or trace output to expose forgotten memory text.

Family rules and conflicts
- Retrieval informs and memory keeps (`docs/interop.md`): `capillary` retrieves bounded context with provenance (`CAP-05`), while `myosotis` governs consent, structural forget, and continuity. Neither impersonates the other.
- `myosotis` stays a zero-dependency pure reference library with no I/O, no model calls, and no peer imports; `bloom` composes `myosotis` and `capillary`.
- Under `CAP-09` context compaction, any summary derived from recalled records links back to its replaced records so a structural forget invalidates derived summaries via epoch mismatch.
- Aligns with `CAP-06` and `CAP-07`: experience receipts and memory records never satisfy an owner gate.

Open owner decisions
- `D11` (pending owner decision): Experience-only memory receipts. Confirm that agents may write experience receipts recording what ran, on which digest, and with what result, while prohibiting any agent-written record from reading as an owner decision, consent grant, or ratified rule.
- Strict recall failure scope (pending owner decision): Confirm whether strict turn-stop on memory read failure applies unconditionally to every run or allows an explicit opt-out when an objective declares no memory access.

Evidence

# Myosotis charter

Mission
Build the memory fabric an agent can be trusted with. Myosotis holds the contracts for memory where the answer to "may this be kept" is a governed decision, and the answer to "forget this" is a structural guarantee.

The name is the point: the flower's ordinary name is forget-me-not, and this system's hardest promise is the opposite direction done right — when the owner says forget, it is forgotten everywhere, structurally, and the fabric can prove its projections are not lying about what they remember.

Principles
1. **Consent precedes keep.** Personal memory enters the store only under a live consent record naming the scope. There is no ambient consent, no inferred consent, and no consent-by-default because the conversation went well.
2. **Classes stay distinguishable.** Organizational knowledge, consented personal memory, active-thread working context, and unconfirmed observations are four different things. The fabric never silently promotes one to another.
3. **Unconfirmed is not established.** An observation that has not been confirmed stays marked unconfirmed and is never presented as knowledge.
4. **Forget is structural.** A real forget removes the record and bumps the store epoch. Every projection stamped before the bump is stale; stale projections fail closed and must be rebuilt from the store. Bypass and rebuild — never resurrect.
5. **Unknown is declared.** A forget that matches no record is reported as unknown. Silence is not an acceptable answer to a forget.
6. **Projection until verified.** Caches, indexes, and summaries are projections. The store is the authority. A projection's claim is only as good as its epoch stamp.

Non-goals
- **Not a chat log.** Reading evidence or posting a message creates no memory. Conversation text is not memory by default.
- **Not retrieval.** Finding and ranking context is capillary's province. Myosotis is what is permitted to be kept and what must be forgotten; capillary is what is fetched and how its provenance is carried.
- **No ambient inference.** The fabric does not guess what a person "probably wants remembered." Memory is created by declared acts — a keep, a note, a save — not by vibes.

# Contract: consent
Label: `specified` (rules), `implemented` (state machine in `src/consent.mjs`).

Shape
```
grant { subject, scope, grantedBy, sequence }   — subject == grantedBy: personal consent in this edition
revocation { subject, scope, sequence }         — kills the grants it names that it does not precede
state { grants, revocations }           — answers hasConsentFor(scope)
```

Rules
1. **Personal consent is granted by the subject.** In this edition, `grantedBy` must equal `subject`. Consent a person cannot themselves give is not consent. Delegated granting (a parent for a child, an org admin for a member) is a real need and is `planned`, named here so it is not invented later by accident.
2. **A grant names a scope.** Consent is not global. A grant for one scope permits nothing in another.
3. **Revocation is immediate and permanent.** A revoked grant no longer permits admission, ever. Re-consent is a new grant after the revocation, on the record.

   `implemented` in `src/consent.mjs`. Order on the record is a `sequence`: a non-negative integer on a grant or a revocation, `null` when not given. A revocation kills a grant for the same subject and scope unless both carry a sequence and the grant's is strictly later; that later grant is re-consent. On a tie, or when either side has no sequence, the revocation wins. A revoked grant never comes back, because its own sequence does not change: only a new grant with a later sequence permits admission again.
4. **Consent gates admission, not existence.** A `personal-consented` record must pass [record validation](records.md) and have a live grant before the store admits it. Revoking consent stops new admission under that grant. The forget contract governs records already in the store.
5. **No implied consent.** Long conversation, friendly tone, repeated asks — none of it grants anything. Only a grant record

What consent does not cover
- `organizational`, `active-thread`, and `unconfirmed` records do not require a consent grant. They are admitted by their own rules because they are not personal memory.
- Consent does not create memory. It permits it. The declared act that creates the record is a separate thing.

Changes
- `0.3.0` — re-consent is implemented. Before `0.3.0`, `consentState` treated any revocation as permanent for its subject and scope, so the re-consent this contract describes was impossible. Grants and revocations now take an optional `sequence`, and every consent record carries `sequence` (`null` when not given). The change is additive: records without a sequence behave exactly as before.

# Contract: continuity
Label: `specified` (rules), `implemented` (the in-process ledger in `src/continuity.mjs`).

A continuity is the one thread of memory a subject is working in. The ledger answers
which continuity a caller is attached to. It holds no memory, grants no consent, and
forgets nothing. The rules are ported from the predecessor's attach, isolate, and
active-lookup rules. Its query and its scope columns are not ported.

Rules
1. **One active continuity per subject.** A subject has at most one active
   continuity. Other subjects' continuities are never read or changed on its behalf.
2. **Lookup only reads.** `lookupContinuity` returns `{ attached: true, continuityId }`
   for the subject's active continuity, or `{ attached: false, continuityId: null }`
   when none is attached. It never opens a continuity, and it returns no ledger.
3. **Attach with no id resumes or opens.** With `continuityId` absent or `null`,
   `attachContinuity` returns the active continuity with `created: false` and the
   ledger unchanged. Only when the subject has none does it open one, with
   `created: true` and a new ledger.
4. **Attach with an id succeeds only for that subject's active id.** The ledger is
   returned as given, with `created: false`. An unknown id, an isolated id, and another
   subject's id are one refusal: `ContinuityError` with code
   `continuity-not-attachable` and the same message every time. The refusal names no
   id, no subject, and no state, so it does not say which of the three it was. An id
   from another ledger is unknown to this one and gets the same refusal.
5. **Isolate opens a new active id.** `isolateContinuity` marks the subject's active
   continuity `isolated`, opens a new active one, and returns both ids as
   `continuityId` and `isolatedId`. An isolated id never attaches again, and no call
   makes it active. With nothing attached, isolate opens a continuity and
   `isolated

In the process
A ledger is a value the caller holds in the process. Nothing is written to a file, a
database, or the network. A new process opens an empty ledger. Its lookup reports none
attached, and an id the earlier process opened is refused like any unknown id. A
durable continuity store is not part of this edition.

What continuity does not touch
- Forget, consent, sensitivity, and provenance are unchanged. `openStore`,
  `admitMemory`, `forgetMemory`, `buildProjection`, `readProjection`, `recallCurrent`,
  and `recallBounded` neither take nor check a continuity. A continuity carries no
  epoch. The forget epoch stays on the store.
- A subject is the string the caller supplies. The ledger does not authenticate it.
  Whatever composes myosotis decides who a caller is before it names a subject.

Not ported
The predecessor keeps continuity as rows in a database table, scoped by several
columns, with a consent epoch, a deletion epoch, a version counter, timestamps, a
privacy mode, and row locks on each continuity. It also refuses memory reads and writes
outside an active continuity. None of that is in this repository.

Changes
- `1.2.0` — additive `openContinuity`, `lookupContinuity`, `attachContinuity`,
  `isolateContinuity`, and `ContinuityError` exports. No record, consent, forget,
  projection, or recall call changes, and every call valid under `1.1.0` stays valid.

# Contract: forget
Label: `specified` (rules), `implemented` (state machine in `src/forget.mjs`).

This is the contract the whole fabric is named for. A forget that cannot be trusted is worse than no memory at all.

The structural forget
1. **A hit removes and bumps.** Forgetting a record that exists removes it from the store and increments the epoch. Both, always, atomically. A remove without a bump is a cosmetic forget, and this fabric does not do cosmetic.
2. **A miss is declared unknown.** Forgetting an id that is not in the store changes nothing and reports `status: 'unknown'`. No epoch bump for a miss — a bump would invalidate every projection for no reason. The answer to a forget of a miss is honest: unknown, not success.
3. **A forget is confirmed and keyed.** Without `confirmed: true` nothing changes, and the result is `refused` with reason `confirmation-required`. A bare id is not a confirmation. A forget without a `key` is refused with `key-required`.
4. **A repeated key is a replay.** The same key for the same id returns `replayed` with the first receipt and the store unchanged: no second epoch bump. The same key for another id is refused with `key-conflict`.
5. **A forget erases the supersede chain.** A record admitted with `supersedes` marks the record it corrects `superseded`: withheld from recall, kept in the store, epoch unchanged. Forgetting a record erases it and every record reachable through `supersedes`, and leaves one tombstone per erased id: `{ id, namedId, digest, epoch }`. `namedId` is the id the forget was asked for. A tombstone holds no text.
6. **A tombstone is not a miss.** A forget of an id that is only a tombstone is `already-forgotten` and names its tombs

Serving a projection
`implemented` in `src/forget.mjs`. The read path enforces rule 7 instead of leaving it to
each consumer:

1. **`buildProjection` stamps and freezes an index.** A projection holds, per current
   record, `{ id, kind, scope, digest, admittedEpoch }`, plus the epoch it was built at.
   It is not a second copy of the text. Neither part can be edited afterwards.
2. **`readProjection` serves only a current projection.** A stamp that differs from the
   store's epoch, in either direction, is refused with reason `stale`. A projection whose
   stamp is not a non-negative integer, or that carries no record list, is refused with
   reason `unverifiable`. A refusal carries `records: null`: nothing is served partially
   or with a warning.
3. **`recallCurrent` rebuilds before it serves.** Given a current projection it returns
   that projection unchanged. Given a stale, unverifiable, or missing one, it rebuilds
   from the store and serves the rebuild, with `rebuilt: true`. Forgotten content cannot
   come back through it. Text is always read from the store: each entry must resolve to an
   active record with the same digest, and an entry that does not resolve (a supersede
   happened, or the digest differs) means a rebuild, even at the same epoch.

Why the epoch exists
Every projection of memory — a recall cache, an index, a summary built for a prompt — carries the stamp of the epoch it was built at. The store's epoch only moves on a real forget. So a stamp mismatch has exactly one meaning: memory changed by forgetting, and anything remembered before it is suspect. This makes forget-correctness structural. A consumer cannot accidentally serve forgotten content from a cache without first choosing to ignore the stamp, and ignoring the stamp is an explicit, visible act.

Prohibitions
- Never un-forget. The epoch never moves backward; records never return.
- Never serve from a stale projection while rebuilding; rebuild first, then serve.
- Never treat "forgotten" as "hidden but keepable." The record is gone from the store; a projection of it is not a copy that was set aside, it is an artifact whose source died.

Bounded recall
`recallBounded({ records, maxChars = 6000, counts? })` selects from the records the
caller supplies. When reading from a store, pass the current records resolved by
`recallCurrent` or `recallAll`. A digest-only projection entry carries no text to select.

`candidateCount` counts the supplied records. `policyEligibleCount` counts entries
with a nonempty id and text, an allowed sensitivity (`public`, `internal`, or
`restricted`), and an active state when a state is supplied. The function keeps
whole eligible records in input order, skipping entries that exceed the remaining
budget. `selectedCount` and `usedChars` describe the returned `records`.

`maxChars` must be a positive integer. The returned `maxChars` is the smaller of the
requested limit and the library ceiling of 6000, measured by JavaScript string length.
If the caller provides `counts`, all three counts must be nonnegative integers with
`selectedCount <= policyEligibleCount <= candidateCount`. They must also match the
actual selection. A count or budget refusal throws `RecallError`.

Changes
- `1.1.0` — adds bounded recall over caller-held records, with sensitivity filtering,
  a character limit, and checked count reporting.

- `0.4.0` — breaking. `forgetMemory` takes `{ id, confirmed, key }`; a bare id is
  refused and changes nothing. Forget erases the supersede chain with digest-only
  tombstones, and a repeated key replays without a second bump. `admitMemory` accepts
  `supersedes` and refuses a reused id. Projections hold ids and digests, not text, and
  `recallCurrent` resolves text from the store. Released as a minor bump because myosotis
  is pre-1.0. A caller that passed a bare id must confirm and key its forget.

- `0.2.0` — `buildProjection`, `readProjection`, and `recallCurrent` are new. Before
  `0.2.0` the stale-projection rule existed only as the `projectionIsValid` boolean, and nothing in `src/`
  refused to serve a stale projection. The change is additive; existing exports behave
  as before.

What this contract does not claim
That a store backend, a projection implementation, or a network service implements any of this. It specifies the rules; `src/` is the tested reference state machine; wiring it to durability is future editions' work.

# Contract: memory records
Label: `specified` (shape), `implemented` (validation in `src/records.mjs`).

Shape
```
{
  id:    string, non-empty   — stable identifier within the store
  text:  string, non-empty   — the memory content itself
  kind:  string, closed set  — one of the four memory classes
  scope: string, non-empty   — who this memory belongs to
}
```

The closed set of kinds
| Kind | Meaning | Consent required |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `organizational` | Knowledge belonging to a scope (team notes, working knowledge). | No — it is not about a person. |
| `personal-consented` | Memory about a person. | Yes — a live grant for the scope. |
| `active-thread` | Working context for the current conversation. | No — ephemeral, never promoted silently. |
| `unconfirmed` | An observation not yet established. | No — but it stays marked unconfirmed. |

Stored fields
`admitMemory` adds, on the stored record: `digest` (64-hex SHA-256 of `text`),
`supersedes` (the id this record corrects, or `null`), `state` (`active` or
`superseded`), `admittedEpoch`, and, once superseded, `supersededBy`. An id is used once
in a store, including an id that is now a tombstone.

Personal memory
`personal-consented` records require `sensitivity` (`public`, `internal`, or
`restricted`) and `provenance: { source: 'explicit-user' }`. The caller supplies that
source when the principal has explicitly confirmed the text. `memoryRecord` validates
these fields and copies the source into a frozen provenance object. `admitMemory`
also requires a live consent grant for the record's scope.

The other three kinds keep the base shape. Projection entries keep their existing
identifiers, digests, and indexing fields without carrying personal provenance or text.

Validation rules
1. A record must have a non-empty `id`, `text`, and `scope`.
2. `kind` must be in the closed set. Unknown kinds are rejected, never defaulted.
3. Records are frozen on creation. Corrections are new records, not in-place edits.

Prohibitions
- No kind promotion outside an explicit, declared act. An `unconfirmed` observation does not become `organizational` knowledge because time passed.
- An `active-thread` record is never treated as durable memory by a consumer.
- `personal-consented` records never enter, or stay, without a consented scope. See the consent contract.

Changes
- `1.0.0` — breaking change. `memoryRecord` and `admitMemory` refuse personal records
  that lack an allowed sensitivity or explicit-user provenance. Re-admit older personal
  records only with metadata supported by an actual confirmation.

# Myosotis interop
How myosotis meets the family. Every behavior attributed to a peer below is sourced from that peer's published repository at the time of writing; where a peer has not shipped the behavior, it is not claimed.

bloom: the proved consumer
Bloom describes memory consumption as:

> Owner-saved notes are durable and scoped... Add note to tell the team what to remember. Forget removes the note, invalidates cached recall, stops an active run, and withholds earlier memory-dependent outputs from future team prompts. Reading evidence or posting a message creates no durable personal note.

Mapping onto myosotis's contracts:

| Bloom behavior | Myosotis contract |
| :--- | :--- |
| Add note → durable, scoped | `memoryRecord` with `scope` required; admission through the consent check when personal. |
| Forget → removes the note | `forgetMemory` hit, confirmed and keyed: remove from store, with what it superseded, and leave digest-only tombstones. |
| Forget → invalidates cached recall | The epoch bump: every projection stamped earlier is stale and fails closed. |
| Forget → stops an active run | Out of myosotis's province: run control belongs to the harness, which consults the store's stamp. |
| Forget → withholds earlier outputs from future prompts | Same epoch discipline: a projection built before the forget never serves again. |
| Reading/posting creates no personal note | The no-ambient-inference non-goal: memory is created by declared acts only. |

The last row deserves emphasis because it is the whole class separation in one behavior: conversation is not memory.

seed: the memory domain
Seed reserves the `memory` domain for tool identifiers. The natural tool faces of a memory store on seed's registry, using seed's closed verb set:

| Tool id | Effect class | Maps to |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `memory.note.create` | write | Admission through `admitMemory`. |
| `memory.note.list` | read | Projection rebuilt at the current stamp. |
| `memory.note.read` | read | Single-record read, same stamp rule. |
| `memory.note.delete` | destructive | `forgetMemory`, with the epoch bump. |

`memory.note.delete` is deliberately the forget face, and it is deliberately classified destructive: a forget is an irreversible owner act, and destructive effects in the harness route the owner gate. A `forget` verb is not coined; the closed verb set stays closed, and `delete` with structural semantics is stronger than a new word.

capillary: the boundary line
Capillary retrieves context and carries its provenance; myosotis governs what may be kept and what must be forgotten. The line:

- A packet capillary returns is **retrieval**. It is what was asked for, with provenance; it is not thereby memory.
- The moment a system decides to **keep** something durable from what was retrieved, that act crosses into myosotis: a record, a kind, a scope, a consent check when personal, an admission epoch.
- A recall cache that exists so retrieval is fast is a **projection** of memory, and the forget contract's epoch governs it exactly as it governs any other projection.

Retrieval informs. Memory keeps. Neither impersonates the other.

Family
The family law and the full table live in the [capillary repository's family doc](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary/blob/main/docs/family.md). Short form: seed for the harness foundation, capillary for retrieval, myosotis for memory, aestivation for admission and review, bloom for the harness. Names are ordinary botanical words; provinces stay distinct.

# Proposals
This folder holds intake proposals for new family capabilities, cross-repository workflow changes, or scope revisions before they enter `docs/timeline/capabilities.json` or a repository capability spec.

Rules
1. **Naming**: Name every proposal `P-YYYYMMDD-<slug>.md` under `docs/proposals/` in the `docs` hub repository.
2. **One PR per proposal**: Open each proposal in its own pull request on `docs`, using [template.md](template.md).
3. **Initial status**: Every proposal opens with `Status: proposed`. Ratifying or declining a proposal or creating or amending a `CAP-NN` entry requires an owner answer under the [Owner questions](../timeline/agent-guide.md#owner-questions) process. Agents never self-ratify proposals.
4. **Public safety**: `docs` is a public repository. Keep hostnames, addresses, ports, credentials, internal names, and operational context out of every proposal file and PR body. Any private details belong directly in the final task message to the owner, never on the public hub.

# P-YYYYMMDD-slug: Proposal title
ID: `P-YYYYMMDD-<slug>`
Title: Proposal title
Status: `proposed`
Date: `YYYY-MM-DD`
Touches: `<CAP-NN or new capability; repository names>`

Idea
One concise paragraph describing the proposed change, why it matters, and what outcome it aims for.

Capability impact
List any existing capabilities (`CAP-NN`) affected or state why a new capability ID is warranted.

Touched repositories
Name the proposed lead repository and every touched repository within the family stack.

Risks and family rules
Describe stack boundary impacts, zero-dependency constraints, claim discipline implications, and reversibility.

Smallest first slice
Define the smallest independently testable first slice (`<repo>`, acceptance test, and ledger update).

Open owner questions
List the concrete decisions the owner needs to rule on before work begins.

Public safety check
Confirm that this proposal contains zero private infrastructure details, credentials, handles, or internal names (send private details directly to the owner in the final task message, never here).

Contracts and schemas for the runtime # Seed Seed is an open, local-first harness foundation for AI agents. It defines the contracts an agent runtime is built on: the run model, tool identity, and the provider adapter. Agent workspaces like [Bloom](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) can orchestrate model-backed workers, tools, and shared artifacts without depending on any single hosted service or third-party harness. **Status: `0.8.0`, specification and contract modules.** The contracts, grammar, and validators in this repository are implemented and covered by `npm test`. The runtime services on the roadmap are specified or planned, not shipped. Nothing in this repository opens a network listener, calls a hosted model, or touches your files today.

Why
Bloom proved the model-agnostic part: a notebook-shaped team workspace that treats any
chat-completions-compatible service as one provider binding of several. The layer below
the model is still rented: a third-party harness decides how tools are called, how runs
are recovered, and how work proves itself. Seed takes that layer back as a small, open,
inspectable foundation:

- **One run model.** Work is an *objective* with *attempts*, recorded intents, and a
  verification receipt, not a loose prompt history.
- **Neutral tool identity.** Tools are addressed by grammar, never by vendor, host, or
  product name, so adapters can be swapped without re-teaching agents.
- **Provider-agnostic by contract.** Any inference service that can complete text can sit
  behind the same `generate` contract Bloom already speaks.

What is here today (`implemented`)
| Module | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `src/tool-id.mjs` | Parse, format, and validate the neutral tool ID grammar; check registry entries, rollback postures, and cross-entry references |
| `src/run-model.mjs` | Objective/attempt records, run statuses, legal transitions, and intent-time tool admission |
| `src/resume.mjs` | Resume pending steps, report supplied failure classes, preview steps in a dry run, and manage in-process run leases |
| `src/admission.mjs` | Fail-closed caller admission over a registry the caller holds |
| `src/registry-documents.mjs` | Check agents and tools documents the caller already parsed: name a document not supplied, and report an agent that names an unknown tool |
| `src/provider.mjs` | Validate provider adapters and normalize generation results |
| `src/model-alias.mjs` | Resolve the alias a caller asks for to a backend model name from a table the caller holds, keeping the two names distinct and labeling deprecated aliases without swapping them |

`npm install && npm test` verifies all of it. There are no runtime dependencies.

Contracts (`specified`, `implemented` where modules cover them)
- [Run model](docs/contracts/run-model.md): objectives, attempts, intents, receipts
- [Tool identity](docs/contracts/tool-id.md): the neutral ID grammar and registry fields
- [Provider adapter](docs/contracts/provider.md): the `generate` contract, compatible with Bloom's team provider

How seed and Bloom fit (`specified`)
Bloom already isolates its model layer behind one provider interface. Seed lands in three
stages, each one usable by Bloom as it ships:

1. **Stage 1, library contracts.** Shared modules: tool IDs, run records, and provider
   validation (this release).
2. **Stage 2, inference endpoint.** A local service exposing an OpenAI-compatible
   chat-completions surface over any configured backend, which Bloom can consume today via
   its provider base URL.
3. **Stage 3, run engine and tool registry.** Durable objectives and attempts, an
   owner gate for effects that leave the run, and a tool registry adapters publish to.

Details and worked examples: [docs/bloom-interop.md](docs/bloom-interop.md).

Documentation
- [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): start here before editing. Stay in this repository's province.
- [Charter](docs/charter.md): mission, principles, non-goals
- [Architecture](docs/architecture.md): planes, authority, and what seed refuses to own
- [Lexicon](docs/lexicon.md): how public repositories stay in generalized terms
- [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md): staged, status-labeled

Design principles
1. Local-first. A clean checkout runs; nothing phones home.
2. One authority per fact. Runs own run state; memory owns memory; tools own effects.
3. Receipts over vibes. A run completes with a verification receipt, not a self-report.
4. Effects are gated. Side effects that leave a run pause for the owner.
5. No vendor names in tool identity. Grammar first; connectors carry the brand.

# Seed architecture decision records
Architecture decision records in `seed` follow the [hub ADR convention](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs/blob/main/docs/adr/README.md) and [ADR template](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs/blob/main/docs/adr/template.md) on `Vidoxlabs/docs`.

ADRs here are numbered sequentially from `0001` as `docs/adr/NNNN-<slug>.md`. Agents write proposals with status `Proposed`; only an owner decision moves a record to `Accepted`, and any runtime dependency proposal requires an ADR first. No ADRs exist in `seed` yet.

# Seed architecture
Status: `specified`. The modules named below exist (`implemented`) where marked; the
services are contract documents until their stage ships.

The four planes
1. **Surfaces** (`external`) — the human-facing workspaces. Bloom is the first: a team
   of agents in one group conversation over a shared desktop. Seed defines no UI contract;
   surfaces consume seed's run and provider contracts.
2. **Harness** (this repository) — the run engine, the tool registry, and the provider
   adapters. This is the part workspaces would otherwise rent from a third-party harness.
3. **Providers** (`plugged in`) — any service that can complete text: a local inference
   server, a hosted chat-completions endpoint, an OpenCode-compatible server. Providers
   are replaceable parts behind one `generate` contract.
4. **Authority stores** (`addressed, never duplicated`) — memory, context, and artifact
   stores that own their facts. Seed addresses them through contracts and keeps no second
   copy.

Inside the harness
- **Run engine** (`specified` per [run model](contracts/run-model.md)). Work is an
  *objective* (an intent plus acceptance criteria) carried out by *attempts*. An attempt
  records its intended effect before the effect runs, holds a lease while it works, and
  *completes only with a verification receipt at the current revision*. An intent is
  written before its effect, so an intent is not proof that the effect landed: a restarted
  attempt resumes only from the steps a receipt proves complete, and an intent with no
  receipt goes to the owner rather than to either a skip or a retry.
- **Tool registry** (`specified` per [tool identity](contracts/tool-id.md)). One place
  that maps neutral tool IDs to connector bindings, effect classes, and schemas. Tools
  are enumerated before a run starts; a run may only call tools admitted to it.
- **Provider adapters** (`implemented as contract validation` in `src/provider.mjs`;
  endpoint adaptation is Stage 2 in the roadmap). Providers take `{ system, prompt, model,
  signal, ... }` and return `{ text, complete, model, usage }` — Bloom's provider contract.
- **Owner gate** (`specified`). Runs move to `waiting_for_owner` when an intended effect
  leaves the run's scopes — writing outside them, spending, sending, creating credentials.
  The gate binds the owner's decision to the exact action digest being approved, and a
  change to the action voids the approval.

Roles, generalized
- The **owner** is the one human whose decisions open gated effects.
- A **coordinator** frames an objective, selects workers, and accepts results; it does not
  call tools.
- **Specialists** are model-backed workers, each with a jurisdiction and a scope of
  admitted tools; tools execute as scoped effects under the run's allowlist.
- A **verifier** is deterministic: it re-reads the admitted evidence, checks hashes, and
  reports. Verification never consumes a model call.
- **Connectors** bind the registry to external systems and default to read-only. Vendor
  identity lives in the connector, never in the tool ID.

The point of generalizing: an ephemeral team's shape (one coordinator, N specialists,
one deterministic verifier) can be stated, inspected, and budgeted without any product,
vendor, or infrastructure name in the statement.

What seed refuses to own
- **No second system of record.** Memory, context, and artifact storage stay with their
  authorities; the run engine holds run facts only.
- **No model server.** Inference is a provider behind the adapter.
- **No silent substitution.** Missing usage, a missing provider, or a failed tool is
  reported as such — never approximated, padded, or replaced.
- **No unclaimed capabilities.** Anything not implemented carries its label on its face
  (`AGENTS.md` claim discipline).

# Bloom interop
Status: stage 1 is `implemented` in this repository; stages 2 and 3 are `specified`.

Bloom (https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) is the first surface seed serves. Since Bloom
0.7.0, Bloom imports seed and runs every team provider behind seed's provider seam. Bloom
has one network provider mode: any service that speaks the chat-completions HTTP surface,
named with `--api-base`. Bloom names no default service. Seed lands in three stages, each
consumable by Bloom the day it ships.

Stage 1 — shared contract modules (`implemented`, `0.2.0`)
Bloom (and any workspace) can adopt seed's modules directly:

- `provider` validation, so an adapter conforms before it is wired in and every generation
  is checked before a caller reads it,
- `tool-id` grammar for neutral tool names in plans and receipts,
- `run-model` records for objective/attempt bookkeeping.

These are dependency-free ES modules. Using them needs no seed process.

### What Bloom has adopted

Bloom 0.7.0 adopted `provider` validation (Bloom commit `3d535e0`):

- Bloom depends on seed as a git dependency pinned to one seed commit. A seed change
  reaches Bloom only when Bloom moves that pin.
- `validateProvider` checks the team provider when Bloom starts. An adapter that does not
  fit the seam stops startup.
- `normalizeGeneration` checks every generation before Bloom's team loop reads it. A record
  outside the contract stops the turn instead of reaching a handoff.
- Seed's generation record has no money field. Bloom carries a reported cost beside the
  record, never inside `usage`, so `usage` holds only the five fields the contract names.
- Bloom's `test/generation-record.test.mjs` holds the adoption: every adapter Bloom ships
  passes seed's checks, and a nonconforming record is refused.

Bloom has not adopted `tool-id` or `run-model`. Those belong to stage 3.

Because Bloom imports seed, a breaking change to `validateProvider`, `normalizeGeneration`,
or the generation record breaks a caller. I

Stage 2 — local inference endpoint (`specified`)
A local service exposing the OpenAI-compatible chat-completions surface over any
configured backend. Bloom 0.7.0 already consumes such a service through its one provider
mode:

```sh
npm start -- --api-base <endpoint-url> --team-model <model-id>
```

The endpoint owns only completion; runs, tools, and memory stay with their owners. When
the endpoint ships, the exact invocation and its verified receipts land in this document
with `observed` labels — not before.

Worked example of the seam, in the shape Bloom adopted (runnable adapter shapes are in
[contracts/provider.md](contracts/provider.md)):

```js
// A workspace composes seed contracts around any backend:
import { validateProvider, normalizeGeneration } from '@vidoxlabs/seed';
const { ok, errors } = validateProvider(adapter);    // once, when the workspace starts
if (!ok) throw new Error(errors.join(' '));
const result = await adapter.generate({ system, prompt, model, signal });
const gen = normalizeGeneration(result);             // every call, before the caller reads it
if (!gen.ok) throw new Error(gen.errors.join(' ')); // never hand on a nonconforming record
```

Stage 3 — run engine and tool registry (`specified`)
Bloom's turn loop upgrades from "prompt in, text out" to objectives and attempts:

- a team's task becomes an **objective** with acceptance and admitted tools,
- each specialist call becomes an **attempt** with recorded intents and receipts,
- tool effects resolve through the **registry**, and gated effects wait for the owner.

Bloom's visible contract — the group conversation, roster, shared desktop, file lineage,
review holds — does not change shape; the run model makes each of its steps inspectable.

What seed does not ask of Bloom
- No hosted accounts. Bloom keeps its local-first, sign-in-free model.
- No required listener. Stage 1 is usable with no seed process running.
- No vendor re-education. Neutral tool IDs mean Bloom's docs never name the backend
  inside the tool call; the connector binding carries it (see
  [contracts/tool-id.md](contracts/tool-id.md)).

Changes
- Bloom 0.7.0 — Bloom imports seed and adopted stage 1 `provider` validation. Bloom's
  OpenCode connection modes are gone, so this document no longer lists a hosted service or
  an OpenCode-compatible server as Bloom modes. The stage 2 example no longer carries an
  address or port.

# CAP-03: Typed tool input and output
- ID: `CAP-03`
- Title: Typed tool input and output
- Lead: `seed`
- Touches: `drosera`, `bloom`
- Horizon: `now`
- Milestone: `M2`
- CLI phase: `P2`
- Status: `in-progress`
- Claim: `specified`
- Depends on: none

Why
`src/tool-id.mjs` checks that a registry entry carries an `inputSchema` object, and `src/run-model.mjs` admits tool IDs per objective, yet neither `seed` nor its consumers enforce a deterministic schema subset over tool inputs or outputs today. Without shared schema validation, malformed model arguments reach tool executors, outputs lack structural guarantees, and workspaces either import heavy external validators or duplicate ad-hoc checks.

What it does
`seed` defines and ships a small, zero-dependency, hand-written schema subset and validator for tool inputs and optional tool outputs:

1. **Closed schema subset**:
   - `type`: `"object"`, `"array"`, `"string"`, `"number"`, `"integer"`, `"boolean"`, or `"null"`.
   - Object keywords: `properties` (map of field name to nested schema), `required` (array of non-empty property names), and `additionalProperties` (`false` only when present, refusing unlisted properties).
   - Array keywords: `items` (single schema applied to every element) and `maxItems` (non-negative safe integer).
   - Scalar and enumeration keywords: `enum` (non-empty array of JSON primitive literals), `minLength` and `maxLength` (non-negative safe integers for strings), `minimum` and `maximum` (finite numbers for numbers and integers).
   - Unknown keywords anywhere in a schema object are refused rather than silently ignored.
2. **Schema checker and value validator**:
   - `checkSchema(schema)` validates that `schema` uses only the closed subset and returns a frozen `{ ok, errors }` result where each error carries a JSON-pointer path (such as `/properties/limit/minimum`) and reason.
   - `validateValue(schema, value)` first validates `schema` (failing closed if malformed) and then checks `value`, returning a frozen `{ ok, errors }` result with JSON-pointer paths (such as `/limit` or `/items/0`).
   - Error messages never echo raw string values that could leak credentials or private content; they n

Contract touchpoints
- `seed`: `docs/contracts/tool-id.md` (adds closed schema subset contract, `checkSchema` / `validateValue` behavior, and optional `outputSchema` on registry entries as an additive minor update); `docs/contracts/run-model.md` (aligns pre-dispatch validation refusal with `schema-invalid`).
- `drosera`: `docs/contracts/tools.md` (optional `inputSchema` and `outputSchema` on `toolFace`, parity against `seed` subset).
- `bloom`: `docs/architecture.md` (pre-dispatch argument validation, single repair turn then `malformed`, output validation sharing repair budget).

Tool IDs and events
### Tool IDs

None defined by this capability.

| Tool ID | Effect | Third-party egress | Owner gate | Summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

### Events

None defined by this capability. Validation and repair events in the team trace belong to `CAP-10`.

| Event | Emitter | Payload summary |
| --- | --- | --- |

Acceptance tests
1. `unknown-schema-keyword-refused`: `checkSchema` rejects any schema containing an unsupported keyword (such as `$ref`, `oneOf`, or `pattern`) and returns frozen `{ ok: false, errors }` with the JSON-pointer path to the offending keyword.
2. `value-validation-json-pointer-no-secret-echo`: `validateValue` checks `type`, `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties: false`, `items`, `enum`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `minimum`, `maximum`, and `maxItems`, reports JSON-pointer error paths, and never echoes sensitive or arbitrary raw string values in error messages.
3. `optional-output-schema-additive`: Existing `0.8.0` registry entries without `outputSchema` remain valid in `isWellFormedRegistryEntry` and `checkRegistry`, while entries supplying a malformed `outputSchema` are rejected.
4. `drosera-face-schema-parity`: `drosera` tool faces accept optional `inputSchema` and `outputSchema`, and a parity check confirms `drosera` accepts and rejects the exact same schema shapes and values as `seed`.
5. `bloom-single-repair-turn-then-malformed`: In `bloom`, invalid tool arguments never invoke the tool executor, trigger at most one repair turn carrying JSON-pointer error paths, and stop as `malformed` if the second attempt still fails `inputSchema`.
6. `output-validation-shares-repair-budget`: In `bloom`, a tool result failing `outputSchema` consumes from the single-turn repair budget and stops cleanly rather than looping or passing unvalidated output into model cont

Slices
- `CAP-03.1` (`seed`, milestone `M2`, status `landed`): Implement the closed schema subset (`checkSchema`, `validateValue`) in `seed` and add optional `outputSchema` to registry entries (`docs/contracts/tool-id.md`, additive minor bump).
- `CAP-03.2` (`drosera`, milestone `M2`, status `proposed`): Add optional `inputSchema` and `outputSchema` validation on tool faces with parity verification against `seed`.
- `CAP-03.3` (`bloom`, milestone `M2`, status `proposed`): Wire pre-dispatch `inputSchema` checking, one repair turn then `malformed`, and `outputSchema` validation sharing the repair budget.

Non-goals
- Implementing full JSON Schema (`$ref`, `allOf`, `oneOf`, `anyOf`, `not`, `pattern`, `format`, remote schema resolution).
- Coercing argument types or silently stripping unknown keys when `additionalProperties: false` is set.
- Adding any runtime dependency or external schema validation package.

Family rules and conflicts
- **Zero runtime dependencies**: Schema checking and validation are pure hand-written JavaScript in `seed` with zero dependencies.
- **Additive compatibility**: `outputSchema` is strictly optional so existing `seed` `0.8.0` callers remain unbroken; adding `outputSchema` and new exports is a minor version bump.
- **No secret echo**: Validation errors identify JSON-pointer paths and expected types or bounds, never repeating raw string payloads that might hold credentials.

Open owner decisions
- `D4` Decided 2026-11-24 in seed#3: Where should the schema subset and validator live? Owner's answer, verbatim: "I need you to approve on recommendations and continue".
  `seed` owns the subset and validator. `drosera` mirrors the subset and verifies parity.

Evidence
- `CAP-03.1` is exercised by six cases in `test/schema.test.mjs` covering nested schema refusal, redacted error paths, bounds, closed objects, and registry compatibility.

Changes
- `2026-11-24`: Record `D4` and ship the closed schema subset with optional registry output schemas (CAP-03, seed#3).
- `2026-11-23`: Added `M2` slice milestones and aligned `D4` wording with the canonical decision record.
- `2026-11-23`: Initial capability specification created (`CAP-01.2` scaffold).

# CAP-06: Tool-call approval decisions
- ID: `CAP-06`
- Title: Tool-call approval decisions
- Lead: `seed`
- Touches: `bloom`, `drosera`
- Horizon: `next`
- Milestone: `M3` (`CAP-06.1` ships at `M3`; `CAP-06.2` to `CAP-06.4` ship at `M4`)
- CLI phase: `P4`
- Status: `proposed`
- Claim: `planned`
- Depends on: `CAP-03`, `CAP-04`

Why
`docs/contracts/run-model.md` defines the `waiting_for_owner` status and rule 5 ("the gate binds to the digest"), and `docs/contracts/tool-id.md` defines `effect` classes and `ownerGate` / `thirdPartyEgress` flags. However, `seed` does not yet define the owner-gate decision record, which decision kinds are valid for each effect class, how owner edits or text responses return to a run, or how deferred pauses fail closed on resume.

What it does
`CAP-06` specifies the digest-bound owner-gate decision contract in `seed`, metadata alignment in `drosera`, and the interactive approval flow and trace events in `bloom`:

1. **Owner-gate decision record (`CAP-06.1` at `M3`)**:
   ```
   { callId, toolId, argsDigest, decision, editedArgsDigest?, reason?, decidedAt }
   ```
   - `callId`: non-empty identifier matching the pending deferred call on the active attempt.
   - `toolId`: well-formed neutral tool ID matching the pending intent.
   - `argsDigest`: 64-hex SHA-256 digest of the canonical pending arguments. Any change to `toolId` or `argsDigest` voids the decision (`run-model.md` rule 5).
   - `decision`: one of `"approve"`, `"edit"`, `"reject"`, or `"respond"`.
   - `editedArgsDigest`: required 64-hex SHA-256 digest when `decision === "edit"`, refused on all other decision kinds.
   - `reason`: optional non-empty string explaining a rejection or holding the owner's reply text for `"respond"`.
   - `decidedAt`: ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string recording when the owner decided.
   - **Plan-digest binding (folded from `CAP-07.3` into `CAP-06.1`)**: the owner-gate decision contract also supports plan approval records bound to a canonical 64-hex SHA-256 `planDigest` (`CAP-07` depends on `CAP-06.1`), failing closed whenever a plan edit alters `planDigest`.
2. **Effect and third-party egress allowances (`CAP-06.1` at `M3`)**:
   - `read` tools with `thirdPartyEgress: false` run freely inside the attempt's admitted `a

Contract touchpoints
- `seed`: `docs/contracts/run-model.md` (owner-gate decision record shape including call and plan-digest binding for `CAP-07`, deferred call kinds `approval`/`question`/`external`, fail-closed resume rule); `docs/contracts/tool-id.md` (effect and `thirdPartyEgress` decision allowances, mandatory `ownerGate` on third-party egress).
- `drosera`: `docs/contracts/tools.md` (face metadata alignment for `ownerGate`, `effect`, and `thirdPartyEgress`).
- `bloom`: `docs/architecture.md` (owner prompt/UI decision flow, `edit` re-validation and model notice, `respond` owner-input labeling, permission events).

Tool IDs and events
### Tool IDs

None defined by this capability.

| Tool ID | Effect | Third-party egress | Owner gate | Summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

### Events

| Event | Emitter | Payload summary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `permission.requested` | `bloom` | Emitted when a deferred `approval`, `question`, or `external` call pauses the run at `waiting_for_owner`, carrying `callId`, `toolId`, `argsDigest`, `effect`, and `thirdPartyEgress`. |
| `permission.resolved` | `bloom` | Emitted when an owner decision (`approve`, `edit`, `reject`, or `respond`) resolves a pending `callId`, recording `decision`, digest match, and outcome before resume. |

Acceptance tests
1. `digest-mismatch-voids-approval`: Changing `toolId`, `argsDigest`, or bound `planDigest` after an `approve` decision is recorded causes resume from `waiting_for_owner` or plan execution to fail closed without running the tool or plan.
2. `destructive-and-credential-disallow-respond`: Submitting `decision: "respond"` for a `destructive` or `credential` tool is refused by validation, while `write` tools permit all four decision kinds.
3. `third-party-egress-always-gates`: A `read` tool with `thirdPartyEgress: true` pauses at `waiting_for_owner` and requires an owner decision before execution.
4. `edit-revalidates-and-informs-model`: An `edit` decision validates replacement arguments against `inputSchema`, verifies `editedArgsDigest`, records the updated intent, and informs the model that replacement arguments ran.
5. `respond-marks-owner-input`: A `respond` decision skips tool execution and injects the owner's response marked explicitly as owner input rather than tool output.
6. `deferred-calls-fail-closed-on-resume`: Runs paused on `approval`, `question`, or `external` deferred calls refuse transition back to `running` if any required decision record is missing, malformed, or unbound.
7. `bloom-emits-permission-events`: `bloom` emits `permission.requested` on pause and `permission.resolved` upon owner resolution with matching `callId` and correlation IDs.

Slices
- `CAP-06.1` (`seed`, milestone `M3`, status `proposed`): Define owner-gate decision record validation, plan-digest binding (folded from `CAP-07.3`, so `CAP-07` depends on `CAP-06.1`), call-digest binding, and effect/egress decision allowances in `seed`.
- `CAP-06.2` (`seed`, milestone `M4`, status `proposed`): Define deferred call states (`approval`, `question`, `external`) and fail-closed `waiting_for_owner` resume checks in `seed`.
- `CAP-06.3` (`drosera`, milestone `M4`, status `proposed`): Align `drosera` face metadata checks with `ownerGate`, `effect`, and `thirdPartyEgress` rules.
- `CAP-06.4` (`bloom`, milestone `M4`, status `proposed`): Implement approval CLI/UI flow, `edit` re-validation and model disclosure, `respond` owner-input labeling, and `permission.requested` / `permission.resolved` events.

Non-goals
- Persisting approval policies across runs ("always allow" wildcard grants) without an explicit future capability and owner decision.
- Letting any model output, specialist verdict, or memory recall record satisfy an owner gate.

Family rules and conflicts
- **Owner is the only gate authority**: Neither `aestivation` review verdicts nor `myosotis` memory entries can ratify or bypass an owner gate (`CAP-07` cross-check).
- **Receipts over self-report**: Approval applies only to the exact `argsDigest` or `planDigest` presented; edited arguments or edited plans re-enter schema validation and intent or gate recording before execution.

Open owner decisions
- **D14 (`CAP-06.1` at `M3` with `CAP-07.3` folded in, pending owner ruling)**: Under review convention `D14`, `CAP-06.1` ships at `M3` (covering plan-digest binding folded from `CAP-07.3`, so `CAP-07` depends on `CAP-06.1`), while `CAP-06.2` through `CAP-06.4` ship at `M4` (`P4`). Kept unless overridden by the owner.
- **D10 (secret-file deny list override, pending owner ruling)**: Under `CAP-05`, the secret-file deny list stays always on and symlinks are not followed by default; an explicit include of a denied path requires a per-call `CAP-06.1` owner approval record.
- **Terminal approval prompt UX for `CAP-06.4` (pending owner decision, not yet numbered)**: pending owner rulings for `bloom` CLI `P4` approval prompts and terminal gate UX details.

Evidence
None yet. Capability is `proposed` with claim `planned`.

Changes
- `2026-11-23`: Separated `CAP-06.4` terminal approval prompt UX into an unnumbered open owner question distinct from `D12` and removed the review-prompt label from `D14` (`CAP-01.2`).
- `2026-11-23`: Moved `CAP-06.1` to `M3` with `CAP-07.3` plan-digest binding folded in (`CAP-07` depends on `CAP-06.1`), assigned `M4` to `CAP-06.2`..`CAP-06.4`, and aligned open owner decisions with `D10` and `D14`.
- `2026-11-23`: Initial capability specification created (`CAP-01.2` scaffold).

# CAP-12: Step graph, checkpoints, resume, interrupts
- ID: `CAP-12`
- Title: Step graph, checkpoints, resume, interrupts
- Lead: `seed`
- Touches: `bloom`
- Horizon: `later`
- Milestone: `M7`
- CLI phase: none
- Status: `proposed`
- Claim: `planned`
- Depends on: `CAP-06`, `CAP-10`

Why
Stage 1 `src/resume.mjs` handles linear in-process step lists (`resumeSteps`) with skipped completed IDs and abort codes, but multi-step workflows also need shared state merging across branches, conditional routing checked before execution, post-step checkpoints with parent links, fork from prior checkpoints, configurable durability modes, per-step retry policies by failure class, and clean interrupt/resume semantics that obey intent-first rule 3.

What it does
`CAP-12` specifies a declarative step graph engine contract in `seed` and its runtime execution in `bloom`:

1. **Step graph over shared state with per-key merge rules**:
   - A graph declares named step nodes operating on a shared state object.
   - Every key in the shared state schema declares a merge rule: `replace` (single writer or deterministic last-in-plan-order overwrite), `append` (ordered list concatenation in deterministic branch order), or a `named reducer` (identifier referencing a caller-supplied pure reducer function in a closed reducer table).
   - Conflicting concurrent writes to a `replace` key within the same parallel superstep fail validation unless ordered explicitly.
2. **Declarative conditional routes checked pre-run**:
   - Edges between steps are declarative route definitions (`from`, optional `condition` name matching a caller-supplied pure predicate table, `to` step ID or terminal state).
   - Before any step executes, the graph validates that every referenced step ID, reducer name, and route condition name exists, and that step bounds or loop limits are explicitly declared (failing closed pre-run if invalid).
3. **Post-step checkpoints and parallel pending writes**:
   - After each step (or parallel superstep), the engine produces a checkpoint record containing `{ checkpointId, runId, attempt, stepId, parentCheckpointId, stateDigest, state, completedWrites, createdAt }`.
   - `parentCheckpointId` links back to the prior checkpoint in a

Contract touchpoints
- `seed`: `docs/contracts/run-model.md` (extends step execution from linear `resumeSteps` to declarative step graphs, checkpoints, interrupts, forks, durability modes, and failure-class retry rules while preserving rules 1-6).
- `bloom`: `docs/architecture.md` (executes step graphs with `CAP-13` persistence, checkpoint tool handlers, and interrupt/resume wiring).

Tool IDs and events
### Tool IDs

| Tool ID | Effect | Third-party egress | Owner gate | Summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `run.checkpoint.read` | `read` | `false` | `false` | Read a recorded step checkpoint by ID or fetch the latest checkpoint for the active run. |
| `run.checkpoint.create` | `write` | `false` | `false` | Record an explicit post-step checkpoint carrying `parentCheckpointId`, `stateDigest`, and `completedWrites`. |
| `run.step.cancel` | `write` | `false` | `true` | Cancel a pending or paused step in the active run and transition cleanly toward `stopping`. |

### Events

None defined in `seed`. Step graph lifecycle and checkpoint events emitted by `bloom` use the `CAP-10` event stream.

| Event | Emitter | Payload summary |
| --- | --- | --- |

Acceptance tests
1. `graph-pre-run-validation-fails-closed`: Missing step targets, unknown reducer names, or unregistered conditional route names throw before any step executes.
2. `state-merge-replace-append-reducer`: Parallel and sequential step writes merge deterministically under `replace`, `append`, and `named reducer` rules, yielding identical `stateDigest` values on replay.
3. `checkpoint-parent-chain-and-parallel-writes`: Every post-step checkpoint links `parentCheckpointId`, records `stateDigest`, and preserves `completedWrites` from parallel peers that succeeded before an interrupt or partial failure.
4. `interrupt-resume-respects-rule-3`: Resuming from an interrupt re-runs the interrupted step from its start, skips prior checkpointed steps, and refuses to silently repeat an unresolved non-idempotent recorded intent.
5. `fork-preserves-prior-checkpoint-lineage`: Forking from an earlier checkpoint starts a new attempt/branch without mutating any state or links in the original lineage.
6. `retry-policy-by-failure-class`: Steps retry transient `external-unavailable` or `external-exec-failed` outcomes up to their cap, and immediately stop without retrying `policy-denied`, `gate-denied`, or `schema-invalid`.
7. `durability-mode-honored`: `per-step` writes checkpoints before advancing each step, `on-interrupt` checkpoints on pause/finish, and `none` stays strictly in memory.

Slices
- `CAP-12.1` (`seed`, milestone `M7`, status `proposed`): Step graph schema, pre-run route/reducer validation, per-key state merge (`replace`, `append`, named reducer), and failure-class retry policies (`seed`).
- `CAP-12.2` (`seed`, milestone `M7`, status `proposed`): Post-step checkpoint records with `parentCheckpointId` and `stateDigest`, parallel `completedWrites`, fork, per-run durability modes, and interrupt pause/resume (`seed`).
- `CAP-12.3` (`bloom`, milestone `M7`, status `proposed`): Runtime graph executor, `run.checkpoint.read` / `run.checkpoint.create` / `run.step.cancel` handlers, and interrupt/fork CLI/UI wiring (`bloom`).

Non-goals
- Writing directly to disk or SQLite from `seed` (persistence belongs to `CAP-13` and `bloom`).
- Executing arbitrary inline code strings in route conditions or reducer declarations (conditions and reducers are named lookups against caller-supplied pure JS maps).

Family rules and conflicts
- **Intent-first rule 3**: Checkpoints never authorize blind re-execution of non-idempotent recorded intents; unclear intents pause for the owner (`CAP-06`).
- **One authority per fact**: Checkpoints store run graph state and digests only, never duplicating `myosotis` memory records or `capillary` context packets.

Open owner decisions
- **Checkpoint retention and built-in reducer set**: Whether `seed` ships a small default table of named reducers alongside caller-supplied reducers, and whether checkpoint pruning/compaction policy lives in `CAP-13` store configuration or per-run options (pending owner guidance when `M7` opens).

Evidence
The in-process resume rules are `implemented` and exercised by `test/resume.test.mjs`,
and by `test/harness-run.test.mjs` for the receipt-over-intent rule across a restart.
Step graphs, checkpoints, fork, and interrupts remain `specified` (`CAP-12.2`), so the
capability claim stays `planned`.

Changes
- `2026-11-24`: Evidence section records the in-process resume coverage, including the receipt-over-intent rule across a restart (`test/harness-run.test.mjs`).
- `2026-11-23`: Added `M7` slice milestones across `CAP-12.1`..`CAP-12.3`.
- `2026-11-23`: Initial capability specification created (`CAP-01.2` scaffold).
