# Capability specification template
Every lead capability spec in `<lead-repo>/docs/capabilities/CAP-NN-<slug>.md` uses the exact 12 sections below in order. Keep all prose plain, with no YAML, no em-dashes, and no private details.

Template
# CAP-NN: Capability title

- ID: `CAP-NN`
- Title: Capability title
- Lead: `<lead-repo>`
- Touches: `<comma-separated peer repos, or none>`
- Horizon: `now` | `next` | `later`
- Milestone: `M0`..`M9`
- CLI phase: `P1`..`P6` | `none`
- Status: `proposed` | `accepted` | `in-progress` | `landed` | `deferred`
- Claim: `planned` | `specified` | `implemented` | `observed`
- Depends on: `CAP-XX`, `CAP-XX.k`, ... | `none`

Why
Explain the problem being solved and why the capability belongs in the family stack at this boundary.

What it does
Specify deterministic behavior, inputs, outputs, invariants, and fail-closed error handling.

Contract touchpoints
List existing contracts in the lead and touched repositories (or state `none` if no runtime contract exists yet).

Tool IDs and events
### Tool IDs

| Tool ID | Effect | Owner gate | Third-party egress | Summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | n/a | n/a | n/a | Replace with rows for each new tool ID (verified against `seed` grammar and `drosera` face rules). |

### Events

| Event | Emitted by | Payload summary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| none | n/a | Replace with rows for each typed event emitted by this capability. |

Acceptance tests
List named deterministic test cases that must pass before any slice or capability claims `implemented`.

Slices
Ordered list of slices (`CAP-NN.1`, `CAP-NN.2`, ...), naming the owning repository, milestone (`M0`..`M9`), and deliverable per slice.

Non-goals
Explicit boundaries stating what this capability does not build or claim.

Family rules and conflicts
Note how this capability honors stack boundaries, claim discipline, zero-dependency rules, and any cross-repo tensions.

Open owner decisions
List open questions and follow the [Owner questions](agent-guide.md#owner-questions) process. Once the owner answers, replace the open item with the line below and add a dated entry under Changes. Add the decision index anchor on the next touch after indexing.

`Decided YYYY-MM-DD in <repo>#<n>: <one-line question>. Owner's answer, verbatim: "<answer>".`

Evidence
Links to test files, probes, and dated observation records once slices land (starts as `none yet` while `planned`).

Changes
Dated changelog entries when the spec or its slices change (`2026-11-23: Initial proposed specification (CAP-01).`).

Multi-point tests for the family # trellis Multi-point testing for the agent family: shape, behavior, consistency, operational. Trellis is the testing member of the bloom agent family. Every member repository keeps its own tests; trellis checks the family from the outside, from four points each: **shape** (the public surface is what it claims), **behavior** (the load-bearing invariants hold under direct calls), **consistency** (the peers agree where they claim to, one grammar, shared conventions), and **operational** (each test suite runs green when actually run). Verdicts are pass, fail, or unknown. A fail always outranks an unknown, an absent checkout is declared unknown, and health claims are dated runs kept as evidence, not standing truths.

The name
A trellis is the lattice a garden grows against. Climbing plants grip a lattice at many points, not one, and the lattice holds because every point it promises to hold is checked. The family is a garden of contract modules, and its health is a multi-point question, never a single green badge.

Status
Version 0.8.0. The probe, grid, and verdict engine is `implemented` as a tested reference library. Family health statements live in `docs/evidence/` as dated observed runs. The engine covers the family's module repositories. The harness and design canon keep their own checks.

Install
```bash
npm install @vidoxlabs/trellis
```

Requires Node >= 22.13. Zero runtime dependencies.

Modules
| Module | What it holds | Label |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `point.mjs` | The four test points and the probe record: deterministic checks, fail closed, dedicated to one point. | `implemented` |
| `score.mjs` | Verdict math: pass, fail, unknown; fail outranks unknown, unknown outranks pass, and nothing is ever silently passed. | `implemented` |
| `grid.mjs` | The multi-point grid: run probes against injected subjects and roll the results up per subject and per point. | `implemented` |
| `probes.mjs` | The default probe lists for each family member and the cross-family consistency probes. A claim a member made after its first release is probed from the version that made it; an older checkout reads unknown. | `implemented` |

The bundle runner, `scripts/family.mjs` (`npm run family`), wires the grid to the canonical family workspace: it loads each peer's modules, runs the default probes, runs each peer's own test suite for the operational point, and prints the dated report the evidence docs record.

The family
The family follows one design law: ordinary botanical words for public products ([the law](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary/blob/main/docs/family.md)).

| Name | Province |
| :--- | :--- |
| [`seed`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed) | Harness foundation: runs, tools, providers |
| [`capillary`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary) | Context retrieval and relations, provenance-first |
| [`myosotis`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/myosotis) | Memory with consent and structural forget |
| [`aestivation`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/aestivation) | Plans, verdicts, and the gate before assembly |
| [`drosera`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/drosera) | Tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks |
| `trellis` (this repo) | Multi-point testing with dated evidence |
| [`bloom`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) | The team workspace harness |
| [`docs`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs) | Family documentation, synced from every public repository |

The line grows against the trellis: the products are the plants; this is the lattice they are checked against.

Documentation
- `AGENTS.md`: start here before editing. Stay in this repository's province.
- `docs/charter.md`: mission, principles, non-goals.
- `docs/architecture.md`: probes, grid, verdicts; engine and bundle runner.
- `docs/contracts/`: the probe and grid contracts.
- `docs/interop.md`: what each peer is probed on, and the boundaries.
- `docs/evidence/`: dated observed family runs, with their receipts.

Development
```bash
npm test       # engine and probe mechanics, no siblings required
npm run family # the bundle runner over the canonical workspace layout
```

Tests use the Node built-in runner. Adding a probe means adding the test that holds it.

License
MIT

The Vidoxlabs name and mark are trademarks of Vidoxlabs LLC. They are not covered by this repository's MIT license.

# Architecture Decision Records
Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for `trellis` live in this directory, numbered sequentially from `0001` (`NNNN-<slug>.md`).

- Format, lifecycle (`Proposed`, `Accepted`, `Superseded by NNNN`, `Deferred`), and review rules follow the hub ADR convention in [Vidoxlabs/docs](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs/blob/main/docs/adr/README.md).
- Agents write `Proposed` ADRs; only an explicit owner decision moves an ADR to `Accepted`.
- Any runtime dependency proposal requires an ADR before adding a package.
- Record every added or updated ADR in `docs/capabilities/index.json` in the same pull request.

# Trellis architecture
Probes ask, the grid runs, verdicts answer.

```
                    injected subjects (never imported by the core)
                              { seed: {namespace, pkg} | null, ... }
                                            │
   probe lists ──────► the multi-point grid ──────► results
   { id, point,      run every probe against             │
     applies,         its subject; absent               ▼
     summary, check }  subject = unknown           verdict math
                                            fail > unknown > pass
                                                        │
                                                        ▼
                                    per-subject, per-point report
                                    (bundle runner prints it, dated)
```

The four points
| Point | The question it asks | How it asks |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `shape` | Is the public surface what the repo claims? | Probes check exports, package discipline: `VERSION` present, the documented entry symbols defined, module type, engines floor, zero runtime dependencies. |
| `behavior` | Do the load-bearing invariants hold under direct calls? | Probes call the subject's functions with known inputs and assert the invariants the member's contract promises: epochs bump, gates hold, hooks fail closed, omissions are declared. |
| `consistency` | Do the peers agree where they claim to? | Cross probes receive the whole subject map: the tool grammar mirrors accept and reject identically, shared conventions hold, versions are declared everywhere. |
| `operational` | Does each test suite actually run green? | The bundle runner spawns each present peer's `npm test` and records the exit code as the point result. |

No point substitutes for another. The grid keeps them separate all the way to the report, so a failure names its point.

The subject map
A subject is `{ namespace, pkg }` — a loaded module namespace and the parsed `package.json` — or `null` for an absent checkout. Absence is a first-class state, not an error: the grid records `unknown` with the reason "checkout absent," and the verdict math carries it honestly. The core learns peers only through this map; it has no path to a peer's files.

The grid and the verdicts
`familyGrid({ subjects, probes })` (or `familyGridAsync`, which awaits asynchronous checks and is what the bundle runner uses) runs every probe whose subject is present, records one result per probe — pass, fail, or unknown, with a detail message — and rolls up a per-subject, per-point summary plus an overall verdict.

The verdict math is a strictness order, not an average:

- any fail makes the verdict `fail`, no matter how many passes;
- with no fails, any unknown makes the verdict `unknown`;
- only all-pass is `pass`.

There is no partial credit and no weighting. The order exists so that the two dishonest summaries — averaging away a failure, and stamping "operational" over unknowns — are both structurally impossible.

The engine and the bundle runner
Two layers, deliberate:

- **The engine** (`src/`) is pure: probe records, fail-closed execution, the grid, the verdict math. It tests green with only this repository present, using fixtures as subjects.
- **The bundle runner** (`scripts/family.mjs`, `npm run family`) resolves the canonical workspace layout — each peer checkout beside the others — loads the present peers as subjects, runs the default probe lists, spawns each peer's `npm test` for the operational point, prints the dated report, and exits nonzero on any fail. Absent peers are reported as unknown; the runner never errors out on absence.

Evidence documents (`docs/evidence/`) record the dated runs of the bundle runner: which members, which points, what verdict, and on what date — with receipts, and with no detail about the machines the runs happened on.

- Folder purpose: holds `trellis` capability ledgers (`index.json`) for touched capabilities (`trellis` leads no capabilities and probes module repositories only, never `bloom` or `docs`).
- Hub timeline: cross-repo roadmap, capability index, and timeline rules live at [Vidoxlabs/docs timeline](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs/blob/main/docs/timeline/README.md).
- Same-PR ledger rule: any PR changing capability status, claim, slices, contracts, tests, PRs, commits, or ADRs updates `index.json`, the owning spec, `docs/CHANGELOG.md`, and affected contract `Changes` sections together.

# Changelog
Earlier contract and release history for `trellis` lives in the `Changes` sections of `docs/contracts/` (`grid.md`, `probes.md`), and dated observed family runs live in `docs/evidence/`.

Unreleased
### Added

- Capability ledger scaffold (`docs/capabilities/index.json`), capability guide, ADR index (`docs/adr/README.md`), and changelog convention (CAP-01, trellis#1).
# Trellis charter

Mission
Keep the family honest from the outside. Trellis holds the contracts for multi-point testing of the public repositories: probes, run against each member's loaded modules, from four points — shape, behavior, consistency, operational — with verdicts that pass, fail, or stay unknown, and with health claims that are always dated runs rather than standing truths.

The name is the doctrine. A trellis is the lattice a garden grows against, and a climbing plant grips it at many points, never one. A family of contract modules is the same shape of thing: its health is not one green badge at the center, it is every load-bearing point holding at once — the exported surface matching the claim, the invariant surviving direct calls, the peers still agreeing where they promised to, the suites actually running. Trellis exists to make that multi-point question answerable by code instead of vibes.

Principles
1. **Multi-point by construction.** Four points per member: shape, behavior, consistency, operational. Each point asks a different question, and none substitutes for another — a module can ship a beautiful surface while its invariants rot, and trellis names which point failed.
2. **Fail closed, in the tester too.** A probe that throws is a failed probe, recorded with its error. Converting an error into a pass, or skipping a probe because it errored, is the exact failure mode this fabric exists to catch in others; it is prohibited here first.
3. **Unknown stays unknown.** An absent peer checkout is a declared unknown with its reason. It is never silently skipped, never counted as a pass, and it never blocks a fail from being reported. A fail outranks an unknown; an unknown outranks a pass.
4. **The core never imports a peer.** Subjects are injected. The published library tests green with only trellis present, and cross-repo truth enters only through the bundle runner over the canonical workspace layout. This keeps the tester honest about what it can know: in isolation, mechanics; in the workspace, the family.
5. **Probes are deterministic code.** A probe checks; it does not judge. Judgment belongs to reviewers and to the admission loop; a probe that wants a model's opinion is mislabeled and has no place in a probe set.
6. **Health is a dated observation.** "The family is operational" is a sentence about a run that happened, recorded in the evidence docs with its dat

Non-goals
- **Not a CI service.** No hosting, no standing dashboards, no network listeners. The bundle runner prints its report to whoever runs it, and the evidence docs hold the dated runs.
- **Not a replacement for peer tests.** Every member keeps its own suite; trellis probes cross-cutting health and invariants from outside. A member whose trellis probes pass and whose own tests fail is failing — the operational point exists to catch exactly that, and the bundle runner runs the member's suite, not a trellis copy of it.
- **Not a load, performance, or security harness.** Behavioral probes check invariants under direct calls, not throughput or audit posture. Those are real needs with their own provinces, named here so they are not invented later by accident.
- **Not a judge of content.** Probes verify that what is shipped matches what is claimed and that invariants hold. Whether a contract is wise is a review question, and the loop that holds it has its own home.

# Contract: the grid
Label: `specified` (rules), `implemented` in `src/grid.mjs` and `src/score.mjs`.

Shape
```
familyGrid({ subjects, probes }) → { results, bySubject, verdict }
familyGridAsync({ subjects, probes }) → Promise of the same grid, each probe awaited in order
subjects   { name: { namespace, pkg } | null, ... } — null means absent
probes     a list of probe records (see probes.md)
results    one execution result per probe, in probe-list order
bySubject  { name: { points: { point: { pass, fail, unknown } }, verdict } }
           plus the '*' rollup for cross probes under the subject '*'
verdict    'pass' | 'fail' | 'unknown' — the overall family verdict
```

Grid rules
1. **Subjects are injected.** The grid receives the subject map; it never loads, imports, or infers a peer. Where a subject map entry is `null`, the grid records the declared unknown rather than skipping the probes: absence is data, not an absence of data.
2. **Probes run in order, once each.** Deterministic input, deterministic grid output. A probe list with a duplicate id is rejected, not merged.
3. **Results are frozen.** The report is built from frozen result records; rolling up never re-runs or re-weighs a check.

Verdict math
The verdict is a strictness order, computed from the results:

```
fail    if any probe failed        — regardless of passes or unknowns
unknown if no probe failed, and any result is unknown
pass    only if every probe passed
```

Two dishonest summaries are structurally impossible under this order:

- **No averaging.** Ten passes cannot outvote one fail. The grid has no weights.
- **No unknown laundering.** "Operational" cannot be stamped over unknowns; an unknown is carried to the top verdict unless a fail outranks it.

Per-subject and per-point rollup
`bySubject` counts each point's pass, fail, and unknown for one subject, and gives that subject its own verdict under the same math. A cross probe (`applies: '*'`) belongs to the family, not to any one member: it rolls into the `'*'` bucket and into the overall verdict. The report therefore answers both questions honestly: "is the family holding," and "which member, at which point, is not."

Operational points and the bundle runner
The operational point's data enters through results the bundle runner records — in the shipped runner, the exit code of each present peer's `npm test`, spawned from the peer's checkout in the canonical layout. The grid accepts those results like any other; the runner prints the dated report and exits nonzero on any fail, so a warm-feeling human or a tool chain over the runner's output cannot mistake a fail for success. An absent checkout keeps its operational result `unknown`, with its reason, exactly as elsewhere.

What the grid never does
- Never re-derives a probe's result from another probe's.
- Never drops a result to make a verdict look better.
- Never claims a subject absent from the subject map.
- Never resolves an unknown without a new run.

# Contract: probes
Label: `specified` (rules), `implemented` (records and execution in `src/point.mjs`).

Shape
```
probe { id, point, applies, summary, check }
id       kebab-case, unique within a probe list
point    one of: shape | behavior | consistency | operational
applies  a subject name ('seed'), or '*' for a cross-family probe
summary  non-empty; what the probe guarantees when it passes
check    a function: (subject, subjects) → { ok, message? } — deterministic code
```

For a named probe, the check receives its subject `{ namespace, pkg }` or `null`.
For a `'*'` probe, the check receives the whole subjects map. Every check may
consult `subjects`; only cross probes depend on more than their own.

Rules
1. **The check is a function.** A probe record without a function is not a probe. Hooks in the tooling fabric established the shape rule; probes inherit it: checks are code the author wrote, deterministic, never prose, never a model call.
2. **Fail closed on throw.** Executing a probe turns an exception into a failed result carrying the error's message, in full, for the report. A probe is never skipped because it threw, and a throw never becomes a pass.
3. **One point each.** A probe names exactly one point. The multi-point discipline is that shape, behavior, consistency, and operational stay separate all the way to the report; a probe that "sort of" checks two points is two probes.
4. **Dedicated subjects.** A named probe applies to exactly one subject. Cross-family questions — agreements between peers — are `'*'` probes, and they declare themselves by their `applies`.
5. **Summaries state the guarantee.** "The forget bumps the epoch and fails stale projections closed" is a summary; "tests the memory" is not. A reader of the report should know what every pass certified.
6. **A claim is probed from the version that made it.** A behavior a member added after its first release is held by a probe that names that version. Against a checkout whose `VERSION` is older, or that declares no `x.y.z` version, the probe is `unknown` and names both versions: probing a claim the subject never made would be a superset (see below). Execution result
```
runProbe(probe, subjects) → { id, applies, point, subject, status, detail }
runProbeAsync(probe, subjects) → Promise of the same result
status   'pass' | 'fail' | 'unknown'
detail   the message that says why
```

- `pass` — the check returned `ok: true`.
- `fail` — the check returned `ok: false`, or it threw; the detail carries the message or the error.
- A check may return a promise when the claim it holds is asynchronous. `runProbeAsync` awaits it, and a rejection is a `fail` like a throw. `runProbe` does not wait: it records `unknown`, naming `runProbeAsync`, because it did not observe the outcome.
- `unknown` — the subject is absent (a named probe whose subject is `null`), or the check returned `{ unknown: true, message }` for a reason it states, such as "grammar agreement needs both checkouts present" when one is missing.

An `unknown` is declared with its reason, carried to the verdict math, and never resolved by wishful re-reading of other results.

What a probe never is
- Not a judge. A probe verifies claims and invariants; opinions about contract quality are review's business.
- Not a leak. A probe's messages quote errors and results, never environment details — what ran matters, where it ran does not.
- Not a superset. A probe checks what is claimed claimed. Probing things the subject never claimed is a defect in the probe, not a failure in the subject.

| capillary | 1 pass | 4 pass | — | 1 pass | pass |
| myosotis | 1 pass | 2 fail, 3 pass | — | 1 pass | fail |
| aestivation | 1 pass | 4 pass | — | 1 pass | pass |
| drosera | 1 pass | 2 fail, 3 pass | — | 1 pass | fail |
| cross-family | — | — | 1 fail, 2 pass | — | fail |

**Family verdict: fail.** Runner exit code: 1. Every member's own `npm test`
passed.

The failures
All five are probes written against the earlier contracts. The members changed
those contracts on purpose in this run's commits, and say so in their own
contract change notes. Trellis records the disagreement and does not repair a
member from this checkout.

- `myosotis-forget-is-structural` and `myosotis-stale-projection-refused`. The
  probes call `forgetMemory(store, id)`. Myosotis 0.4.0 requires
  `{ id, confirmed: true, key }`, and a bare id is refused with no state
  change. The probes therefore see no removal and no epoch bump. The second
  probe also shows that a projection now holds ids and digests, not text.
- `drosera-cookbook-references-resolve` and `drosera-skill-names-refuse-vendors`.
  The probes build skills from `name`, `summary`, and `instructions`. Drosera
  0.4.0 also requires `procedure`, `guardrails`, and `verification`, so every
  such skill is refused, including names the contract allows.
- `vendor-list-agreement` (consistency). The probe reads "drosera refuses this
  word" from a refused skill. Drosera now refuses every skill without the three
  new lists, so the probe reports a vendor disagreement that the two vendor
  lists do not have. This is a probe input defect, not observed drift between
  seed and drosera.

What repairs this
The repair is a later trellis task: build skills with the three new lists, and
forget with a confirmed, keyed request, gated by `since('0.4.0', ...)` so the
earlier releases keep their earlier probes. No member needs to move for that.

- It does not claim the members are deployed, hosted, or running as services.
- It does not claim health beyond the five module repositories at the commits
  above, on the run date.

# Trellis interop
How trellis meets the family. Every behavior attributed to a peer below is sourced from that peer's published repository; the default probes cite the contract each check holds. The core never imports a peer — subjects are injected, and cross-repo truth enters only through the bundle runner over the canonical workspace layout.

seed — the grammar anchor
Probed on:

- **shape** — the tool-id contract surface: `VERSION`, `parseToolId`, `formatToolId`, `isValidToolId`, `isWellFormedRegistryEntry`, `RESERVED_DOMAINS` all present; package discipline held.
- **behavior** — grammar edges reject exactly as the contract says (vendor segments, infrastructure-like segments, unknown verbs, over-long IDs), valid IDs parse to their parts, and a registry entry validates or names its errors.
- **behavior, from 0.2.0** — admission holds at intent: an attempt copies its objective's admission list, an intent naming a tool off it is refused, and an attempt with no list admits nothing. An entry with no rollback reads as `unsupported`, and a registry whose compensating tool is not registered names it.
- **consistency** — the reserved domains still hold the anchors the family leans on: the memory domain and the context domain. Peers' interop docs point here; the point holds the promise.

capillary — declared packets
Probed on:

- **shape** — the retrieval surface: `VERSION`, `recordSource`, `buildContextPacket`, `relationRecord`, `isSoundLedger`, `BLOOM_BASELINE` present.
- **behavior** — honest packets: budget-driven truncation is declared (`shortened`, `carried`, `cut`), out-of-budget items land in `omitted` with their reason, a source without a 64-hex digest never enters, and the ledger soundness audit catches dangling endpoints and duplicate relations.
- **behavior, from 0.2.0** — a source that could not be read is recorded as unknown with a null digest; its excerpts never enter a packet, even with a digest attached, and the packet lists it.
- The probes hold capillary's oldest rule, inherited from the systems it revamps: a packet declares what it did.

myosotis — the structural forget
Probed on:

- **shape** — the memory surface: `MEMORY_KINDS`, `memoryRecord`, `requiresConsent`, `consentState`, `openStore`, `admitMemory`, `forgetMemory`, `recallAll`, `projectionStamp`, `projectionIsValid`, `VERSION` present.
- **behavior** — the forget contract, under direct load: a real forget removes the record and bumps the epoch; a projection stamped before the bump fails closed after it; a forget miss is declared `unknown` with no state change; personal-consented memory is refused without a live grant; the kind set stays closed.
- **behavior, from 0.2.0** — a projection built before a forget is refused and serves nothing, and current recall rebuilds without the forgotten record.
- **behavior, from 0.3.0** — consent follows the sequence: a grant after a revocation is re-consent, a later revocation ends it, and a tie or an unsequenced side goes to the revocation.

aestivation — the gate that does not bend
Probed on:

- **shape** — the loop surface: `STAGE_KINDS`, `validatePlan`, `planProposal`, `DECISIONS`, `verdictRecord`, `latestVerdict`, `isSoundVerdictLedger`, `assemblyGate`, `VERSION` present.
- **behavior** — the gate order under direct load: an approved but invalid plan stays held (`plan-invalid`; deterministic outranks judgment), a revise verdict refuses to record without reasons, and a revise-then-approve ledger ends permitted with both verdicts kept.
- **behavior, from 0.2.0** — a hand-built approval with no judge holds the gate as `ledger-unsound` and is never surfaced as the verdict.
- **behavior, from 0.3.0** — given the plan digest, an approval of that exact plan permits, and an approval of a changed plan holds as `review-stale`.

drosera — fail closed, resolve early
Probed on:

- **shape** — the tooling surface: `EFFECT_CLASSES`, `parseToolId`, `toolFace`, `toolPack`, `skill`, `skillPack`, `EVENTS`, `hook`, `hookPack`, `runHooks`, `recipe`, `cookbook`, `checkRecipe`, `VERSION` present.
- **behavior** — hook dispatch fails closed (a throwing check is a failed check), a face with a non-closed effect is rejected, and cookbook reference resolution catches a dangling face at check time.
- **behavior, from 0.2.0** — every pack revalidates its entries: a frozen object that is not a valid face, skill, hook, or recipe is refused.
- **behavior, from 0.3.0** — a skill name with a vendor word is refused, whole words only, and protocol words stay allowed.

Cross-family — where the peers agree
- **Grammar mirror agreement** — drosera mirrors seed's tool-id grammar locally, by doctrine; the cross probe feeds both parsers the same corpus of valid and invalid IDs and passes only when they accept and reject identically. Either checkout absent: declared unknown — agreement is a two-member property, and it is not observed by wishing.
- **Vendor list agreement** — drosera's `VENDOR_NAMES` claims to be the vendor half of seed's forbidden segments. The cross probe tries a corpus: the vendor words both contracts name, drosera's own list, candidate vendor words neither lists, and seed's protocol words. Every word drosera refuses in a skill name must be a segment seed refuses; every corpus word seed refuses that drosera allows must be a protocol word; and drosera must allow the protocol words. Seed does not export its list, so a vendor seed adds outside the corpus is not seen. Either checkout absent, or drosera older than 0.3.0: declared unknown.
- **Version discipline** — every present subject declares a `VERSION` in `x.y.z` form. The point does not require the versions to be equal; it requires the declarations to exist, because trellis' shape claims in the evidence docs speak of what the modules said about themselves.

Claims made after a first release
A probe marked "from" a version is held only against a checkout at or past it. An older checkout reads `unknown` for that probe, with both versions named, rather than failing a claim it never made or passing one nobody checked. The rule is in `docs/contracts/probes.md`.

The family members not probed here
Bloom, the family's team workspace, and videsign, the design canon, are not subjects of the engine: the engine probes module repositories with exported surfaces, and each of those carries its own contract discipline in its own home. Their absence from the grid is a boundary, not a judgment, and this section names it so a future change would be a decision, not an accident.

Evidence
Runs of the bundle runner are recorded in `docs/evidence/` as dated observations: which members ran, each point's verdict, and the overall verdict. They are receipts, not standing claims — the next health statement is the next run.

# Memory Field (ADR-018) Implementation Plan
> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Ship a shared, deterministic memory-field primitive (constellation + pipeline) that vidoxlabs.dev renders at build time and ViWeb renders at runtime, with the same look from one source.

**Architecture:** Follows the ADR-013 stage precedent. `lib/memory-field.js` is pure (layout, SVG, text equivalent, contrast report, pipeline SVG); `lib/memory-field.css` carries every visual and the four motions from emitted tokens; `npm run tokens` ships both to `dist/`; the MCP tool `memory_field` returns SVG plus report; `dist/standard.json` carries `rules.memoryField`.

**Tech Stack:** Node (CommonJS, `node:test`), SVG, CSS (tokens via `--vi-colors-*`), MCP stdio server.

**Spec:** `SKILL.md` § ADR-018 (written in Task 1). Design approved in session 2026-11-18 (sections 1 and 2; sections 3 to 5 written into the ADR on the owner's instruction to keep going).

Global Constraints
- Animated properties: `transform` and `opacity` only (ADR-008). No `stroke-dashoffset` animation.
- Durations and easings come from tokens: 150/200/300/500ms, ambient drift 32s, pulse 6s.
- Every motion renders its final state under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` and under `[data-motion="paused"]` on the root (WCAG 2.2.2).
- No inline `style` attribute in emitted SVG; colour from classes only (`style-src 'self'`).
- Meaningful (lit) lines reach ≥ 3:1 on every surface of their theme (WCAG 1.4.11, ADR-013 item 4). Rest edges are `aria-hidden`.
- Link tokens stay ≥ 15 ΔE00 from every persona and status hex and ≥ 20 ΔE00 from each other.
- No persona colour marks a link type (ADR-004, ADR-017 item 8). Never colour alone: each code also has a dash or marker and a text label.
- Deterministic: no `Math.random`, no clock. Same input and seed give byte-identical output.
- Budget: ≤ 300 nodes and ≤ 3,000 edges, else typed error `MEMORY_FIELD_OVER_BUDGET`.

chunks.text: # Vivarium Seven systems, one agent platform. Vivarium is a personal agent platform. A person raises an assistant with a character and a job, gives it memory they consent to keep, and works alongside it: it reads what they point it at, asks before it acts outside its bounds, and leaves a record of what it did. It runs on the person's own machine first, and every route it takes to a model, a file, or a service is one the person switched on. This repository is the umbrella, not the product. It pins the seven systems at exact commits, records what each one owns, and gives a code agent the context it needs to work in the family without guessing. No product code lives here: the code lives in the seven repositories, and this tree is the one snapshot that says which code that is. bloom is Vivarium's user interface; the other six systems are the parts behind it.

The systems
| System | Role | Layer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [seed](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed) | Harness floor: run records, tool identity, provider adapters, the shared contracts | floor |
| [capillary](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary) | Context: bounded retrieval with sources attached, and relations | peer |
| [myosotis](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/myosotis) | Memory: consent to keep, structural forget | peer |
| [drosera](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/drosera) | Tools: tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks | peer |
| [aestivation](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/aestivation) | Review and delegation: plans, verdicts, questions to the person, the assembly gate | peer |
| [bloom](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) | User interface: the desktop and web app, first-run setup, the head agent; the only composer | composer |
| [trellis](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/trellis) | Testing from outside the call path: shape, behavior, consistency, operational probes | outside |

The floor holds the contracts. The four peers do not import each other; they meet at seed. bloom is the only composer: it is where a person raises an agent and where the parts are put together. trellis tests from outside the call path, so a failure in the tree is not a failure the tree can hide.

System map
<!-- vivarium:map:start -->
```mermaid
flowchart BT
    bloom["bloom · interface"]
    capillary["capillary · context"]
    myosotis["myosotis · memory"]
    drosera["drosera · tools"]
    aestivation["aestivation · review"]
    trellis["trellis · probes"]:::outside
    seed["seed · harness floor"]:::floor

    bloom -->|imports drosera 7a396c0| drosera
    bloom -->|imports seed 0d158cd| seed
    bloom -.->|contracts| seed
    capillary -.->|contracts| seed
    myosotis -.->|contracts| seed
    drosera -.->|contracts| seed
    aestivation -.->|contracts| seed
    capillary -.->|"context to memory, planned"| myosotis
    trellis -.->|probes| bloom
    trellis -.->|probes| capillary
    trellis -.->|probes| myosotis
    trellis -.->|probes| drosera
    trellis -.->|probes| aestivation
    trellis -.->|probes| seed

    linkStyle 2,3,4,5,6,7 stroke-dasharray: 6 4
    linkStyle 8,9,10,11,12,13 stroke-dasharray: 2 4
    classDef floor stroke-width:3px
    classDef outside stroke-dasharray: 4 3
```

Solid is an import today, labelled with the pinned short SHA. Dashed is a contract. Dotted is a probe from outside the call path. Edges marked planned are not built yet.
<!-- vivarium:map:end -->

Quick start
```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/vivarium.git
cd vivarium
npm run check
npm run sync   # move every system to the latest main and regenerate the manifest
```

Already cloned it without the systems? Run `git submodule update --init --recursive`.

`npm run check` is offline and deterministic. It fails when a generated file drifts from the pins, when a submodule is not at its gitlink, when a relative link or a `systems/` path does not resolve, or when a public-safety rule trips. `npm test` runs the unit tests for the tool itself.

How changes flow
1. **Change a system in its own repository.** A pull request there, its own tests, its own review. Nothing in this repository edits a submodule.
2. **The pin moves here.** Either the scheduled bump opens a pull request with the new pins and the regenerated manifest and map, or a person runs `npm run sync` and opens `chore(systems): bump <names>`. Either way the pin is a commit that is on that system's `main`.
3. **Readers get the prose from the docs hub.** [docs](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs) syncs every system's README and documentation, so this repository links to those pages instead of copying them.
4. **`docs` is linked, not pinned.** It is product-neutral and may serve more than one product, so it is not part of the snapshot. Neither is [videsign](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/videsign), the design canon this repository's banner follows.

Links

| --- | --- |
| [docs](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs) | The documentation hub, with every system's documentation synced |
| [videsign](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/videsign) | The design canon, including the family banner system |
| [docs/system-map.md](docs/system-map.md) | The generated map and the full pin table |
| [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) | The context file a code agent reads before touching the tree |
| [docs/product/](docs/product/) | The product specs: naming, first-run setup, model access, context access |
| [templates/agent-setup/](templates/agent-setup/) | The agent schema, the setup script, and three generic example agents |
| [docs/vision/design-brief.md](docs/vision/design-brief.md) | The living product brief: direction, not claims |
| [docs/adr/](docs/adr/) | The decision records, from the umbrella layout to the web app's context routes |
| [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) | How to work in the umbrella, and what belongs in a system instead |

# 0001: Umbrella with git submodules
- **Status**: Proposed
- **Date**: 2026-11-25
- **Decided by**: maintainers of this repository
- **Amends**: none

Context
Vivarium is one product made of seven systems, each in its own public repository with its own
history, tests, CI, and release cadence. A person who wants to work on the product needs one
checkout in which the seven are at commits that are known to work together, and a code agent
needs one file it can read to know which commits those are.

Three things are true of the systems:

- They are separate repositories, and a change to one belongs in that one.
- They are read together: bloom pins seed and drosera, the peers meet at seed's contracts, and
  trellis tests the tree from outside.
- They move independently, and a pin can be six hours stale without anyone noticing.

Decision
This repository is an umbrella that pins the seven systems as git submodules under `systems/`
and records the pins in a generated `vivarium.json`. `systems.config.json` holds what each
system is and owns; `npm run sync` moves every pin to the latest `main` and regenerates the
manifest, the map, and the README blocks; `npm run check` fails when the generated files drift
from the pins, when a submodule is not at its gitlink, when a link does not resolve, or when a
public-safety rule trips. Pins move only through pull requests.

Consequences
- **A pin is a pull request.** The bump workflow opens one every six hours when something
  moved, with the compare links. A pin is never pushed straight to `main`.
- **Cloning needs one extra word.** `git clone --recurse-submodules`, or
  `git submodule update --init --recursive` afterwards. A plain clone gives an empty `systems/`
  and `npm run check` says so.
- **Drift is visible, not silent.** The generated files are committed, so a stale manifest is a
  failing check rather than a note nobody reads.
- **Two histories, on purpose.** Each system keeps its own history, and this repository's
  history is the history of the pins. Blaming a file means deciding which of the two to blame.
- **Submodule edits can be lost.** A change made inside `systems/<name>/` is not committed
  here, and a `sync` would move past it. The rule is in `AGENTS.md`: change a system in its own
  repository.

Alternatives
**A monorepo.** All seven under one history. It would make a cross-system change one pull
request, and it would take seven repositories' CI, ledgers, and release notes and merge them
into one, which is a change of governance, not of layout. Rejected: each system's history and
release cadence is worth more than the convenience.

**A package-only umbrella.** Publish the seven to a registry and pin versions in a
`package.json`. It would remove submodules, and it would hide the code a person is meant to
read: this is an open, local-first family, and a version number is not a snapshot you can
inspect. It also needs a publish decision for every system. Rejected.

**A docs-only index.** One README that links the seven repositories, no pins. It would be
trivial to maintain and it would tell a code agent nothing about which commits work together.
Rejected: the pins are the product of this repository.

The Dependabot alternative, not adopted
Dependabot has a `gitsubmodule` ecosystem and would open one pull request per submodule per
day. It is not enabled here, because:

- each pull request would move one pin and leave `vivarium.json`, `docs/system-map.md`, and the
  README blocks stale, so the required `check` would fail on every one of them;
- the seven pull requests would compete for the same generated files, so merging one would
  stale the other six.

The ready snippet, for the day someone adds the follow-up job that runs `npm run sync` on a
Dependabot branch:

```yaml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: gitsubmodule
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: daily
```

Adopting it needs one more piece: a workflow that, on a Dependabot pull request, checks out the
branch, runs `npm run sync`, commits the regenerated files, and pushes once. Without that piece,
the bump workflow stays the primary path.

Why `docs` and `videsign` are linked, not pinned
`docs` is product-neutral and may serve more than one product; its existing sync already copies
every system's documentation, so pinning it would freeze a hub that is meant to be current for
readers, and would put a product-neutral repository inside one product's snapshot. `videsign`
is the design canon: a versioned reference, not a runtime dependency, and it is consumed by
more than this repository. Both are linked from the README and from `AGENTS.md`.

Changes
| Date | Change | By |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-11-25 | First written | |

# 0002: Internal agents use the public setup
- **Status**: Accepted (owner decision, 25 November 2026)
- **Date**: 2026-11-25
- **Decided by**: the owner
- **Amends**: none

Context
Vidoxlabs runs its own work with internal agents. The temptation is to give them a private
path: a private overlay repository, a private branch, or a fork of the templates with the
company's own names in it. Every one of those would mean the owner's own agents are built by
code no user sees, and that a capability internal agents need can live somewhere users cannot
ask for it.

The product also has to be able to answer a plain question: "can I make an agent like that?"
If the answer is "yes, if you had our private layer", the answer is no.

Decision
There is no private overlay, no private branch, and no private fork.

- Vidoxlabs' internal agents are ordinary user agents, created in the app through the same
  first-run setup, the same templates, and the same editors as anyone's.
- They live in the owner's user data, never in a repository. This repository and the seven
  systems ship generic templates only.
- If internal agents need something the setup cannot express, that is a missing feature for
  every user. It is specified here in public, in `docs/product/`, and built for everyone.
- Public CI keeps personal names and private details out. `npm run check` hashes forbidden
  words and scans for patterns; a personal name in a template is a failing check, not a
  review note.

Consequences
- The owner's own experience and a user's experience are the same experience, by construction.
- A feature internal agents want becomes public work with public tests. That is slower, and it
  is the point.
- The templates in `templates/agent-setup/` must stay generic. Three examples, no personal
  names, no keys, no endpoints.
- Anything that cannot be said in public cannot be part of how internal agents work; it stays
  in the owner's own user data, outside every repository.

Alternatives
**A private overlay repository.** Rejected: a hidden layer undermines user trust and splits the
owner's experience from the user's. It would also make "how do I do what your agents do"
unanswerable.

**Private branches in the public repositories.** Rejected: a branch is still code that exists
in a public repository's history and gets reviewed, tested, and eventually merged, and it would
teach contributors that some work bypasses review.

**A private fork.** Rejected: it doubles the maintenance and guarantees the two copies drift,
and the drift is invisible until an internal agent behaves differently from what users get.

# 0003: First-run setup and no default autonomy
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Date**: 2026-11-25
- **Decided by**: the owner
- **Amends**: none

Context
An agent that acts on a person's files, accounts, and money has to have a bound on what it does
without asking. The easy design is a default: pick level 3, let the person change it later.
That design makes the most important decision in the product on the person's behalf, and it
does it silently, at the moment they are least likely to look.

An agent that asks the wrong way is nearly as bad: a question with no explanation reads as
noise, and a question that cannot be traced back to a setting teaches the person nothing about
the machine they are running.

Decision
1. **No autonomy level is preselected anywhere.** Not in the setup screen, not in the schema,
   not in the app, not in an example agent. `agent.schema.json` requires `autonomy.level` and
   carries no `default`; the setup script's autonomy step has no selected choice; an example
   carries the literal placeholder `chosen-in-setup`. `npm test` fails if a `default` keyword
   appears in the schema.
2. **Setup is a scripted eight-step conversation**, not a settings form: model routes, workflow
   style (simple or advanced), autonomy level, question delivery, context routes, and a first
   agent, then a review screen showing each answer with the place to change it. The data lives
   in `templates/agent-setup/setup-script.json`; the prose is
   `docs/product/first-run-setup.md`.
3. **Every question the agent asks links to the setting that caused it.** The question card
   says "You set this agent to …", with a Change link that opens that exact setting, not the
   top of the settings tree.
4. **Every step says where to change it later**, by the same `settings.*` path the question
   card uses.

Consequences
- An agent cannot start until a person chooses a level. Setup can be paused; it cannot be
  skipped into a default.
- The autonomy screen is the longest in setup. That is deliberate.
- A new action class needs a level, or an explicit "inherits the agent's level", which is a
  schema change and a record in this repository.
- Tests can assert the absence of a default, so the rule does not depend on anyone remembering
  it.

Alternatives
**A default of level 3, changeable later.** Rejected: it decides for the person, and the person
who never opens settings is exactly the one who would be surprised.

**A default that adapts from the first few questions.** Rejected: it hides the decision behind
behaviour the person cannot see, and it makes the level non-reproducible.

**Setup as a settings tree, entered anywhere.** Rejected: an agent needs the six choices before
its first run, in an order that explains each one. A tree gives orderless access and no
explanation.

| 2026-11-25 | First written | |

# 0004: Model access routes
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Date**: 2026-11-25
- **Decided by**: the owner
- **Amends**: none

Context
A personal agent needs a model, and the model is the one part of the product that costs money
on every use. There are three honest ways a person can pay for that: they already pay a vendor
for a subscription, they pay a vendor directly for API use, or they run a model on hardware
they own.

The dishonest ways are familiar: resell someone's plan, hold their key on a server and forward
requests, or give away credit that a vendor will eventually invoice. Each changes who bills
whom without changing what the person sees, which is the worst kind of surprise.

Decision
Vivarium launches with three routes, and only three:

1. **A subscription the person already has**, used through the vendor's official sign-in
   program. The person pays the vendor, on the plan they chose before Vivarium existed.
2. **The person's own API key**, paid to the vendor at the vendor's prices.
3. **A model on the person's own machine**, paid for in hardware and electricity.

- **No hosted plan at launch**, and **no broker**: no relay holds a person's key and forwards
  requests on their behalf.
- **Hosted credits: later, maybe.** If credit is ever offered, it is separate, clearly priced,
  opt-in, and the three routes keep working without it.
- **Keys stay with the person by default.** The desktop app keeps a key in the operating
  system's credential store. The web app uses the paired companion by default, so the browser
  never holds the key. Storage on the web account is an explicit, encrypted opt-in, not a
  default.
- **A subscription program that requires the vendor's own runtime is used only through the
  desktop app or the paired companion.** The web app does not impersonate a vendor's runtime
  and does not scrape a session.
- **An agent definition holds route kinds and labels, never a key, a token, or an endpoint.**
  The schema has no field for one, and the public-safety scan fails a file that carries a key
  shape.

The reasoning and the route table live in `docs/product/model-access.md`.

Consequences
- The person's bill is always a bill from someone they chose, and Vivarium's price list does not
  include tokens.
- A feature that needs a server-side model call must be traced to one of the three routes, or
  it does not ship. That will rule some ideas out.
- The web app depends on a paired companion for key-based routes. That is a real cost: without
  a companion, the web app is limited to routes that need no key of the person's.
- Route order is a user setting, so two people with the same agent can get different answers.
  The record of which route answered belongs in the run record, not in a guess.
- Vendor terms change. The documentation link in settings is where a change is described, and
  this page deliberately restates no prices or quotas.

Alternatives
**A hosted plan with bundled credit.** Rejected at launch: it puts Vivarium between the person
and the vendor's bill, and it needs a margin decision before the product has users.

**A key broker.** Rejected: it would make Vivarium the custodian of every user's key, which is
the largest possible security surface for the smallest possible convenience.

**API keys only.** Rejected: most people who would use this already pay for a subscription, and
telling them to pay twice is a worse product.

**Local models only.** Rejected as the only route: it excludes the person whose machine cannot
run one, and it makes the first run a hardware conversation.

# 0005: Web-app context routes
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Date**: 2026-11-25
- **Decided by**: the owner
- **Amends**: none

Context
The desktop app can read a file because it runs where the file is. The web app cannot: it runs
on a server, and the person's device is somewhere else, behind a network they do not control.
Every product that has faced this has chosen between three bad options — pretend the server can
see the device, ask the person to paste things, or ship a browser extension nobody trusts.

There is a fourth option: make the connection outbound from the device, so nothing on the
person's machine listens for the internet.

Decision
Vivarium launches with the desktop app and a cloud-hosted web app; mobile comes later. The web
app reaches device context only through five opt-in routes:

| Route | Reaches | Connects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Upload and drag-in | one file or folder the person chose, one time | ordinary upload |
| OAuth connector | one account on one service | the vendor's consent screen |
| Browser extension | the page the person is on, when they press it | an extension they install |
| The agent's own browser | public pages the agent visits itself | a hosted browser session |
| Paired companion | folders and applications the device shares | an outbound-only connection from the device |

The companion pairing flow:

1. A **one-time code**, shown in the app with a short expiry, typed into the companion.
2. An **outbound-only connection** opened by the companion and held open. No inbound listener,
   no published address.
3. **The same autonomy settings, enforced locally.** The companion applies the agent's policy
   before it acts, using the same policy record; a command from the server cannot raise it, and
   where the two disagree the stricter wins.
4. **Revocable from either side**, taking effect at the next action.

The **hand-off rule**: a step that can only happen on the device is named as such, runs on the
paired companion under the same policy, and comes back with the device's name attached. With no
companion, the step waits; the web app never fakes a local result and never wi

Consequences
- The web app is honest about what it cannot reach, and the honest answer is visible in the
  interface rather than in a footnote.
- A web user who wants local files needs a companion. That is a real limit, and it is the price
  of not opening a port on someone's machine.
- The companion must be built and tested as its own surface, with its own probes in trellis.
- Two enforcement points for the autonomy policy, app and companion, must agree. The policy
  record is the single source, and a disagreement resolves to the stricter.
- Context arrives by reference with its source attached (capillary), so a route's name travels
  with the packet and a person can see what was read and from where.

Alternatives
**Server-side access to the device over a tunnel.** Rejected: it means an inbound path to a
person's machine, which is a security product of its own and one we are not building.

**Paste-only context.** Rejected as the only route: it is safe and useless for anything larger
than a paragraph.

**A browser extension as the only route.** Rejected: it reaches pages, not files or
applications, and it asks for broad permissions on every site to be useful.

**Mobile first.** Rejected: the two surfaces that make the product legible are the desktop and
the web app; mobile adds a third enforcement point before the first two agree.

# Decision records
One file per decision that shapes this repository or the product it describes. A record says
what was decided, why, what it costs, and what else was considered. It is a record, not a
discussion: the discussion belongs in the pull request that lands it.

| Record | Title | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [0001](0001-umbrella-with-submodules.md) | Umbrella with git submodules | Proposed |
| [0002](0002-internal-agents-use-the-public-setup.md) | Internal agents use the public setup | Accepted, owner decision, 25 November 2026 |
| [0003](0003-first-run-setup-and-no-default-autonomy.md) | First-run setup and no default autonomy | Accepted |
| [0004](0004-model-access-routes.md) | Model access routes | Accepted |
| [0005](0005-web-app-context-routes.md) | Web-app context routes | Accepted |

Statuses
- **Proposed** — written and open for review; not yet binding.
- **Accepted** — decided. The owner's decision when it changes what a person gets or pays for;
  a maintainer's when it is internal to this repository.
- **Superseded by NNNN** — kept for the record, replaced by a later decision.
- **Rejected** — considered and not taken, with the reason.

Adding a record
1. Copy [template.md](template.md) to `NNNN-short-title.md`, using the next number.
2. Fill every section. A Consequences section with nothing uncomfortable in it means the
   decision was not examined.
3. Add a row to the table above, and an entry to
   [docs-timeline.md](../docs-timeline.md).
4. Quote the owner's words when the decision is his, with the date and the channel, redacting
   anything private.

Numbers are never reused, including for a rejected record.

# NNNN: Title in sentence case
- **Status**: Proposed | Accepted | Superseded by NNNN | Rejected
- **Date**: YYYY-MM-DD
- **Decided by**: the owner, or a maintainer of this repository
- **Amends**: a record number, or none

Context
What is true now that makes a decision necessary. Facts, not preferences: what exists, what
does not, what breaks without a decision. Link the code, the contract, or the pull request
that shows it.

Decision
What was decided, in the present tense, in a few sentences. A reader should be able to act on
this section alone.

Consequences
What follows, including what is now harder, what is now impossible, and what must be watched.
Every cost named here is one we accept knowingly.

Alternatives
What else was considered, and why it was not taken. One short paragraph each: the option, its
appeal, the reason it lost.

Changes
| Date | Change | By |
| --- | --- | --- |
| YYYY-MM-DD | First written | |

# Vivarium workspace
Vivarium is a public repository. Everything committed here can be read by anyone, so write
as if a stranger will read it: no private paths, addresses, hostnames, ports, handles,
secrets, or personal details, and no internal agent names beyond "internal agents".

This file is for code agents. A person can read it too, but the README is the front door.

What Vivarium is
Vivarium is a personal agent platform: a person raises an assistant with a character and a
job, gives it memory they consent to keep, and works with it. It runs locally first, asks
before it acts outside the bounds the person set, and records what it did. Every route it
takes to a model, a file, or a service is one the person switched on.

This repository is the umbrella for seven systems. It pins them at exact commits and gives
an agent the context to work across them; it holds no product code. The product direction
lives in [docs/vision/design-brief.md](docs/vision/design-brief.md), and it is direction, not a
claim about what runs today.

### Naming

Vivarium is the product. bloom is Vivarium's user-interface system, not the product. Say
Vivarium for the product and bloom only for the interface system. docs is a separate,
product-neutral documentation hub; it is linked, not pinned.

Read order
1. This file.
2. `vivarium.json` — the pins, versions, layers, and which system imports which.
3. `docs/system-map.md` — the picture and the pin table.
4. The target system's own `AGENTS.md` (see the table below).
5. That system's `docs/`.

Inside a submodule, that repository's `AGENTS.md` wins over this file where it is stricter or
more specific. Read it before you plan a change there.

How the systems relate
| Layer | Systems | What the layer means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| floor | seed | The contracts every other system builds against. |
| peer | capillary, myosotis, drosera, aestivation | Peers do not import each other; they meet at seed's contracts. |
| composer | bloom | The only place the parts are put together, and the only user interface. |
| outside | trellis | Tests the tree from outside the call path, so the tree cannot hide a failure. |

**Imports today**, read from each system's `package.json` at the pinned commit: bloom pins
seed and drosera. No peer imports another, and nothing imports bloom. `vivarium.json` records
each pin; `docs/system-map.md` draws the edges. Derive the edges from the manifest, not from
memory, because a pin move can add one.

**What each system owns in Vivarium** is in `systems.config.json` under `owns`, one list per
system. Examples: seed owns the run contracts, the provider adapters, the model ladder, the
budgets, and the autonomy policy record; myosotis owns consent to keep and structural forget;
aestivation owns plans, verdicts, the questions to the person, and the assembly gate. When a
change belongs to a responsibility, it belongs in that system's repository.

Where each system's rules live
| System | Its own rules |
| --- | --- |
| seed | `systems/seed/AGENTS.md` |
| capillary | `systems/capillary/AGENTS.md` |
| myosotis | `systems/myosotis/AGENTS.md` |
| drosera | `systems/drosera/AGENTS.md` |
| aestivation | `systems/aestivation/AGENTS.md` |
| bloom | `systems/bloom/AGENTS.md` |
| trellis | `systems/trellis/AGENTS.md` |

Never edit a submodule from the umbrella
`systems/<name>/` is another repository at a pinned commit. A change there belongs in a pull
request in that repository, reviewed by that repository's rules. Then the pin moves here,
through the bump workflow or a `chore(systems)` pull request. Never commit a pin to a commit
that is not on that system's `main`, and never tidy a submodule's files from a branch here.

Verification
```bash
npm test        # unit tests for the umbrella tool
npm run check   # drift, submodule health, cross-links, public safety, no TypeScript
```

Both run before every commit, and CI runs both plus the `systems` matrix, which runs each
system's own tests at its pin. `npm run check` is offline and deterministic; if it reports
drift, run `npm run sync` and commit what it rewrites.

Internal agents are ordinary user agents
Vidoxlabs' own agents are created in the app through the same first-run setup, templates, and
editors as any user's, and live in the owner's user data, not in any repository. This
repository ships only generic templates. If something cannot be expressed through setup, it
is a missing feature for everyone, and it is specified here in public. The decision is
[ADR-0002](docs/adr/0002-internal-agents-use-the-public-setup.md). Never add personal agent names or
private details.

Product behaviour an agent must preserve
- **No default autonomy level.** A person chooses one in setup; nothing is preselected and
  nothing quietly assumes a level. The decision is
  [ADR-0003](docs/adr/0003-first-run-setup-and-no-default-autonomy.md).
- **Model access only through routes the person controls.** A subscription the person already
  pays for, their own API key, or a local model. The decision is
  [ADR-0004](docs/adr/0004-model-access-routes.md).
- **The web app reaches device context only through opt-in routes**, and a device-only step
  hands off to the paired companion. The decision is
  [ADR-0005](docs/adr/0005-web-app-context-routes.md).

Commits and pull requests
- Conventional commit messages that describe the change. No co-author trailers. No branch
  names in commit messages or pull request titles.
- One concern per branch and per pull request. Never force-push, rebase a published branch,
  amend a pushed commit, or rewrite history; fix forward.
- Never commit secrets, tokens, or `.env` files. Name a secret in documentation; never write
  its value.
- A claim about a system links to that system's README, docs, or code, and carries the
  system's own label when it is not implemented yet: implemented, specified, planned,
  observed.
- Merging is the owner's decision. Open the pull request, keep it green, and leave it for the
  merge order recorded in [SETUP.md](SETUP.md).

`CLAUDE.md` holds one line pointing here, matching the family.

# Development timeline
Newest first. One entry per slice: what landed, the pull request, and the pins at that time.
Times are ET.

25 November 2026
**Brief vocabulary in the agent setup** — PR #10. The schema's `autonomy.overrides` now uses the
design brief's five action classes (read, write, external, spend, credential) instead of the
placeholder set, the setup script carries the brief's five level names, and the question card
quotes a level by its product name. A test locks the class names, so a future edit cannot drift
from section 2.3 of the brief. Pins unchanged.


**Owner decisions and the canonical brief** — PR #9. `docs/vision/design-brief.md` is replaced with
the owner's second edition, verbatim, with only the required one-line header added under the title;
the reconstruction it replaces was written from the owner decisions of the same date and is now
history. `SETUP.md` records the four decisions taken with it: the seven `systems` checks become
required only after the first pin-bump run is green, pin bumps are merged by the owner with no
auto-merge, the bump workflow stays the path over Dependabot, and the docs source list stays in
`docs/sync.md` with no new capability row. Pins unchanged.

**Docs hub source** — PR in `Vidoxlabs/docs` #4: adds `vivarium` to `sources.json`, so the hub's
existing sync carries this repository's README, `AGENTS.md`, and `docs/`. Pins unchanged.

**Setup and close** — PR #8. `SETUP.md`, the owner checklist and merge order, the last timeline
entries, and a final `npm run sync` and `npm run check` on the top of the stack. Pins unchanged.

**Community files** — PR #7.

# Context access
Status: `specified`. The routes and the pairing flow below are what bloom and drosera build
against; the companion and its tool faces are `planned`. capillary owns what a route returns,
with its source attached.

Why there is a route at all
The web app runs on a server, so it cannot read a person's disk, their clipboard, or their
local applications. Rather than claim otherwise, Vivarium reaches device context only through
routes the person turns on, one at a time, each with a visible switch and a visible scope.

The five web-app routes
| Route | What it reaches | How it connects | What the person sees when it is on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Upload and drag-in | A file or a folder the person chose, one time | Ordinary upload from the browser to the app | The file's name in the conversation, with the copy stored until they delete it |
| OAuth connector | One account on one service: files, mail, calendar, issues | The vendor's consent screen, then a token the app holds | "Connected to … on <date>", the scopes granted in plain words, and a Disconnect button |
| Browser extension | The page the person is on, when they press the button | An extension they install, which sends the page's text and URL on request | A badge on the page and an entry in the conversation saying which page was read |
| The agent's own browser | Public pages the agent visits itself | A hosted browser session owned by the agent, no access to the person's browser | Each URL it opened, in order, with the time |
| Paired companion | The device the companion runs on: files, folders it watches, local applications it exposes as tools | An outbound-only connection from the device to the app, started by a one-time code | The device's name, the folders it shares, and a live "connected" state with a Disconnect |

A route is off until it is turned on. Turning one on never turns another on. Revoking a route
takes effect at the next action, not at the next restart.

Pairing a companion
1. **One-time code.** The app shows a six-word code and a short expiry. Nothing is paired
   until the person types that code into the companion on the device.
2. **Outbound only.** The companion opens the connection to the app and holds it open. The
   app never dials the device, so there is no port to open, no address to publish, and no
   inbound listener on the person's machine.
3. **The same settings, enforced locally.** The companion applies the agent's autonomy policy
   before it does anything, using the same policy record the app reads. A level the person
   lowered in the app is already in force on the device; a command that arrives from the
   server cannot raise it. Where the two disagree, the stricter wins.
4. **Visible, and revocable from either side.** The device can unpair itself without the app.
   The app can revoke a device without the device. Either way the connection is torn down and
   the token is dropped.

Hand-off for a device-only step
Some steps can only happen on the device: reading a local file, running a command, operating
an application that has no API. The rule:

- **The web app does not pretend.** It says the step needs the device and offers the hand-off.
- **Hand-off means a paired companion.** If there is one, the step runs there, under the same
  autonomy policy, and the result comes back with the device's name attached. If there is
  none, the step waits: the person can pair a device, switch to the desktop app, or drop the
  needed file in.
- **No silent substitution.** The web app never fakes a local result, never asks the person to
  paste something a route could have carried, and never widens a scope to avoid the hand-off.

What a code agent must preserve
- A route is opt-in, named, scoped, and revocable. Adding a route kind amends [ADR-0005](../adr/0005-web-app-context-routes.md).
- Context arrives by reference with its source attached (capillary), not as an anonymous
  blob, and never widens what the agent may do.
- The companion is outbound-only. A design that needs an inbound connection to the device is
  a different design, and it needs the owner's decision.
- Nothing about a person's machine (paths, addresses, device identifiers) is committed to this
  repository. `npm run check` fails a file that carries one.

# First-run setup
Status: `specified`. The eight screens below are the contract bloom builds against; seed's
records for them are `planned` and do not exist yet. Nothing on this page is implemented.

Purpose
A person opens Vivarium for the first time and ends up with an agent they chose: a name, a
character, a job, a model route, a workflow style, an autonomy level, a way to be asked
questions, and the context routes they turned on. Setup is a conversation, not a settings
form: each screen asks one thing, explains it in plain words, and says where to change it
later.

The machine-readable version of these eight steps is
[`templates/agent-setup/setup-script.json`](../../templates/agent-setup/setup-script.json), so
the setup screen renders data rather than a hand-written flow.

The eight screens
### 1. Welcome: what this is

- **Asks**: begin, or look around first and finish setup later.
- **Copy**: "Vivarium gives you an agent you raise yourself. It remembers what you let it
  remember, asks before it acts outside your bounds, and shows you what it did. Setup takes a
  few minutes and every answer can be changed later."
- **Stores**: the resume point only. Proposed record: `setup.answers`, field `progress`.
- **Change later**: `settings.about`.

### 2. Model routes: where the agent thinks

- **Asks**: at least one route. A subscription the person already pays for, their own API
  key, or a model on this machine. Routes are ordered: the first that answers is used.
- **Copy**: "Choose at least one route to a model. A subscription you already pay for, your
  own API key, or a model running on this machine. Keys stay with you: the desktop app keeps
  them in this computer's credential store."
- **Stores**: the ordered route kinds and their labels. Never a key, never an endpoint. The
  key itself goes to the operating system credential store, or to the companion when the app
  is the web app. Proposed record: `agent.definition`, field `modelRoutes`.
- **Change later**: `settings.models.routes`.

### 3. Workflow style: how much you want to see

- **Asks**: simple or advanced.
- **Copy**: "Simple keeps the machinery out of the way and shows the result. Advanced shows
  the plan, the tools it used, and the settings behind each decision while the work runs.

The question-card rule
Every question the agent asks the person during work follows one shape:

> **You set this agent to _Work alongside_.**
> It wants to send the summary to a colleague.
> [Allow once] [Always allow for this kind of action] [Change the setting]

- The first line quotes the setting that caused the question, in the person's own words, and
  the word **Change** opens that exact setting (`settings.autonomy.level`, not the top of the
  settings tree).
- The question is one action, in plain words, with the target named.
- "Always allow" writes an override for that action class and shows the new level before it
  is saved.
- A question never asks about two things at once, and never bundles a settings change with an
  approval.

What is stored, and where
| Record (proposed) | Holds | Owner | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `setup.answers` | which screen was answered, when, and the script version | seed | planned |
| `agent.definition` | id, display name, character, job, workflow style, model routes, context routes, tool grants, memory scope, standing rules, packs | seed | planned |
| `autonomy.policy` | the level and per-kind overrides, read on every action | seed | planned |

seed's current contracts (`docs/contracts/run-model.md`, `provider.md`, `tool-id.md`,
`edge-gate.md`) do not define these records yet. Until they do, the shapes here are
`specified` and the validator in
[`scripts/lib/agent-setup.mjs`](../../scripts/lib/agent-setup.mjs) is the only check.

What setup must never do
- Preselect an autonomy level, a workflow style, a model route, or a context route.
- Store a key, a token, or an endpoint in the agent definition.
- Turn a context route on because it was on for another agent.
- Hide a choice behind an "advanced" toggle that the simple style cannot reach.

# Model access
Status: `specified`. This page describes what Vivarium launches with; no adapter for these
routes is shipped yet. seed owns the provider adapters and the model ladder.

The three launch routes
| Route | Who pays | Who holds the credential | What the person sees in settings |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A subscription the person already has, used through the vendor's official sign-in program | the person, to the vendor, on the plan they chose before Vivarium existed | the vendor's own session, on the device or the companion, never copied into an agent definition | "Use a subscription I already have", with the vendor's sign-in screen |
| The person's own API key | the person, directly to the vendor, at the vendor's prices | the operating system credential store on desktop; the paired companion by default for the web app | "Use my own key", with the key field masked and a link to the vendor's billing page |
| A model on this machine or this device | the person, in hardware and electricity | nothing leaves the machine | "Use a model on this machine", with the model's name and size |

An agent has an ordered list of routes. The first route that can answer is used; the rest are
fallbacks. Changing the order changes which model answers first, and nothing else.

What launches, and what does not
- **No hosted plan at launch.** Vivarium does not sell tokens, does not resell a vendor's
  plan, and does not put itself between the person and the vendor's price list.
- **No broker at launch.** There is no relay that holds a person's key and forwards requests
  on their behalf.
- **Hosted credits: later, maybe.** If Vivarium ever offers credit, it is a separate, clearly
  priced thing the person opts into, and the three routes above keep working without it.

Where keys live
| Surface | Default | Opt-in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Desktop app | The device credential store, read by the app, never written to a file Vivarium owns | — |
| Web app | The paired companion holds the key and makes the request; the browser never sees it | Encrypted storage on the web account, only if the person turns it on and sets it up explicitly |
| Agent definition | Never a key, never a token, never an endpoint. Only a route kind and a label | — |

The rule follows from the schema:
[`agent.schema.json`](../../templates/agent-setup/agent.schema.json) allows a route kind and a
short label, and the pattern check in `npm run check` fails a file that carries a key shape.
A key pasted into a description is a finding, not a feature.

Subscription routes
A subscription program that requires the vendor's own runtime is used only through the
desktop app or through the paired companion. The web app does not pretend to be that runtime
and does not scrape a session. If a vendor offers no sign-in program that a third-party app
may use, that route is not offered: the person uses an API key or a local model instead.

Vendor terms
Each route is governed by the vendor's own terms, and the person agrees to them with the
vendor, not with Vivarium. The design brief's sources list the terms that were read when the
routes were chosen; this page does not restate prices, quotas, plan names, or limits, because
a number copied here would be wrong within a month. When a vendor's terms change, the route's
documentation link in settings is the place to say so.

What this means for a code agent
- Do not add a fourth route kind without an ADR that amends [ADR-0004](../adr/0004-model-access-routes.md).
- Do not write a key into an agent definition, a log, a test fixture, or an error message.
- Do not add a hosted plan, a relay, or a bundled credit without the owner's decision: it
  changes who bills whom.
- A route is a *kind* plus a *label*. Everything specific to a deployment stays in the
  person's own configuration, never in this repository.
