# Naming
Status: `specified`. This page is the rule for user-facing copy; nothing here claims a
feature runs today. The framing it serves is [the design brief](../vision/design-brief.md).

The rule
- **Vivarium is the product.** One product, one name, one front door.
- **bloom is Vivarium's user-interface system**, not a product. Say Vivarium for the product
  and bloom only for the interface system.
- **docs is a separate, product-neutral documentation hub.** It is linked, not pinned,
  because it may serve more than one product and it already syncs every system's
  documentation.

The family rule from the systems themselves: public repositories use only proper nouns of
things a public repository backs, plus generalized role terms. Vivarium is an ordinary word,
which fits that rule.

How the seven read in user-facing copy
People meet one product. The seven are described as parts of it, in plain words, and never as
separate products with their own front doors.

| System | Say it like this | Never say |
| --- | --- | --- |
| seed | "The foundation: the records, the contracts, and the connection to each model." | "the seed product" |
| capillary | "Where context comes from, with the source still attached." | "the context app" |
| myosotis | "Memory: what it keeps, with your consent, and what it forgets for good." | "the memory product" |
| drosera | "The tools and skills it can use, and the packs you can add." | "the tools platform" |
| aestivation | "How it plans, reviews its own work, and asks you before it goes ahead." | "the review engine" |
| bloom | "The app you open." After first mention only: "the interface". | "the bloom platform", "bloom by Vidoxlabs" |
| trellis | "The checks that run from outside, so a failure cannot hide." | "the test product" |

Where the names appear
- **Repository names** stay as they are: `seed`, `bloom`, `capillary`, `myosotis`, `drosera`,
  `aestivation`, `trellis`. A repository name is an address, not a product.
- **Product copy, help text, and settings** use Vivarium for the product and the plain
  description above for the part. A person should never have to learn seven names to use one
  product.
- **Code and contracts** use the system names, because a code agent needs to know which
  repository owns a responsibility. `systems.config.json` holds that mapping.

What this means for a pull request
If a change renames something a person reads, the question is: does it rename a part of
Vivarium, or does it rename Vivarium? A part keeps its system name in code and its plain
description in copy. Renaming the product is not a documentation change; it is a product
decision, and it belongs to the owner.

# Advanced system plan
Status: `planned`. This page extends [system-work.md](system-work.md): the same
rules apply, and none of this replaces it. Every item below is an advanced slice
for a later task **in that system's own repository**. Nothing here is a claim
that the work exists, and nothing here opens a pull request or an issue in a
system repository. Where a slice extends one already named in system-work.md, the
"extends" column says so; new slices get their capability ids from the owning
repository when that repository plans them, not from this page.

Each section names what the pinned system has **today**, with the system's own
label (`implemented`, `specified`, `planned`), and then the advanced slices that
grow it. "Today" claims link to the pinned source and carry its label; they are
not upgraded on this page.

The eight focus areas
| Focus | Owning system or systems | Extends |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Better agent tools | drosera, with seed's tool identity | D1, D2, D3 |
| Context efficiency | capillary | C1, C2, C3 |
| Agent memory | myosotis | M1, M2, M3 |
| Personality | seed, with the setup templates | S1, S2 |
| Agent internal communications | aestivation, with bloom's assembly | A1, A2, A3 |
| User interaction | bloom | B1 to B5 |
| Testing frameworks | trellis | T1 to T4 |
| Planning with implementation | seed and aestivation | S3, S5 |

---

1. Better agent tools (drosera, with seed)
Goal: an agent's tools are admitted through one gate, described by honest
metadata, and revoked the moment the person says so.

**Today** (all `implemented` at the pinned commit): drosera ships the pack
format and tool faces ([src](../../systems/drosera/src/pack.mjs)), the
cookbook packs ([src](../../systems/drosera/src/cookbook.mjs)), the skill
documents and their markdown shape ([src](../../systems/drosera/src/skills.mjs)),
and the workspace coding hooks
([src](../../systems/drosera/src/workspace-coding.mjs)). seed defines tool
identity, the controlled verb grammar, and each registry entry's effect
(`read | write | destructive | credential`), third-party egress and owner-gate
flags ([tool-id contract](../../systems/seed/docs/contracts/tool-id.md),
`implemented`).

**Advanced slices.**

| Slice | What it adds | Extends / depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One admission path | Every tool call, from any surface, passes the same admission gate. No flag, mode or harness bypasses it, and a run without a policy denies every non-read and says so, rather than inventing a default level | Depends on seed's `autonomy.policy` (S3) |
| Approvals bound to the exact request | An approval covers one tool id, one argument digest and one run, never a session or a "kind of action". The card the person answers shows the resolved program that will run, not only the typed command line | Extends S3; feeds bloom's approval screen (B3) |
| Action classes fr

2. Context efficiency (capillary)
Goal: the agent sees what it needs, with its sources attached, inside a budget
the person can see — by reference, not by copying the workspace into the prompt.

**Today** (`implemented` at the pinned commit): capillary packs bounded
codebase and conversation packets
([src](../../systems/capillary/src/codebase-packet.mjs),
[src](../../systems/capillary/src/conversation.mjs)), keeps provenance on
records ([src](../../systems/capillary/src/provenance.mjs)), guards reads
against stale epochs ([src](../../systems/capillary/src/epoch-guard.mjs)), and
maintains relations between what the agent knows and where it came from
([src](../../systems/capillary/src/relations.mjs)).

**Advanced slices.**

| Slice | What it adds | Extends / depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Route-named packets | Context from each of the five web routes arrives by reference, with the route named in the packet's source | C1 |
| Source records for everything | An upload, a connector item, a page or a paired device gets a source record, so a packet can always say where it came from | C2 |
| Budgeted assembly | The composer asks capillary for a packet under a token budget; the packet says what it included and what it left out, instead of silently truncating | Depends on seed's run budgets |
| Records that persist honestly | Transcript and working-record shapes ride the packer with the same provenance and epoch rules as codebase packets | Grows CAP-05 in capillary |
| The memory ha

3. Agent memory (myosotis)
Goal: the person consents to what is kept, can scope it per agent, and a forget
is real — no stale read brings it back.

**Today** (`implemented` at the pinned commit): myosotis keeps consent as
grants and revocations ([src](../../systems/myosotis/src/consent.mjs)),
recalls under scope ([src](../../systems/myosotis/src/recall.mjs)), and
forgets structurally with epoch-stamped projections, proven by a test that
reads after the forget
([src](../../systems/myosotis/src/forget.mjs),
[test](../../systems/myosotis/test/confirmed-forget.test.mjs)).

**Advanced slices.**

| Slice | What it adds | Extends / depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Per-agent scope | Memory scope is `agent` or `shared`, enforced on read as well as write, so one agent cannot read what another kept privately | M1 |
| Consent states before keeping | `ask-each-time` and `ask-once` are recorded before anything is kept, and the record says which one applied | M2, with capillary C3 |
| No resurrection | A forget cannot be undone by a stale projection, a cached packet or a re-ingested copy; read-after-forget is the acceptance test | M3, with capillary's epoch guard |
| Scoped recall | Recall answers only within the consenting scope, and a refusal names the scope it protected | Depends on per-agent scope |

---

4. Personality (seed, with the setup templates)
Goal: an agent's character, job and way of working are first-class records that
ride the definition — stable across sessions, owned by the person, never a grant
of authority.

**Today**: the setup templates carry the fields
([agent schema](../../templates/agent-setup/agent.schema.json), `specified`)
and the first-run flow defines how a person answers them
([first-run setup](../product/first-run-setup.md), `specified`). seed has the
closed schema style and the registry-document validation it will reuse
([src](../../systems/seed/src/schema.mjs), `implemented`). The decision that
internal agents use the same public setup is
[ADR-0002](../adr/0002-internal-agents-use-the-public-setup.md).

**Advanced slices.**

| Slice | What it adds | Extends / depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Templates never run | An `agent.template` holds placeholders and can never execute; `setup.answers` turns a template into an `agent.definition`, which refuses placeholders anywhere | S1, S2 |
| Character and job as records | Display name, character, job and workflow style are part of the definition record, so a persona is data the person owns and edits, not prompt text a harness owns | S1 |
| Persona continuity | The character record is stable across sessions and surfaces, and a change to it is a visible edit, not a silent drift | Depends on the definition record |
| Standing rules are records, not prose | A standing rule matches one exact tool and scope, c

5. Agent internal communications (aestivation, with bloom's assembly)
Goal: when agents work together, the collaboration is records — bounded
delegation, reviewed results, one trace — and nothing can forge the person's
channel.

**Today** (`implemented` at the pinned commit): aestivation carries plans
([src](../../systems/aestivation/src/plan.mjs)), verdicts of approve or revise
([src](../../systems/aestivation/src/verdict.mjs)), held reasons at the gate
([src](../../systems/aestivation/src/gate.mjs)), intent fencing for untrusted
turns ([src](../../systems/aestivation/src/intent.mjs)) and corrections
([src](../../systems/aestivation/src/correction.mjs)).

**Advanced slices.**

| Slice | What it adds | Extends / depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A question to the person | A question record carries the setting path that caused it, so the app can render "You set this agent to … Change" and the answer lands on that setting | A1, with seed S5 |
| Execution roles, not fixed identities | A small closed set of execution roles (coordinator, specialist, reviewer, verifier) binds user-created agents per run; an agent's identity is the person's, a role is the run's | Feeds bloom's assembly; distinct from S1 |
| Delegation that only narrows | A delegation record is validated, bounded and cancellable, and can only narrow the delegate's authority, never widen it | Depends on S3's classes |
| Verdicts a verifier cannot mint | Review sign-off is asymmetric — the verifier cannot produce what

6. User interaction (bloom)
Goal: the person sees what an agent will do, answers exactly what it asked, and
can change any answer at the setting it came from.

**Today**: the terminal commands and the coding loop are the working surface —
bloom's ledger keeps the capability `specified` with its three slices
`landed` ([capability index](../../systems/bloom/docs/capabilities/index.json)),
and the README describes them as implemented; reconciling that label is bloom's
own task. The setup script the screens will render is
[specified](../../templates/agent-setup/setup-script.json).

**Advanced slices.**

| Slice | What it adds | Extends / depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First-run setup, resumable and editable | The eight screens render from the setup script, open with nothing selected on the autonomy screen, survive restart, and persist in the person's data — never in a repository | B1, with S2 |
| Every answer carries its Change link | The review screen shows each answer with a link that opens that exact setting | B2 |
| The questions inbox | Question cards arrive with the setting link and the answer returns to that setting; an approval shows the resolved program and is bound to the exact request | B3, with seed S5 and the admission path |
| Pairing | A one-time code with expiry, a device list, and revoke from either side; the companion stays outbound-only | B4, with ADR-0005 |
| Two shells, one definition | Desktop and web read the same agent definition and autonomy policy; n

7. Testing frameworks (trellis)
Goal: the tree is tested from outside the call path, so no system can hide a
failure — and the verdicts are dated evidence, not vibes.

**Today** (`implemented` at the pinned commit): trellis scores the family grid
([src](../../systems/trellis/src/grid.mjs)), runs point probes
([src](../../systems/trellis/src/probes.mjs)) and keeps per-point scoring
([src](../../systems/trellis/src/score.mjs)).

**Advanced slices.**

| Slice | What it adds | Extends / depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The probe set, with negative tests | One probe per guarantee — setup with no preselected autonomy, definitions, admission, provenance, consent and forget, plan holds, delegation authority, trace integrity, provider neutrality, boundaries, hygiene — each asserting both the pass and the refusal | T1 to T3, grown |
| Dated verdicts on revisions | A verdict says pass, fail or unknown for a named revision, and unknown is a recorded state when evidence is missing — never a silent pass | With the family grid |
| The pairing probe | A companion that cannot be reached inbound, and a token that stops working after revoke | T2 |
| A grid entry per pin | Every repository's pin is tested from outside before it merges, so the umbrella cannot drift ahead of what it pins | T4 |
| Fail-closed is tested too | A missing corpus, an unreadable record and an absent policy fail with a stated error and a nonzero exit — the tests assert the refusal, not just the happy path | Cross-cuttin

8. Planning with implementation (seed and aestivation)
Goal: planning is not a prompt trick — it is records that pause, ask, clear,
implement and verify, and the run can always say what it is waiting for.

**Today** (`implemented` at the pinned commit): seed's run model has the
waiting-for-owner status and the pause-and-resume contracts
([run-model contract](../../systems/seed/docs/contracts/run-model.md),
[src](../../systems/seed/src/resume.mjs)), admission per objective
([src](../../systems/seed/src/admission.mjs)), and the provider seam and model
profiles for route selection
([src](../../systems/seed/src/provider.mjs),
[src](../../systems/seed/src/model-profile.mjs)).

**Advanced slices.**

| Slice | What it adds | Extends / depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The policy read on every action | An `autonomy.policy` record — level plus per-class overrides, no default value anywhere — is read on every action, and no agent runs without one | S3 |
| Route kinds on the ladder | Subscription, own key, local model: a kind and a label per route, never a credential, and setup can finish without a route while the agent stays not-runnable with a typed reason | S4, [ADR-0004](../adr/0004-model-access-routes.md) |
| The question record | The action, the setting that caused it, the target and the answer — one record the inbox renders and the setting consumes | S5, with A1 |
| Holds that clear on one line | A plan pauses on a hold, shows its clearing condition, and resumes when the person

Sequencing
The order in [system-work.md](system-work.md) holds here: seed's contracts come
first because the other slices read them, the peers meet at those contracts,
bloom composes, and trellis tests the tree from outside. Within that:

1. seed: the definition, answers, policy and question records (focus 4 and 8) —
   every other area reads them.
2. drosera and capillary: the admission path and the packet budget (focus 1 and
   2), against seed's action classes.
3. myosotis: scope and consent states (focus 3), with capillary's hand-over.
4. aestivation: the question record, delegation and verdicts (focus 5), against
   seed's records.
5. bloom: setup, the inbox, pairing and the shells (focus 6), composing the
   records the others hold.
6. trellis: the probe set and dated verdicts (focus 7), last, so it tests what
   actually shipped.

The research step every slice starts with
Each system repository has a research rule: before planning a change to a module
that serves a capability, the plan starts from the recorded evidence for that
capability — the claims, the decision axes with the test that holds each one,
and the open gaps — never from general knowledge. A capability with neither
evidence nor a recorded gap is stopped and reported, not planned. See each
system's own `AGENTS.md` for the exact calls. Slices on this page follow that
rule like any other: the owning repository plans them against its evidence, and
until that evidence step runs, "planned" here means direction, not a schedule.

What is not in this list
The same exclusions as [system-work.md](system-work.md) apply: anything that
changes who bills whom, opens a port, or publishes personal data is an owner
decision, and the decision records say so.

# Vivarium design brief
Living document. Edit by PR; record changes in docs-timeline.md.

- Status: living document, second edition (owner decisions of 25 November 2026 folded in)
- Date: 25 November 2026
- Scope: the Vivarium umbrella over seven public systems: `seed`, `bloom`, `capillary`, `myosotis`, `drosera`, `aestivation`, and `trellis`
- Audience: the owner, contributors, and the code agents that build Vivarium

Market figures and vendor policies below were read on 25 November 2026 from the sources in section 9. They move month to month. Re-check them before quoting them anywhere public.

### Owner decisions in this edition (25 November 2026)

1. **One setup path for everyone.** There is no private overlay. Vidoxlabs' own internal agents are created in the app through the same first-run setup and editors any user goes through, so the team uses the product exactly as users do (section 2.5).
2. **Model access at launch:** the person's existing subscriptions where the provider officially supports sign-in from other apps, their own API keys, and local or on-device models. No hosted plan and no broker at launch; hosted credits are "later, maybe" (section 3.4).
3. **Platforms:** desktop app and a cloud-hosted web app first; mobile later. The web app reaches device context through an optional paired companion and other opt-in routes (section 5.5).
4. **No default autonomy level.** A scripted first-run setup has the person choose autonomy and simple or advanced workflows, and

1. What Vivarium is
Vivarium is the public product name and the umbrella for one product idea: **a personal agent platform where people raise personified assistants that remember them, learn their work, and act with them and for them.** The seven systems are the organs of that platform:

| System | Role in Vivarium | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `seed` | Harness floor: run records, tool identity, provider adapters, the contracts everything else speaks | "What is a run, a tool, a provider, a budget?" |
| `bloom` | User interface: the desktop and web app a person opens, the first-run setup, the head agent, the workspace the agent and person share | "Where do I set up my agents, talk to them, and watch them work?" |
| `capillary` | Context: bounded retrieval with sources attached, and the relations between things | "What does the agent need to know right now, and where did it come from?" |
| `myosotis` | Memory: consent to keep, structural forget | "What does the agent remember about me and itself, and who allowed it?" |
| `drosera` | Tools: tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks | "What can the agent do, and how does it find the right tool?" |
| `aestivation` | Review and delegation: plans, verdicts, questions to the person, the assembly gate | "Should this step run, who does it, and what do we ask the person first?" |
| `trellis` | Testing from outside the call path: shape, behavior, consistency, operational probes | "Does it actually work, and did it stay working

2. Focus area 1: agent creation and delegation
### 2.1 The problem

- People differ. Some want to approve every step and edit every workflow. Others want something that just works and never asks a question they cannot answer.
- Vidoxlabs runs its own internal agents on the same architecture. People should be able to see that the product the company uses is the product they get, with no hidden layer. At the same time, the company's own agent names, notes, and goals are personal data and do not belong in public repositories.

### 2.2 Options

| Option | How it works | Tradeoffs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A. Fixed presets | Ship three or four ready-made assistants; users pick one | Dead simple; no real personalization; weak long-term retention |
| B. Full builder only | Users define personas, tools, triggers, and policies from scratch | Maximum control; most people never finish setup |
| C. One agent model, two editors | Every agent is the same data object (persona, memory scope, tool grants, autonomy level, workflows). A simple editor creates it by conversation; an advanced editor exposes every field | One code path; users can graduate from simple to advanced without migrating; needs careful defaults |

### 2.3 Autonomy levels

Autonomy is a deliberate design choice, separate from model capability and tool access. Research on agent autonomy levels describes a ladder from the person as operator, through collaborator, consultant, and approver, to observer ([Feng, McDonald, and Zhang

3. Focus area 2: affordable model access
### 3.1 The problem

Agents burn tokens. People who cannot run models locally and do not want another subscription or an API bill will not adopt a product whose every task costs money they did not plan for. Many target users already pay for a chat or coding subscription and expect to reuse it.

### 3.2 What the market allows today

| Route | Status on 25 Nov 2026 | Tradeoffs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bring your own API key (any provider) | Universally allowed; usage billed to the key owner | Cheapest for Vidoxlabs; friction for non-technical users; surprise bills without budgets |
| Bring your own ChatGPT plan | OpenAI's "Sign in with ChatGPT" lets Go, Plus, Pro, and Business users spend their plan allowance in participating apps. Terms require requests to come from the user's own local runtime or a runtime only they control, tokens stored locally, no charge to use the plan, and plan use only inside the connected app ([terms](https://openai.com/policies/sign-in-with-chatgpt-terms/), [help](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001542-using-your-chatgpt-plan-in-other-apps-and-sites)) | Zero extra cost for many users; tied to one vendor's program, participation rules, and plan limits. Because the terms require the user's own local runtime, Vivarium's web app uses this route only through the user's desktop app or paired companion (5.5), never from Vidoxlabs servers |
| Bring your own Claude plan | Not permitted: Anthropic reserves consumer-

4. Focus area 3: scope of work
### 4.1 The problem

People use agents for three broad jobs: building code and tools; work such as reading PDFs, research, and reports; and everyday conversation and errands. Building three products dilutes the effort. Building one generic chat box produces a lesser product that the next model release makes obsolete.

### 4.2 Options

| Option | Tradeoffs |
| --- | --- |
| A. Pick one vertical (for example coding) | Clear story; crowded market; leaves the personal-assistant thesis unproven |
| B. Generic assistant | Broad; nothing a frontier vendor's own app does not do better |
| C. Personal core plus installable skill packs | The core (persona, memory, context, tools, review, autonomy) is shared; each job is a pack of skills, tools, workflows, and tests. Needs a strong pack format and good starter packs |

### 4.3 Recommendation

Option C. Build the layer that gets **more** valuable as models improve, not less:

- **Owned by the user, compounding over time:** memory of the person, each assistant's own memory of itself, workflows, and standing rules. These survive model changes and are exportable.
- **Model-agnostic:** a better model is an upgrade for Vivarium, not a replacement for it.
- **Three starter packs at launch,** each with acceptance tests in `trellis`:
  1. *Build:* code and tool work in a real work tree, with plans reviewed by `aestivation`.
  2. *Work:* documents, PDFs, research, and reports, with every claim tied to a source by `c

5. Focus area 4: connectors and tooling
### 5.1 The problem

Every API or tool-server connector needs its own sign-in, keys, or OAuth grant. Tokens expire, updates break them, tool definitions flood the context window, and agents pick the wrong tool when two look alike. Managing twenty connectors is a chore nobody signs up for. The owner's working theory: let the agent use a computer the way a person does, either the person's own device or a computer of its own.

### 5.2 State of the art (25 Nov 2026)

- **Computer use is now credible.** Leading agents report scores above the original human baseline on the verified OSWorld desktop benchmark, with top submissions reported near 90% against a 72% human baseline measured on the earlier task set ([OSWorld-Verified](https://www.llmboard.ai/benchmarks/osworld-verified-485)). It is still slower and costlier per step than a direct API call, and benchmark tasks are not the long tail of real apps.
- **Operating systems are building the "agent's own seat".** Windows 11's agent workspace gives each agent its own account and its own Windows session, running in parallel with the person's session, with access only to folders and apps the person shares. It is a preview feature, off by default ([Microsoft](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/ai/ai-features/experimental-agentic-features), [Windows blog](https://blogs.windows.com/windowsexperience/2025/10/16/securing-ai-agents-on-windows/)). Microsoft also offers full cloud PCs for agent

6. Focus area 5: interfaces and platforms
### 6.1 Market share (StatCounter, October 2026, share of web page views, not installed base)

| Segment | Share | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Desktop worldwide | Windows 76.6%, macOS 15.7%, Linux 5.7%, ChromeOS 2.0% | [Dr. Windows summary of StatCounter](https://www.drwindows.de/news/browser-und-betriebssysteme-im-oktober-2026) |
| Mobile worldwide | Android 72.4%, iOS 27.6% (12-month average about 69% / 31%) | [Spreadcast summary of StatCounter](https://spreadcast.app/resources/android-vs-ios-market-share) |
| Mobile United States | iOS 52.0%, Android 48.0% (12-month average about 59% iOS) | same |
| All platforms worldwide | Android 44.7%, Windows 28.9%, iOS 17.5%, macOS 5.9%, Linux 2.2% | [Dr. Windows](https://www.drwindows.de/news/browser-und-betriebssysteme-im-oktober-2026) |

Reading: mobile is where people are; the desktop is where agents can do real work today; Windows dominates desktops; iOS leads in the United States; Android leads everywhere else.

### 6.2 Rollout order (decided 25 November 2026)

1. **Desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux) and a cloud-hosted web app, together.** One interface (`bloom`) in both. The desktop app runs agents on the person's own machine; the web app runs agents in the cloud and reaches the device through the routes in 5.5. Windows gets first-class attention because of its share; macOS because early adopters and developers are there; Linux because it costs little extra.
2. **Companion pairing

7. Cross-cutting principles
- **Claims match evidence.** Every capability stays labelled `implemented`, `specified`, `planned`, or `observed`, as the systems already require.
- **One change, one repository.** The umbrella pins and explains; it never edits a system. Changes land as pull requests in the owning system.
- **Model-agnostic, device-agnostic, connector-light.** Prefer routes that need no new sign-in.
- **The person stays in charge.** Autonomy is chosen, visible, and revocable; credentials always ask.

8. Decisions and open questions
Decided by the owner on 25 November 2026:

| # | Question | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Where do the internal agents live? | Nowhere special: they are user-created agents, made through the same in-app setup as any user's, kept in the owner's own user data. No overlay, branch, or fork (2.5) |
| 2 | How do people pay for models at launch? | Existing subscriptions through official sign-in programs, their own API keys, and local models. No hosted plan or broker at launch; hosted credits later, maybe (3.4) |
| 3 | First surface? | Desktop app and cloud-hosted web app; mobile later (6.2) |
| 4 | Default autonomy? | None. Chosen in first-run setup, changeable later, with the setting linked from every question (2.3, 2.4a) |
| 5 | Codename or product name? | Product name: Vivarium. `bloom` is its user-interface system |
| 6 | Should the umbrella also pin `docs` and `videsign`? | No. `docs` stays product-neutral (it may serve future products) and already syncs every system's documentation; `videsign` is design canon. Link both |

Still open:

| # | Question | Options | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7 | Cloud seat for always-on agents: build or rent? | (a) rent cloud PCs; (b) self-host; (c) defer | (c) until the desktop app and web app ship |
| 8 | Subscription programs beyond ChatGPT? | Track each vendor's program; adopt only official ones | Adopt official programs only; never handle consumer-plan credentials outside the vendor's

9. Sources (read 25 November 2026)
- Feng, McDonald, Zhang, "Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents": https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12469
- OpenAI, Sign in with ChatGPT Terms: https://openai.com/policies/sign-in-with-chatgpt-terms/
- OpenAI Help, Using your ChatGPT plan in other apps: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001542-using-your-chatgpt-plan-in-other-apps-and-sites
- Anthropic, Claude Code legal and compliance: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance
- OpenAI API pricing (standard and batch): https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing
- Gemini API rate limits: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits
- OpenRouter limits: https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/limits
- Apple Foundation Models framework: https://developer.apple.com/foundation-models-framework/
- Android on-device inference: https://developer.android.com/blog/posts/build-intelligent-android-apps-on-device-inference
- HyDRA hybrid routing (arXiv): https://arxiv.org/html/2605.17106
- TrueFoundry routing benchmark: https://www.truefoundry.com/blog/engineering/llm-cost-routing-benchmark/
- Anthropic, advanced tool use: https://www.anthropic.com/research/advanced-tool-use
- Anthropic, code execution with tool servers: https://www.anthropic.com/research/code-execution-with-mcp
- Model Context Protocol, client best practices: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2025-11-25/develop/clients/client-best-practices
- Model Context Protocol, authorization: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specifi

# Architecture Decision Records

This folder defines the Architecture Decision Record (ADR) convention for the `docs` hub and every peer repository in the Vidoxlabs family.

## Naming and numbering

- Each repository keeps its own `docs/adr/` directory with its own `README.md` pointing to this hub convention.
- Files are named `NNNN-<slug>.md` using a four-digit zero-padded number starting at `0001` per repository (`0001-<slug>.md`, `0002-<slug>.md`, and so on).

## Status lifecycle

Every ADR carries one of four statuses:

- `Proposed`: Drafted by an agent or contributor for review.
- `Accepted`: Ratified by an owner answer recorded under the [Owner questions](../timeline/agent-guide.md#owner-questions) process.
- `Superseded by NNNN`: Replaced by a newer accepted ADR in the same repository.
- `Deferred`: Parked by owner decision without adoption.

## Governance rules

- **Agents propose ADRs**: Only an owner answer recorded under the [Owner questions](../timeline/agent-guide.md#owner-questions) process moves an ADR to `Accepted`, `Superseded`, or `Deferred`.
- **Dependencies require an ADR first**: Per [engineering-law.md](../engineering-law.md), repositories keep zero runtime dependencies (`bloom` pins only `seed`). Any proposal to introduce a dependency must open and win owner acceptance as an ADR before any dependency enters `package.json`.
- **Format**: Follow [template.md](template.md) with plain Markdown headings and zero YAML frontmatter.

docsPages.body: Plans, verdicts, and the assembly gate # aestivation Plan proposal, deterministic validation, review verdicts, and the assembly gate. Aestivation is the admission and review member of the bloom agent family. Before work opens, it happens here: a plan is proposed, a deterministic rule pack validates it, reviewers record approve or revise verdicts, and a gate holds automatic assembly until the plan is both valid and approved. A revision verdict stops assembly; the reasons say what to change; the next plan is a new proposal. ## Status Version 0.5.0. The plan rule pack, verdict ledger, and assembly gate are `implemented` as a tested reference library. A durable ledger, live reviewers, and service interfaces remain `specified` or `planned`. ## Install ```bash npm install @vidoxlabs/aestivation ``` Requires Node >= 22.13. Zero runtime dependencies. ## Modules | Module | What it holds | Label | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `plan.mjs` | Plan proposals: objective plus ordered steps, the SHA-256 digest of each proposal's content, and the deterministic rule pack that validates stages, titles, and order. | `implemented` | | `verdict.mjs` | Verdict records (approve or revise) that may name the plan digest they reviewed, the append-only ledger, and the soundness check over every record. | `implemented` | | `intent.mjs` | Read-only intent assessments that name missing sources and ground personal recall in admitted memory references. Tool and memory-write lists stay under caller admission. | `implemented` | | `correction.mjs` | Corrections within existing scope after an exact-digest revise verdict, with new frozen proposals, a two-replan limit per in-process lineage, and a check that refuses superseded results. The judge cannot apply the patch. | `implemented` | | `gate.mjs` | The assembly gate: one function that checks the ledger, holds a review of a different plan version as stale, and composes validation and verdicts into permitted or held, with the reason. | `implemented` | ## The name Aestivation is the arrangement of petals in a bud before it opens. That is the entire doctrine: the work of arranging before the opening. Nothing assembles until the arrangement has been validated and reviewed. When it opens, it opens because the gate said so for stated reasons. ## The rule pack The baseline deterministic rules a plan must pass: 1. A plan has at least one step. 2. Every step names a known stage: `research`, `work`, `review`, `assemble`, or `verify`. 3. Every step has a non-empty title. 4. When review and assemble are both present, review precedes the first assemble. 5. When verify is present, it is the final step. The same plan validates the same way every time, and no review can wave it through. The split runs both ways: no rule pack approves a plan on a reviewer's behalf. Judgment and rules are separate lanes; the gate composes them. ## The family The family follows one design law: ordinary botanical words for public products. | Name | Province | | :--- | :--- | | [`seed`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed) | Harness foundation: runs, tools, providers | | [`capillary`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary) | Context retrieval and relations, provenance-first | | [`myosotis`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/myosotis) | Memory with consent and structural forget | | `aestivation` (this repo) | Plans, verdicts, and the gate before assembly | | [`drosera`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/drosera) | Tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks | | [`trellis`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/trellis) | Multi-point testing with dated evidence | | [`bloom`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) | The team workspace harness | | [`docs`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs) | Family documentation, synced from every public repository | ## Documentation - `AGENTS.md`: start here before editing. # Aestivation architecture

Four whorls, one gate.

```
            ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
            │                  the bud                     │
            │                                              │
 proposal ──►│  rule pack ──► verdict ledger ──► the gate  │──► assembly permitted
   {objective,                                 held?        (or held, with reason)
    steps[]}    deterministic   judgment,        reason:
                yes/no          with reasons     plan-invalid
                                                 ledger-unsound
                                                 awaiting-verdict
                                                 review-stale
                                                 revisions-requested
            └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## The proposal

A plan is an objective plus ordered steps. Each step names a stage from a closed set — `research`, `work`, `review`, `assemble`, `verify` — and carries a title. The proposal is the unit of review: reviewers read it whole, and a revised plan is a new proposal, not an edit of the old one in place. Each proposal carries the SHA-256 digest of its content, so a verdict can name exactly which version it reviewed.

## The rule pack

Deterministic validation of shape and order. Same input, same verdict, every time, no exceptions, no authority. The baseline pack:

- at least one step;
- known stages only;
- non-empty titles;
- review before the first assemble when both are present;
- verify is the final step when present.

A caller can swap in a stricter pack. It cannot swap in a looser one that outputs `ok` for plans these rules reject — the baseline is a floor, and the gate consults the pack it was given, whose rules are on its face.

## The verdict ledger

Review is recorded, not remembered. Each verdict names its plan, carries a decision from `{approve, revise}`, names the judge, and — when the decision is revise — carries at least one reason. The ledger is append-only: soundness means every verdict references a known plan and every record is well-formed. The latest verdict for a plan is the one that counts; history stays underneath it.

## The gate

One composition, one answer. Given a validation result and a ledger, the gate answers: is automatic assembly of this plan permitted? Held reasons, in order:

1. `plan-invalid` — the rule pack rejected it. Deterministic outranks judgment; an approval cannot rescue an invalid plan.
2. `ledger-unsound` — the ledger holds a malformed record, or, when known plans are given, a reference to an unknown plan. Judgment counts only from a ledger the gate can trust.
3. `awaiting-verdict` — no verdict exists for the plan. Unreviewed plans do not self-assemble.
4. `review-stale` — given the plan's digest, the latest verdict reviewed a different version or named none. The proposal reviewed is the proposal assembled.
5. `revisions-requested` — the latest verdict is revise. The reasons say what to change; the plan comes back as a new proposal.

Permitted means one thing: valid plan, approved by the latest verdict. Not good, not owner-ratified, not deployed — permitted to assemble, with the ledger showing exactly why.

## What this edition is

`src/` implements the four parts as pure functions over plain data: the rule pack, verdict construction and ledger soundness, and the gate. No I/O, no persistence, no concurrency. A durable ledger behind this state machine is `specified` in the contracts; the mapping onto any particular store is deliberately out of scope here.

# CAP-07: Plan review and approval loop

- ID: `CAP-07`
- Title: Plan review and approval loop
- Lead: `aestivation`
- Touches: `seed`, `bloom`
- Horizon: `next`
- Milestone: `M3`
- CLI phase: `P3`
- Status: `proposed`
- Claim: `planned`
- Depends on: `CAP-06.1`

## Why

Multi-step workspace runs need an explicit, deterministic plan-review and owner-approval loop so plans carry role-bound steps, hold when a clarifying question is open, enforce a strict step status machine, bound revisions per run, and never mistake a reviewer verdict or model belief for owner ratification.

## What it does

- **Plan payload extensions (`CAP-07.1`)**: a plan proposal carries `request` (the task request), `seats` (role IDs only from the closed set `chair`, `framing`, `risk`, `coherence`, `sequencing`), `knownFacts` (explicit grounded facts), `steps` (each carrying a seat role ID from that closed set, a stage, a title, and an `action`), `summary`, and an optional `clarifyingQuestion`. When `clarifyingQuestion` is present, the plan is held until the owner answers; no execution step advances while held.
- **Step status machine (`CAP-07.1`)**: every plan step holds a status in the closed set `{ planned, awaiting-review, approved, rejected, running, done, failed, cancelled }`. Transitions follow the full deterministic table below; every transition absent from the table (including skipping review, reversing direction, or leaving terminal statuses `rejected`, `done`, `failed`, `cancelled`) is illegal and refused.

| From status | Allowed next statuses | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `planned` | `awaiting-review`, `cancelled` | Submitted for review or cancelled before review |
| `awaiting-review` | `approved`, `rejected`, `cancelled` | Review outcome recorded or cancelled while awaiting review |
| `approved` | `running`, `cancelled` | Execution begins after assembly gate and owner approval, or cancelled |
| `rejected` | (none, terminal) | Rejected step ends; revision opens a new proposal version |
| `running` | `done`, `failed`, `cancelled` | Step finishes, fails, or is cancelled |
| `done` | (none, terminal) | Completed step |
| `failed` | (none, terminal) | Failed step |
| `cancelled` | (none, terminal) | Cancelled step |

- **Review verdicts and assembly gate**: review verdicts remain `aestivation`'s responsibility (`approve`, or `revise` with mandatory reasons). `assemblyGate` stays closed on `plan-invalid`, `ledger-unsound` (any malformed verdict record or dangling plan reference), `awaiting-verdict`, `review-stale` (digest mismatch), and `revisions-requested`.
- **Owner plan approval separated from review (`CAP-07.2`, `CAP-06.1`)**: owner approval is a separate act. The owner accepts, edits, or rejects the plan; the decision is recorded as a `seed` owner-gate record (`CAP-06.1` at `M3`) bound to the plan's canonical SHA-256 `planDigest`. `aestivation` never ratifies on the owner's behalf, and memory records, model beliefs, or reviewer `approve` verdicts never count as owner approval. Editing the plan produces a new `planDigest` and invalidates prior verdicts or owner approvals.
- **Per-run revision cap (`CAP-07.2`)**: each run enforces an explicit per-run revision cap. Reaching the cap stops further revision rounds and holds the plan with a stated reason instead of looping without bound.

## Contract touchpoints

- `aestivation/docs/contracts/plan.md`: plan payload fields (`request`, `seats`, `knownFacts`, `steps` with seat role ID and `action`, `summary`, optional `clarifyingQuestion`), step status machine, and per-run revision cap (`CAP-07.1`, `CAP-07.2`).
- `aestivation/docs/contracts/verdict.md`: `approve` and `revise` verdict records with mandatory reasons on `revise` and append-only ledger soundness checks.
- `aestivation/docs/contracts/gate.md`: `assemblyGate` precedence (`plan-invalid`, `ledger-unsound`, `awaiting-verdict`, `review-stale`, `revisions-requested`) and non-ratification guarantee.
- `seed/docs/contracts/run-model.md`: `seed` owner-gate decision record binding to `planDigest` (`CAP-06.1` at `M3`).
- `bloom/docs/architecture.md`: loop wiring and emission of `plan.*` events (`CAP-07.4`).

## Tool IDs and events

### Tool IDs

No new tool IDs are introduced by `CAP-07`.

| Tool ID | Effect class | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

### Events

| Event | Emitted by | Payload summary |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `plan.proposed` | `bloom` | `planId`, `planDigest`, `request`, `seats` (role IDs), `steps`, `summary`, optional `clarifyingQuestion` |
| `plan.verdict` | `bloom` | `planId`, `planDigest`, `decision` (`approve` or `revise`), `judge` role ID, `reasons` |
| `plan.gate` | `bloom` | `planId`, `planDigest`, `permitted`, `held` reason (if held), ledger soundness status |
| `plan.decision` | `bloom` | `seed` owner-gate decision (`approve`, `edit`, `reject`, `respond`) bound to `planDigest` |

## Acceptance tests

- `step-status-legal-transitions`: every legal transition in the eight-status table succeeds and returns a frozen step record.
- `step-status-illegal-moves-refused`: every illegal move not listed in the transition table (across all 8 x 8 pairs plus unknown statuses, including `planned` to `running`, `planned` to `approved`, and any exit from terminal states `rejected`, `done`, `failed`, `cancelled`) is explicitly tested and refused.
- `clarifying-question-holds-plan`: a plan containing `clarifyingQuestion` holds execution until the owner answers.
- `unsound-ledger-closes-assembly-gate`: a malformed verdict or unknown plan reference causes `assemblyGate` to hold with `ledger-unsound` and `verdict: null`.
- `review-verdict-and-memory-never-ratify`: a reviewer `approve` verdict, model belief, or memory entry never counts as owner approval; execution remains blocked until a `seed` owner-gate record (`CAP-06.1`) bound to `planDigest` records owner acceptance or edit.
- `owner-edit-updates-plan-digest`: an owner edit yields a new `planDigest`, invalidating any earlier verdict or decision for the superseded digest.
- `revision-cap-holds-with-stated-reason`: reaching the per-run revision cap refuses further revision attempts and holds the plan with a stated reason.

## Slices

- `CAP-07.1` (`aestivation`, `M3`, `proposed`): Plan payload extensions, clarifying question hold, and step status machine.
- `CAP-07.2` (`aestivation`, `M3`, `proposed`): Revision cap and separation of review verdict from owner approval.
- `CAP-07.4` (`bloom`, `M3`, `proposed`): Plan review loop wiring and plan events (`plan.proposed`, `plan.verdict`, `plan.gate`, `plan.decision`).

## Non-goals

- Executing or scheduling plan steps inside `aestivation` (execution belongs to `bloom` and `seed`).
- Letting `aestivation`, a model reviewer, or memory ratify a plan on the owner's behalf.
- Defining seat instruction files or character personas (seats use closed role IDs only).
- Adding persistence or I/O inside `aestivation` (durable storage belongs to `CAP-13`).

## Family rules and conflicts

- Role IDs only: `seats` and step assignments use only `chair`, `framing`, `risk`, `coherence`, and `sequencing`, never persona names.
- Deterministic checks outrank reviewer judgment: `assemblyGate` rejects invalid plans and unsound ledgers regardless of any `approve` verdict.
- `aestivation` remains a zero-dependency pure reference library with no I/O, no model calls, and no peer imports.

## Open owner decisions

- **D14 (pending owner decision)**: Under the review sequencing convention, `CAP-06.1` (`seed` owner-gate record binding to `planDigest`) lands at `M3` with `CAP-07.3` folded into `CAP-06.1` (`CAP-07.4` preserved without renumbering), and `CAP-07` depends on `CAP-06.1` at `M3` ahead of `CAP-06.2` through `CAP-06.4` at `M4`.
- Per-run revision cap default and owner plan-gate threshold (pending owner decision, not yet numbered): confirm the default per-run revision cap and whether owner plan approval gates every multi-step plan or only plans exceeding declared effect thresholds.

## Evidence

- Status `planned`: Phase 0 specification created. Baseline plan validation, verdict ledger soundness, `assemblyGate`, read-only intent assessment, and bounded two-replan corrections are implemented and verified by `npm test` in `aestivation` (`0.5.0`); `CAP-07.1` and `CAP-07.2` extensions remain to be implemented.

## Changes

- `2026-11-23`: Initial Phase 0 specification (`CAP-01`).
- `2026-11-23`: Folded `CAP-07.3` into `CAP-06.1` and updated dependency to `CAP-06.1` (`D14`).
- `2026-11-23`: Removed `D12` attribution from the unnumbered revision-cap and owner plan-gate threshold open question and formatted capability IDs in Changes (`CAP-01.5`).

# Aestivation charter

## Mission

Build the loop that decides, before work opens, whether the work may open. Aestivation holds the contracts for planning: propose, validate deterministically, review with reasons, and hold assembly at a gate. The loop's judgments are recorded, its rules are plain, and nothing automatic assembles until the plan has passed both lanes.

The name is the doctrine. Aestivation is the arrangement of petals in the bud before it opens. Petals that never arrange do not open well; work that never gets planned does not assemble well. Everything here happens before the opening — and the opening itself is a gated, stated event.

## Principles

1. **Deterministic first, judgment second.** The rule pack runs on every plan, the same way every time. An invalid plan is held no matter who approved it. Rules and review are separate lanes; the gate composes them, and neither can substitute for the other.
2. **Verdicts carry their reasons.** A revise verdict always states what to change. An approve verdict may carry reasons too — an approval with no explanation is weaker than one with its basis on its face, but it is a valid verdict.
3. **The ledger is append-only.** A verdict is a record of a moment in review. It is never edited. Re-review after revision is a new verdict appended to the plan's history.
4. **Revise stops assembly.** When a plan's latest verdict is revise, the gate holds. Automatic assembly does not proceed on a maybe.
5. **The loop never ratifies for the owner.** A verdict records review; a gate opening permits assembly. Neither is the owner's assent. Effects that exceed the plan's scope — publishing, deploying, deleting, spending — are gated effects, and they route the owner's gate in the harness, not the reviewer's pen.
6. **Held states say why.** A gate that holds names the reason: plan-invalid, ledger-unsound, awaiting-verdict, review-stale, revisions-requested. "No" without a reason teaches nothing.

## Non-goals

- **Not a scheduler.** Aestivation does not run the steps. The harness runs work; this loop decides whether the arrangement admits it.
- **Not a judge of quality.** The rule pack checks shape and order. Reviewers judge content. Neither claims to measure whether the work is good, and the gate certifies neither.
- **Not an approval substitute.** The loop's outputs are records and a gate state. Ratification — the owner's act of accepting the outcome — happens outside this loop, always.

# Contract: the assembly gate

Label: `specified` (rules), `implemented` (in `src/gate.mjs`).

## Shape

```
assemblyGate({ validation, verdicts, planId, planDigest?, knownPlanIds? }) → { permitted, held, validation, ledger, verdict }
```

## The gate's one question

Is automatic assembly of this plan permitted? The answer is composed from the validation and the verdict ledger, in a fixed order:

| Order | Condition | Held reason |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | `validation.ok === false` | `plan-invalid` |
| 2 | the verdict ledger is unsound | `ledger-unsound` |
| 3 | no verdict exists for the plan | `awaiting-verdict` |
| 4 | a `planDigest` was given and the latest verdict names a different one, or none | `review-stale` |
| 5 | latest verdict is `revise` | `revisions-requested` |
| — | none of the above: valid plan, sound ledger, latest verdict `approve` (of this exact version, when a digest was given) | (permitted) |

The held reasons are closed and exported in this order as `HELD_REASONS`.

## Why the order is the order

1. **Deterministic outranks judgment.** An invalid plan is held even when a reviewer approved. The rule pack's rejection cannot be overruled by a pen, and this ordering is what makes that principle structural rather than aspirational.
2. **Judgment counts only from a ledger the gate can trust.** The gate checks the whole ledger with the verdict contract's soundness rules before it reads any verdict. One malformed record anywhere, such as an approval with no judge or a revise with no reason, makes the ledger unsound and holds the gate. When `knownPlanIds` is given, a verdict naming an unknown plan, or a gated `planId` that is not itself known, is also unsound. Without `knownPlanIds` the gate checks record well-formedness only.
3. **Unreviewed never self-assembles.** A valid plan with no verdict waits. Silence is not approval and absence is not consent.
4. **A review covers the version it read.** Given the plan's `planDigest`, the gate holds as `review-stale` when the latest verdict for the plan names a different digest or none. A step added, removed, or retitled after review changes the digest, so the old approval no longer opens the gate. The latest verdict still counts: a later review of another version leaves this version stale rather than reaching back to an older approval. Without `planDigest` the gate does not check versions and answers as before.
5. **Revise is a stop, not a pause of opinion.** The latest revise verdict holds assembly until a new proposal earns a new verdict. The title of the held reason names the path out: the revisions were requested, so make them.

## Output semantics

- `permitted: true` means the two lanes passed over a sound ledger: valid, approved. Nothing more.
- `permitted: false` always carries a `held` reason from the table above. There is no naked refusal.
- The gate returns the validation, the ledger soundness result (`{ ok, errors }`), and the latest verdict alongside its answer, so a caller never re-derives what the gate already judged.
- When the ledger is unsound, `verdict` is `null`: a verdict from an untrusted ledger is never surfaced as the answer.

## Prohibitions

- The gate never ratifies. Permission to assemble is not owner assent; effects exceeding the plan's scope route the owner's gate in the harness.
- The gate never judges content. If the rule pack and the reviewers both passed it, the gate opens whether or not a third party would have preferred different work.
- The gate never mutates its inputs. It composes; it does not rewrite the ledger or re-validate with different rules.

## Changes

- `0.2.0` — the gate checks ledger soundness, adding held reason `ledger-unsound` (order 2), the optional `knownPlanIds` input, the `ledger` output, and `HELD_REASONS`. Before `0.2.0` the verdict contract said an unsound ledger is refused by the gate, but the gate read verdicts unchecked, so a hand-built approval with no judge could permit assembly. Gate answers over ledgers built with `verdictRecord` are unchanged. A caller that matches on `held` values should handle the new reason.
- `0.3.0` — the optional `planDigest` input and held reason `review-stale` (order 4). A malformed `planDigest` is refused with an error. Without `planDigest`, answers are unchanged. A caller that matches on `held` values should handle the new reason.

# Contract: plan

Label: `specified` (shape), `implemented` (rule pack in `src/plan.mjs`).

## Shape

```
proposal { id, objective, steps[], digest }
step     { stage, title }
stage    one of: research, work, review, assemble, verify
```

## The closed set of stages

| Stage | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `research` | Gathering evidence and reading context. |
| `work` | Making changes, producing artifacts. |
| `review` | Judgment on the proposal's outputs, recorded as verdicts. |
| `assemble` | Automatic assembly of the plan's outputs. |
| `verify` | Deterministic verification of the assembled result. |

## Baseline rule pack

1. **Non-empty.** A plan with zero steps is not a plan.
2. **Known stages.** A step naming an unknown stage is rejected, not guessed.
3. **Titled.** A step without a title is rejected.
4. **Review precedes assemble.** When both are present, the first `review` step comes before the first `assemble` step. Assembly without review before it is the failure mode this loop exists to prevent.
5. **Verify is final.** When a `verify` step is present, it is the last step. Deterministic verification comes after assembly, before anything opens.

All five are shape and order rules. None of them judges content.

## Validation output

```
{ ok: boolean, errors: string[] }   — errors carries every violated rule, not the first
```

A validation result is data. The gate consumes it; a caller may not string-match a validation's prose, because prose changes and rules stay.

## The plan digest

`implemented` in `src/plan.mjs`. `planDigest(proposal)` is the SHA-256, in 64 lowercase hex, of the proposal's content as canonical JSON: `{ id, objective, steps }`, every step with all of its fields, object keys sorted, undefined members dropped, no whitespace. `planProposal` stores it as `digest`. Key order does not change the digest; any change to the id, the objective, a step's fields, or the step list does. A verdict names this digest to say which version of the plan it reviewed (see the verdict contract), and that is how "the proposal reviewed is the proposal assembled" is checked.

## Intent assessment

`implemented` in `src/intent.mjs`. An intent assessment is advice about a request:
`{ label, needs, confidence, authority: 'advisory', evidencePolicy }`, frozen. `needs` lists evidence
needs from `project-knowledge`, `live-state`, `durable-memory`, and `none`.

1. **It grants nothing.** An input carrying `tools`, `allowedTools`, `memoryWrites`,
   `grants`, `scopes`, or `actions` is refused.
2. **It is read-only.** `admitWithIntent(admission, assessment)` returns the admission's
   `allowedTools` and `memoryWrites`, copied and frozen, unchanged. The input is not
   mutated. A `durable-memory` need sets `memoryRecallAdvised`: advice to read, never a
   write.
3. **Only a real record composes.** A look-alike object, or a copy of a record, is
   refused, so a forged assessment cannot add a tool.
4. **Missing evidence is named.** `evidencePolicy.missingSource` is `state-unavailable`.
   The caller can supply `availableSources` with evidence types it verified. Composition
   returns a frozen `evidence` record with `missingSources` and a `statement` naming
   each gap. The statement is `null` when all required evidence is available.
5. **Personal recall uses admitted memory.** `evidencePolicy.personalRecall` is
   `admitted-memory-only`. A `durable-memory` need is met only by nonempty
   `admission.admittedMemory`, a list of references already admitted by the caller.
   The evidence record copies those references for a recall need. Conversation history,
   an assessment's input fields and the generic source list cannot satisfy that need.

## Corrections

`implemented` in `src/correction.mjs`. `correctPlan({ previous, verdict, author,
objective?, steps? })` answers a revise verdict:

1. The verdict must be a `revise` of `previous.id` at `previous.digest`. An approval is
   refused with `correction-not-needed`; a review of another version, or of no named
   version, with `review-mismatch`.
2. The previous proposal is not edited. The correction is a new frozen proposal with the
   same id and a new digest, and a record `{ planId, previousDigest, digest, reviewedBy,
   author, reasons }`. A correction that leaves the digest unchanged is refused with
   `correction-unchanged`.
3. The judge who asked for the revision cannot apply it: an `author` equal to the
   verdict's judge, or no author, is refused with `reviewer-cannot-apply`.
4. An approval of the previous digest does not open the gate for the correction. The
   gate holds it as `review-stale` until the new digest is reviewed.
5. Each parent proposal can spend two successful replans in its in-process lineage.
   `correctPlan` retires the old digest when it returns the next proposal. A correction
   from a retired proposal or back to a retired digest is refused with `order-superseded`.
   The third replan is refused with `replan-exhausted`. Refusals spend no replan.
6. Before consuming a result, call `assertCurrentPlanResult(proposal, { planId,
   planDigest })` with the proposal instance held by the run. The check refuses retired
   digests with `order-superseded` and other mismatches with `result-mismatch`. Retain
   the returned proposal for the next review or result check. A reconstructed proposal
   starts a separate in-memory lineage.
7. The caller declares expansion with `scopeExpanding`, `expandWorkspace`,
   `expandPaths`, or `newCriterionGrant`. Both flags default to `false` and both
   scope values default to `null`. A true flag or a non-null scope value throws
   `ScopeExpansionError` with code `authority-required` before any change to the
   lineage or budget. The previous proposal remains current.

## Prohibitions

- No silent step injection. The proposal reviewed is the proposal assembled; steps appearing after review are a new proposal.
- No stage migration inside a plan object. A plan is frozen on creation.
- No rule pack may approve on a reviewer's behalf, and no reviewer verdict may waive a rule.

## Changes

- `0.5.0` — `correctPlan` accepts optional scope fields and refuses requested
  expansion. `ScopeExpansionError` extends `CorrectionError`. Calls within the
  existing scope keep the original correction contract.

- `0.4.0` — intent assessments and corrections are new. Additive: no existing export
  changed.

- `0.3.0` — `planDigest` and the proposal's `digest` field are new. Additive: validation and proposal construction are otherwise unchanged.

# Contract: verdict

Label: `specified` (rules), `implemented` (ledger in `src/verdict.mjs`).

## Shape

```
verdict { planId, planDigest, decision, judge, reasons[] }
decision  one of: approve, revise
```

## Rules

1. **A verdict names its plan.** `planId` is required and must reference a known proposal. The ledger's soundness check rejects dangling references.
2. **A verdict may name the version it reviewed.** `planDigest` is the 64-hex `planDigest` of the proposal the judge read, or `null` when not given. A malformed digest makes the record invalid. When the gate is given a plan digest, a verdict counts only for the version it names (see the gate contract).
3. **A verdict names its judge.** A review without a reviewer is not a review. `judge` is a non-empty string; who judges is the ledger's provenance.
4. **Revise carries reasons.** A `revise` decision without at least one reason is rejected. A reviewer who wants changes says what changes.
5. **Approve may carry reasons.** An approval is valid with an empty reasons list, though an approval that states its basis is the better record.
6. **The ledger is append-only.** Verdicts are frozen on creation. Correction happens by appending, never by editing history.
7. **The latest verdict counts.** A plan may be reviewed many times across revisions; the verdict in force is the last one recorded for it.

## Ledger soundness

```
isSoundVerdictLedger(verdicts, knownPlanIds) → { ok, errors[] }
```

A ledger is sound when it is a list, every verdict is a well-formed record by rules 1 through 4 (the same checks `verdictRecord` applies), and every `planId` references a known plan. Errors carry the verdict's index. An unsound ledger is refused by the gate with held reason `ledger-unsound` — the gate does not grade verdicts it cannot trust.

`implemented` in `src/verdict.mjs` and `src/gate.mjs` as of `0.2.0`; before it, soundness checked only plan references and the gate did not check it at all.

## Changes

- `0.3.0` — the optional `planDigest` field; every verdict record now carries it (`null` when not given). Additive: verdicts without it are well-formed as before.

## Prohibitions

- No verdict speaks for the owner. A verdict records review; ratification is a separate act by a separate authority, always outside this loop.
- No backdating. The ledger records in order; the order is the record.
- No editing verdicts into approval. The path from revise to permitted is a new plan and a new verdict, on the record.

# Aestivation interop

How aestivation meets the family. Every behavior attributed to a peer below is sourced from that peer's published repository at the time of writing; where a peer has not shipped the behavior, it is not claimed.

## bloom: the proved shape

Bloom describes the plan-and-review loop as the interplay of its planner, validators, and review specialists:

> The head proposes an ordered plan... A deterministic rule validates the response and the stage order. A reviewer records approve or revise. A revision verdict stops automatic assembly... A review verdict of "revise" pauses assembly... address the author with the requested changes and attach the review when continuing.

Mapping onto aestivation's contracts:

| Bloom behavior | Aestivation contract |
| :--- | :--- |
| The head proposes an ordered plan | `planProposal`: objective plus frozen, ordered steps. |
| A deterministic rule validates response and stage order | The rule pack: `validatePlan` with the baseline five rules. |
| A reviewer records approve or revise | `verdictRecord`: decision from `{approve, revise}`, judge, reasons. |
| A revision verdict stops automatic assembly | `assemblyGate` held reason `revisions-requested`. |
| Review "revise" pauses, author re-proposes with changes attached | Append-only ledger: the revise verdict stays; the revised plan is a new proposal; the latest verdict counts. |
| "Review approved" / "Changes requested" strings | `decision: 'approve'` / `decision: 'revise'` as data, not prose. |

The one deliberate difference: bloom's review specialists emit strings into a message stream; aestivation holds the same loop as typed records a harness can compose deterministically.

## seed: carrying the effects

Aestivation has no tool domain of its own on seed's registry. It is not a connector; it is the loop code the harness runs. Three integrations, all in-process:

1. **Plan validation is a deterministic check.** In bloom the rule is stated as a validator the harness runs without model agency; on seed's run model the same rule runs as verification code the harness executes — the plan enters a `verify`-class checkpoint as data, and the rule pack's output is read as data.
2. **Verdict recording is work product.** A review specialist's judgment lands in the ledger through ordinary harness messages; the verdict record is constructed from the decision, the judge, and the reasons, and it is `data`, not an effect.
3. **Gated effects route the owner gate.** When assembly, publishing, or any scope-exceeding effect follows from a permitted gate, that effect is a gated effect on the harness, with the owner's assent required — permission to assemble is the loop's verdict, ratification is the owner's act, and the loop never confuses the two.

Nothing in this section requires myosotis: verdicts and plans are loop records, not memory. If a harness chooses to remember a review, that act crosses into myosotis under its own contracts.

## capillary: evidence into review

Review reads evidence. When a reviewer's reasons cite material, the retrieval of that material is capillary's province — packets with provenance, budgets, and bounded reads. Aestivation consumes none of it directly; the harness hands the reviewer what capillary retrieved, and the verdict records what the reviewer said. The boundary stays clean: capillary proves where evidence came from, aestivation records what was judged and gates what follows.

## Family

The family law and the full table live in the [capillary repository's family doc](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary/blob/main/docs/family.md). Short form: seed for the harness foundation, capillary for retrieval, myosotis for memory, aestivation for admission and review, bloom for the harness. Names are ordinary botanical words; provinces stay distinct.

docsPages.body: Workspace, CLI, and terminal UI # Bloom Give a head agent a brief and watch a team work through it in one group conversation. Specialists can research public sources, review the findings, and assemble a Markdown guide. Each contribution is a file on a shared desktop that you can open, attach to another task, or download. [Download the latest release](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom/releases/latest) · [View the phone layout](docs/previews/phone.png) ![Bloom’s scripted research team sharing its findings, review and guide in one workspace](docs/previews/workspace.png) ## Try it Download `bloom-VERSION.zip` from the [latest release](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom/releases/latest) and extract it, or clone this repository. Install Node.js 22.13 or newer and run this command from the project folder in a terminal on macOS, Linux, or Windows. The release ZIP already holds Bloom's one runtime dependency, seed; in a clone, run `npm install` first. ```sh npm run demo ``` Open the local address the demo prints, choose **Create a team** and give the head agent a name. Use **Add file** to paste some project notes, select **Try a sample task**, and send it. Open the assembler’s file in the group chat. The demo is scripted and requires no key. Its outputs and usage display identify it as a demonstration. Run `node bin/bloom.mjs eval --smoke` to check the built-in coding fixture offline and print its deterministic report. ## Connect a model endpoint Teams and coding sessions run on any service that speaks the chat-completions HTTP API (`POST {base}/chat/completions`). Bloom names no default service. The endpoint lives only in the private `config.json` in Bloom's data directory, described under **Terminal commands** below, and neither the web workspace nor the terminal takes it on the command line. ```sh npm start -- --workspace '' ``` The web workspace follows the terminal's rules: local providers only, the configured key setting, and the model profile saved by `bloom doctor --probe`. Team calls send the brief and admitted evidence to that endpoint. Without a provider, Bloom still opens the workspace, notes and files, and a team turn stops with a message pointing at `config.json`. Every provider runs behind [seed](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed)'s provider seam: Bloom checks the adapter when it starts and checks every reply against seed's record before the team reads it. A reply outside that record stops the turn. **Coding sessions** run the coding loop in the chosen folder when a provider is configured. The browser shows streamed text, a row for every model call and tool call, and an approval card before every write and every command. The scripted demo runtime shows the same view without a model. [docs/live-test.md](docs/live-test.md) is the runbook for a first live run in a throwaway sandbox. ## Terminal commands **Implemented.** After `npm install`, run `npm link` to install the `bloom` command from this checkout. Try the scripted runtime with `bloom chat --demo`, or run it once with `bloom run --headless --demo --json "Inspect the project"`. Headless runs reject requests by default. Use `--approve-policy allow-read` to allow read requests. A configured local model can run the existing team loop. In the terminal data directory, use a private `config.json` with `version: 1`, one entry under `providers` with `kind: "chat-completions"` and `baseURL` set to your OpenAI-compatible API base, and `models.aliases` containing an alias, backend model ID and workload. Set `models.default` to that alias or choose one with `--model`. Loopback is local by default. For a server on your private network, set `locality` to `local`. Enable `allowInsecureHttp` only if that server uses plain HTTP. Set `apiKeyEnv` to the name of an environment variable if the server requires a key. The team loop uses the desktop and saved specialists. `--team NAME --workspace PATH` records a team session's workspace. **Implemented:** `bloom chat --workspace PATH` without `--team` runs the coding loop in that folder: the model reads, searches, edits and runs `node`, `npm` or `git` there, and Bloom asks before every write and every command. A headless `bloom run --workspace PATH` never writes. Read the command gate and its residual risk in [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) before pointing it at a folder you care about. Terminal cloud providers need `--allow-cloud` inside a sandbox from `scripts/make-sandbox.mjs`; the web workspace stays local only. `bloom doctor` checks the local installation and endpoint rule without displaying the address. `bloom doctor --probe` also asks the configured provider what it supports, saves its model profile, and names the provider only by its config name and locality. Cloud providers need `--allow-cloud` on probe and chat. `bloom sessions list` lists session IDs. `bloom sessions export ID --jsonl` writes the stored events in order, and `bloom replay FILE --step` displays them one at a time. Use `--data-dir` to select the data directory, including when you read a demo session. `bloom memory --help` lists note commands. Forget requires `--confirm`. ## Work with a team - **Assign work.** Set the head agent’s **Jurisdiction** and describe the deliverable. Add a specialist under **Personas** before starting a new team with a configured model. The head assigns work to saved personas and team members. The scripted demo includes three example specialists. Select a recipient or type `@Reviewer: check the latest draft` for a direct assignment in the group. A review verdict of “revise” pauses assembly. Address the author with the requested changes and attach the review when continuing. - **Reuse specialists.** Use **Save as persona** on a roster member, or **+ New** under **Personas** in the left sidebar, to keep a specialist's name, **Jurisdiction**, voice, stage and optional model. Every head agent sees the library when it plans and can recruit a persona by name; the saved fields are used as they are, and the head only writes the assignment. **Add to team** puts a persona on the open team's roster for a direct `@Name:` message. Editing or deleting a persona leaves teams that already recruited it unchanged. - **Share evidence.** Paste up to three public HTTPS URLs in a brief or use **Add file** on the **Shared desktop** for a web page, GitHub repository README, or text. Bloom records the source and its digest. The head can select files from the shared catalog. The source reader retrieves public text over IPv4 and records excerpts. Specialists receive bounded excerpts and see which sources were shortened. - **Inspect a handoff.** Open a file in the conversation or inspector. Its detail includes the author, SHA-256, and input-file relationships. Each revision is a separate Markdown file. For an edit made in another application, import the changed text as a new source. - **Manage memory.** Use **Add note** under **Notes** to tell the team what to remember. Leave **Always use** checked for standing instructions, or turn it off for background facts that should reach a specialist only when they match the task. **Share with every team** makes a note available to all teams on this computer. Specialists can suggest facts to keep; they appear under **Suggested by agents** and are never used until you **Keep** them. **Activity** lists exactly which notes each specialist received. **Correct** replaces a note. **Forget** removes it. Either one invalidates cached recall, stops an active run, and withholds earlier outputs built from that note from future team prompts. Previous messages, exported files, provider logs and copies on the local disk have separate lifetimes. - **Ask another team.** When another team's **Jurisdiction** covers part of a brief, the head agent can ask it one question per task. Both conversations show the question and the answer. The other team answers from its jurisdiction, notes shared with every team, and its non-private posts and files, never its private notes. The asking team pays for the call. A busy team is skipped. **Stop** in the other team ends only the answer. - **Control usage.** Under **Model and limits**, the team form accepts a per-run **Model calls** limit and an optional **Token limit**. Bloom checks the token limit between calls. One call can cross it. Missing metering stops further calls when a token limit is active. Expand **Usage** under **Activity** for per-agent usage, provider-reported cache reads and writes, and cost when supplied. Local recall hits and provider token caching have separate counters. Model outputs and tool effects are never replayed as cache hits. - **Use the desktop.** One persistent `Desktop/` folder belongs to the local installation. Teams share ordinary files. Check a file and ask the team to change it: a specialist can revise it, rename it or file it into a folder. Each change is a new version, marked `v2`, `v3` and so on, and **Open** lists the other revisions. Team-note-derived files have room-scoped access through the harness. For a graphical Linux desktop over that same folder, install Docker with Compose, run `npm run desktop -- --demo` alongside the demo, and open the local address the command prints. For real profiles omit `--demo`. Stop it with `npm run desktop -- --demo --down`. Docker first downloads the desktop image. The desktop provides a persistent graphical environment for the operator. Team agents interact with its files through Bloom. [Webtop](https://docs.linuxserver.io/images/docker-webtop/) ## Storage and extension points Bloom serves the browser on loopback and stores SQLite history and desktop files under `~/.bloom` (`~/.bloom/demo` for the demo). Pass `--data-dir PATH` to select a different folder and pass the same argument to the optional desktop command. Existing ViBloom data directories are detected. Use one server per data directory. A running local account can access its files. Closing the browser leaves the local server working. Stopping the server interrupts active work. Agents start at [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). Stay in this repository's province. [Architecture and design sources](docs/architecture.md) explains the VI, OAI and LA roles, the portable memory implementation, design-token synchronization, and verification boundaries. ```sh npm test npm run test:network ``` ## License Bloom is available under the [MIT license](LICENSE). The bundled Geist fonts retain the [SIL Open Font License](public/fonts/Geist-OFL.txt). The Vidoxlabs name and mark are trademarks of Vidoxlabs LLC. They are not covered by this repository's MIT license.
