# Vivarium design brief

Living document. Edit by PR; record changes in docs-timeline.md.

- Status: living document, second edition (owner decisions of 25 November 2026 folded in)
- Date: 25 November 2026
- Scope: the Vivarium umbrella over seven public systems: `seed`, `bloom`, `capillary`, `myosotis`, `drosera`, `aestivation`, and `trellis`
- Audience: the owner, contributors, and the code agents that build Vivarium

Market figures and vendor policies below were read on 25 November 2026 from the sources in section 9. They move month to month. Re-check them before quoting them anywhere public.

### Owner decisions in this edition (25 November 2026)

1. **One setup path for everyone.** There is no private overlay. Vidoxlabs' own internal agents are created in the app through the same first-run setup and editors any user goes through, so the team uses the product exactly as users do (section 2.5).
2. **Model access at launch:** the person's existing subscriptions where the provider officially supports sign-in from other apps, their own API keys, and local or on-device models. No hosted plan and no broker at launch; hosted credits are "later, maybe" (section 3.4).
3. **Platforms:** desktop app and a cloud-hosted web app first; mobile later. The web app reaches device context through an optional paired companion and other opt-in routes (section 5.5).
4. **No default autonomy level.** A scripted first-run setup has the person choose autonomy and simple or advanced workflows, and shows where to change both later (section 2.4a).
5. **Vivarium is the public product name.** `bloom` is Vivarium's user-interface system, not the product (section 1).
6. **`docs` is not pinned by the umbrella.** It is product-neutral, may serve future products, and already syncs every system's documentation; Vivarium links to it and does not duplicate it (section 8).

---

## 1. What Vivarium is

Vivarium is the public product name and the umbrella for one product idea: **a personal agent platform where people raise personified assistants that remember them, learn their work, and act with them and for them.** The seven systems are the organs of that platform:

| System | Role in Vivarium | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `seed` | Harness floor: run records, tool identity, provider adapters, the contracts everything else speaks | "What is a run, a tool, a provider, a budget?" |
| `bloom` | User interface: the desktop and web app a person opens, the first-run setup, the head agent, the workspace the agent and person share | "Where do I set up my agents, talk to them, and watch them work?" |
| `capillary` | Context: bounded retrieval with sources attached, and the relations between things | "What does the agent need to know right now, and where did it come from?" |
| `myosotis` | Memory: consent to keep, structural forget | "What does the agent remember about me and itself, and who allowed it?" |
| `drosera` | Tools: tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks | "What can the agent do, and how does it find the right tool?" |
| `aestivation` | Review and delegation: plans, verdicts, questions to the person, the assembly gate | "Should this step run, who does it, and what do we ask the person first?" |
| `trellis` | Testing from outside the call path: shape, behavior, consistency, operational probes | "Does it actually work, and did it stay working?" |

The umbrella repository pins all seven by commit, so a person or a code agent sees one coherent snapshot of the platform instead of seven moving targets.

**Naming.** People use *Vivarium*; *bloom* is the part of Vivarium they see and touch. Write "Vivarium" for the product and "bloom" only for the interface system. The other six systems are likewise parts of Vivarium, never products of their own in user-facing copy.

### Positioning statement (scope of work)

> **Vivarium gives you agents that work with you and for you.** You create a few personified assistants, each with its own character and job. They keep a memory of you that you control, use the apps and accounts you already have, and handle the work you hand them: code and tools, documents and research, and the everyday errands and conversations in between. You decide how much they do on their own.

What this statement commits to:

1. **Personal before general.** The value is an assistant that knows you and your workflows, not a smarter chatbot. Memory (`myosotis`) and context (`capillary`) are the moat.
2. **Works with what you have.** Your devices, apps, logins, and model subscriptions. Not twenty new integrations.
3. **You set the leash.** Autonomy is a setting, not a surprise.

What it does not commit to: being the best coding agent, the best document analyzer, or the best companion app on day one. Vivarium wins by being the place those jobs meet the same memory and the same assistants.

---

## 2. Focus area 1: agent creation and delegation

### 2.1 The problem

- People differ. Some want to approve every step and edit every workflow. Others want something that just works and never asks a question they cannot answer.
- Vidoxlabs runs its own internal agents on the same architecture. People should be able to see that the product the company uses is the product they get, with no hidden layer. At the same time, the company's own agent names, notes, and goals are personal data and do not belong in public repositories.

### 2.2 Options

| Option | How it works | Tradeoffs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A. Fixed presets | Ship three or four ready-made assistants; users pick one | Dead simple; no real personalization; weak long-term retention |
| B. Full builder only | Users define personas, tools, triggers, and policies from scratch | Maximum control; most people never finish setup |
| C. One agent model, two editors | Every agent is the same data object (persona, memory scope, tool grants, autonomy level, workflows). A simple editor creates it by conversation; an advanced editor exposes every field | One code path; users can graduate from simple to advanced without migrating; needs careful defaults |

### 2.3 Autonomy levels

Autonomy is a deliberate design choice, separate from model capability and tool access. Research on agent autonomy levels describes a ladder from the person as operator, through collaborator, consultant, and approver, to observer ([Feng, McDonald, and Zhang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12469)). Vivarium adopts a five-step version in its own terms and pairs it with **action classes**, so a level never means "anything goes":

| Level | Name in the product | The agent... | Often suits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Ask me first | proposes every step; the person runs or approves each one | people trying a new agent or a new kind of task |
| 2 | Work alongside | plans with the person, does reversible steps, hands back on anything else | advanced users who like control |
| 3 | Check in | leads the work, asks only when a preference or a fact is missing | people who want progress with occasional questions |
| 4 | Handle it | acts on its own except blockers, credentials, spending, and consequential actions | trusted, well-tested workflows |
| 5 | Run in the background | acts on its own within budgets and standing rules; the person reads the journal and can stop it at any time | scheduled, well-tested routines |

| Action class | Examples | Level 1-2 | Level 3 | Level 4 | Level 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Read | read a file, search, summarize | ask / auto | auto | auto | auto |
| Reversible write | draft, branch, local edit with undo | ask | auto | auto | auto |
| External or irreversible | send, post, submit, delete, merge, deploy | ask | ask | ask | standing rule only |
| Spend | purchase, paid API beyond budget | ask | ask | ask | within a set budget only |
| Credential | sign in, share a secret, grant access | ask | ask | ask | ask |

A **standing rule** is a written permission for one exact action and scope ("send the Friday status email to this list"), created by the person, visible in settings, and revocable. Credentials always ask.

**There is no default level.** Vivarium never preselects one. The person chooses during first-run setup (section 2.4a) and can change it at any time, for all agents or per agent.

### 2.4 Simple and advanced workflows

- **One representation.** A workflow is a plan graph that `aestivation` already knows how to validate: trigger, steps, tool grants, checks, and the questions to ask the person.
- **Simple editor.** The person describes the job in words ("every Monday, read my inbox for invoices and put them in a sheet"). The agent drafts the plan, shows it as a short checklist, runs it once while the person watches, and saves it.
- **Advanced editor.** The same plan as an editable graph or text file, with triggers, budgets, per-step autonomy overrides, and `trellis` tests attached.
- **Graduation.** Any simple workflow opens in the advanced editor; nothing is converted or lost.

### 2.4a First-run setup (scripted, on first app start)

Why: people rarely look for a setting they do not know exists. If an agent stops to ask a question the person never chose, they conclude the app is broken. If they chose "ask me first" themselves and the question says so, they know it is a setting and where to change it. Setup makes every behavior that shapes the experience a choice the person made.

The script, in order (each screen has a plain-language explanation, an example, and "you can change this later in Settings"):

| Step | The person chooses | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Welcome | nothing | What Vivarium is in two sentences; how long setup takes; that every answer can be changed later |
| 2. Model access | one or more routes: an existing subscription (official sign-in programs only), an API key, or a local model | Shows who bills them for each route (their provider, never Vidoxlabs). A route is needed before an agent can run; setup can continue without one and says what will not work yet |
| 3. Workflow style | Simple or Advanced | Simple: describe jobs in words, see a checklist. Advanced: the full plan editor. Switchable any time; nothing is lost (2.4) |
| 4. Autonomy | a level from 1 to 5, with **no option preselected** | Each level shows the action-class row it implies and one worked example ("you ask for a weekly report: at this level the agent..."). Credentials always ask at every level, and the screen says so |
| 5. Questions | where questions arrive (in-app inbox, notifications, batched digest) and quiet hours | Sets expectations for how often the person will be asked, given step 4 |
| 6. Context access | optional sources: the companion app, a browser extension, account connectors, file upload | Each is off until chosen; each shows what it can and cannot read (5.5) |
| 7. First agent | start from a template or from a blank agent; name, character, job | Simple style creates it by conversation; Advanced shows every field |
| 8. Summary | confirm | One screen restating every choice, with the exact place to change each: Settings, then Autonomy (global) and Agent, then Autonomy (per agent) |

Rules that keep setup honest:
- Setup answers are stored as the agent definition and the autonomy policy record (`seed` contracts), not as UI state, so every system reads the same choice.
- Every question an agent asks because of the chosen level carries a short line: "You set this agent to *Check in*. Change" linking to the setting.
- Setup can be re-run from Settings at any time; re-running never deletes agents or memory.
- `trellis` tests that no autonomy option is preselected, that every question card links to its setting, and that the summary matches what was stored.

### 2.5 Internal agents use the same setup as everyone

The rule: **there is no private layer.** Vidoxlabs' internal agents are ordinary user-created agents. The owner creates them in the app, through the same first-run setup, editors, templates, and settings any user has, and the team uses the product the way users do.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Public["Public (Vidoxlabs org, MIT)"]
    V["vivarium (umbrella, pins seven systems)"]
    S["seven systems"]
    T["generic agent-setup templates"]
    V --> S
    V --> T
  end
  subgraph Person["Each person's own user data (any user, including Vidoxlabs)"]
    A["their agents: names, characters, jobs"]
    C["their setup answers: autonomy, workflow style, model routes"]
    M["their memory and connections"]
  end
  T -- "first-run setup and editors" --> A
  S -- "runs" --> A
```

- **Public core.** `vivarium` and the seven systems ship the app, the setup script, and **generic** agent templates (for example a planner, a builder, a researcher). They never ship anyone's personal agents.
- **Personal agents stay personal.** Agents a person creates, including Vidoxlabs' own, live in that person's local user data (or their own encrypted account data in the web app), never in a repository.
- **Same path, same fixes.** If an internal agent needs something the setup or editors cannot express, that is a missing feature for every user and is built in public. There is no private patch, fork, or overlay.
- **Guards.** Public CI rejects forbidden strings (stored as hashes, so the list itself reveals nothing) and operational detail, so personal names and private details never land in public files.
- **Dogfooding.** The owner configures the team through the same steps a new user takes, so friction the owner feels is friction users feel, and it gets fixed for both.

### 2.6 Recommendation

Option C, with no default autonomy level (the person chooses in first-run setup, 2.4a), the action-class table as the policy contract, and internal agents created through the same setup as every user's (2.5).

| Piece | Owner system |
| --- | --- |
| Agent definition, setup answers, and autonomy policy record (contract) | `seed` |
| Plan graph, per-step admission, questions to the person, delegation to specialist agents | `aestivation` |
| First-run setup, agent creator, simple and advanced editors, autonomy setting, questions inbox | `bloom` |
| Per-agent memory scope and consent | `myosotis` |
| Tool grants per agent | `drosera` |
| Autonomy-policy conformance tests (an agent at level N never takes a class it may not) | `trellis` |

---

## 3. Focus area 2: affordable model access

### 3.1 The problem

Agents burn tokens. People who cannot run models locally and do not want another subscription or an API bill will not adopt a product whose every task costs money they did not plan for. Many target users already pay for a chat or coding subscription and expect to reuse it.

### 3.2 What the market allows today

| Route | Status on 25 Nov 2026 | Tradeoffs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bring your own API key (any provider) | Universally allowed; usage billed to the key owner | Cheapest for Vidoxlabs; friction for non-technical users; surprise bills without budgets |
| Bring your own ChatGPT plan | OpenAI's "Sign in with ChatGPT" lets Go, Plus, Pro, and Business users spend their plan allowance in participating apps. Terms require requests to come from the user's own local runtime or a runtime only they control, tokens stored locally, no charge to use the plan, and plan use only inside the connected app ([terms](https://openai.com/policies/sign-in-with-chatgpt-terms/), [help](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001542-using-your-chatgpt-plan-in-other-apps-and-sites)) | Zero extra cost for many users; tied to one vendor's program, participation rules, and plan limits. Because the terms require the user's own local runtime, Vivarium's web app uses this route only through the user's desktop app or paired companion (5.5), never from Vidoxlabs servers |
| Bring your own Claude plan | Not permitted: Anthropic reserves consumer-plan OAuth for its own apps and forbids third parties from routing requests through Free, Pro, Max, or Ultra credentials ([legal and compliance](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance)). An unmodified Claude Code binary signed in by the user is allowed | Use API keys or cloud-provider credentials for Claude; or drive the user's own unmodified Claude Code install as a tool |
| Free tiers | Gemini API free tier around 20 requests per day per project on Flash models; OpenRouter free variants around 50 requests per day (1,000 after a credit purchase) ([Gemini limits](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits), [OpenRouter limits](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/limits)) | Fine for a trial and for triage; far too small for real agent work |
| On-device models | Apple's Foundation Models framework gives free, offline inference on Apple Intelligence devices; Android's ML Kit Prompt API runs Gemini Nano locally on supported phones ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/foundation-models-framework/), [Android](https://developer.android.com/blog/posts/build-intelligent-android-apps-on-device-inference)) | Free and private; small models; good for routing, summarizing, classifying, and drafting, not for long agent runs |
| Local desktop models | Local model runtimes on a capable PC or Mac | Free per token; hardware-bound; quality gap on long tool-using runs |
| Vidoxlabs-hosted credits or a broker | Vidoxlabs buys tokens and resells metered usage, or routes through a third-party broker | Simplest for users, but asks people to trust a new company with their prompts and their spend before it has earned that trust; margin and abuse risk sit with Vidoxlabs. Not at launch |

### 3.3 Cost levers that work regardless of route

| Lever | Evidence | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Model ladder and routing**: a small or on-device model triages and handles easy steps; a frontier model only for hard steps | Published router evaluations report roughly 40-70% cost savings at 97-98% of strong-model quality, and a 2026 hybrid router reports 54% savings within 0.3 points of the strong baseline. Savings depend on traffic mix, and misrouted hard prompts hurt quality ([HyDRA](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.17106), [TrueFoundry benchmark](https://www.truefoundry.com/blog/engineering/llm-cost-routing-benchmark/)) | `seed` provider adapters and budget record; `aestivation` decides per step |
| **Prompt caching**: stable system prompt, persona, and tool index first, volatile content last | Cached input is billed at about one tenth of fresh input on current OpenAI list prices ([OpenAI pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing)) | `seed` request shape; `capillary` packet ordering |
| **Batch for background work** | Batch processing is listed at half the standard price ([OpenAI pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing?pricing=batch)) | `aestivation` marks steps that can wait |
| **Context discipline**: bounded packets, summaries, references instead of copies | Fewer input tokens on every turn | `capillary`, `myosotis` |
| **Tool search instead of tool dumps** | Loading tools on demand cut one reported setup from about 77K to 8.7K context tokens while raising tool-selection accuracy ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/advanced-tool-use), [MCP client guidance](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2025-11-25/develop/clients/client-best-practices)) | `drosera` |
| **Budgets with hard caps** | Prevents surprise bills and runaway loops | `seed` budget record; `bloom` shows spend live |

### 3.4 Recommendation

1. **Launch provider-neutral, with three routes the person already controls:** an existing subscription through an official sign-in program (today, "Sign in with ChatGPT" where the program allows it), their own API key from any provider, and local or on-device models. Present them in plain words ("Use my plan", "Use my own key", "Run on this device"). Vidoxlabs never bills for model use at launch, and never handles consumer-plan credentials outside the vendor's own flow.
2. **Ship the model ladder by default:** on-device or small cloud model for triage, chat, and summaries; a mid-tier model for most tool steps; a frontier model only when `aestivation` marks a step as hard or a check fails.
3. **Every agent has a monthly budget** with a hard cap and a visible meter. Level 5 agents cannot exceed it.
4. **Hosted credits: later, maybe.** No hosted plan and no broker at launch: early users want low cost or free, and asking them to route prompts and money through a new company raises the trust question before the product has answered it. Revisit only once there are users who ask for one bill, priced at cost plus a stated margin.
   - **Keys stay with the person.** In the desktop app, API keys live in the operating system's credential store. In the web app, keys are kept on the paired companion by default; storing a key in the web account is an explicit opt-in, encrypted, with the trade-off explained.
5. **Measure cost per finished task** in `trellis` operational probes, so a change that doubles token use fails CI.

Owners: `seed` (provider adapters, model ladder, budget contract), `capillary` (packet size and cache-friendly ordering), `drosera` (tool search), `aestivation` (per-step model choice, batching), `bloom` (provider sign-in and spend meter), `trellis` (cost regression probes).

---

## 4. Focus area 3: scope of work

### 4.1 The problem

People use agents for three broad jobs: building code and tools; work such as reading PDFs, research, and reports; and everyday conversation and errands. Building three products dilutes the effort. Building one generic chat box produces a lesser product that the next model release makes obsolete.

### 4.2 Options

| Option | Tradeoffs |
| --- | --- |
| A. Pick one vertical (for example coding) | Clear story; crowded market; leaves the personal-assistant thesis unproven |
| B. Generic assistant | Broad; nothing a frontier vendor's own app does not do better |
| C. Personal core plus installable skill packs | The core (persona, memory, context, tools, review, autonomy) is shared; each job is a pack of skills, tools, workflows, and tests. Needs a strong pack format and good starter packs |

### 4.3 Recommendation

Option C. Build the layer that gets **more** valuable as models improve, not less:

- **Owned by the user, compounding over time:** memory of the person, each assistant's own memory of itself, workflows, and standing rules. These survive model changes and are exportable.
- **Model-agnostic:** a better model is an upgrade for Vivarium, not a replacement for it.
- **Three starter packs at launch,** each with acceptance tests in `trellis`:
  1. *Build:* code and tool work in a real work tree, with plans reviewed by `aestivation`.
  2. *Work:* documents, PDFs, research, and reports, with every claim tied to a source by `capillary`.
  3. *Everyday:* conversation, reminders, errands, and messages, with memory governed by `myosotis`.
- **One assistant can hold several packs.** The person does not choose a product; they give their assistant a new skill.

Owners: `drosera` (pack format: skills, tools, hooks, cookbooks), `seed` (pack and agent contracts), `myosotis` and `capillary` (the compounding layer), `trellis` (per-pack acceptance tests), `bloom` (pack install and discovery).

---

## 5. Focus area 4: connectors and tooling

### 5.1 The problem

Every API or tool-server connector needs its own sign-in, keys, or OAuth grant. Tokens expire, updates break them, tool definitions flood the context window, and agents pick the wrong tool when two look alike. Managing twenty connectors is a chore nobody signs up for. The owner's working theory: let the agent use a computer the way a person does, either the person's own device or a computer of its own.

### 5.2 State of the art (25 Nov 2026)

- **Computer use is now credible.** Leading agents report scores above the original human baseline on the verified OSWorld desktop benchmark, with top submissions reported near 90% against a 72% human baseline measured on the earlier task set ([OSWorld-Verified](https://www.llmboard.ai/benchmarks/osworld-verified-485)). It is still slower and costlier per step than a direct API call, and benchmark tasks are not the long tail of real apps.
- **Operating systems are building the "agent's own seat".** Windows 11's agent workspace gives each agent its own account and its own Windows session, running in parallel with the person's session, with access only to folders and apps the person shares. It is a preview feature, off by default ([Microsoft](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/ai/ai-features/experimental-agentic-features), [Windows blog](https://blogs.windows.com/windowsexperience/2025/10/16/securing-ai-agents-on-windows/)). Microsoft also offers full cloud PCs for agents in preview.
- **Phones expose actions, not screens.** Android AppFunctions lets apps publish typed functions that authorized agents can call (Android 16+, experimental), and Apple's App Intents expose app actions to Siri and system intelligence, now open to all developers in a preview ([Android](https://developer.android.com/ai/appfunctions), [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents)).
- **Browser agents in your logged-in sessions work but are attackable.** Researchers demonstrated zero-click prompt-injection attacks against browser agents acting inside signed-in sessions; vendors add classifiers and approvals but say the risk is not zero ([SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/zero-click-ai-browser-hacking-claude-and-chatgpt-atlas-hijacked-via-emails-x-posts/), [Claude help](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12902428-use-claude-in-chrome-safely)).
- **Credentials can be filled without the model seeing them.** Password managers now let an agent request a login, the person approves, and the extension fills it outside the model's view ([1Password](https://support.1password.com/1password-for-agents/)).
- **Tool-server auth is maturing.** The current tool-protocol spec requires OAuth 2.1 with short-lived tokens and adds enterprise-managed authorization ([spec](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization)). It reduces the mess; it does not remove one sign-in per service.

### 5.3 The two device models, honestly

| | Agent drives the person's device | Agent has its own computer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Context and logins | Everything is already there | Starts empty; needs files and sign-ins shared into it |
| Contention | Person and agent fight over one mouse, keyboard, and focus | None; both work at once |
| Safety | Mistakes land on the person's real session | Mistakes land in a sandbox first |
| Supervision | Person sees everything, but only while watching | Needs a journal and a live view |
| Redundant storage | None | Risk of copied files and stale duplicates |
| Cost | Free | A second machine or a cloud PC |

### 5.4 Recommendation: "a seat beside you"

Neither extreme. Give the agent **its own seat on the person's machine**: a separate session or profile on the same device, sharing what the person chooses, plus an optional cloud seat for always-on work.

1. **Own seat, shared context.** The agent works in its own desktop session, browser profile, and working folders on the person's device. It reads the person's files by reference through `capillary` (pointer plus digest, not copies), so there is one source of truth and no stale duplicates. Where the OS offers an agent workspace (Windows today), use it; elsewhere, use a separate user profile or a contained virtual desktop.
2. **An access ladder instead of a connector zoo.** The agent tries the cheapest reliable route first:

   | Rung | Route | Sign-in burden |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | 0 | Local files, clipboard, and OS-native app actions (App Intents, AppFunctions, Windows agent connectors) | None |
   | 1 | The agent's own browser profile, signed in once by the person; secrets filled by the person's password manager outside the model's view | Once per site, renewed by the browser like any person's session |
   | 2 | API or tool-server connectors only for high-value, high-frequency services, loaded on demand through tool search | One sign-in screen for all of them, with health checks and renewal handled by `drosera` |
   | 3 | Vision-based computer use as the universal fallback for anything else | None beyond rung 1 |

3. **No contention on phones (later).** When mobile arrives, the phone is the remote control, not the workstation: chat, voice, the questions inbox, notifications, and OS-native actions. Long tasks run in the desktop app, the web app, or a companion.
4. **Supervision without staring.** Every action goes to a journal with screenshots for visual steps; reversible actions get undo; external or irreversible actions follow the autonomy table in section 2.3; a live view lets the person watch or take over at any time.
5. **Injection defense by design.** Content the agent reads is data, never instructions; actions triggered while reading untrusted content are held for review by `aestivation`; the browser seat has no access to the password vault except through the approve-and-fill flow.
6. **Optional cloud seat** for 24/7 routines, later, with the same journal and policies.

### 5.5 How the cloud web app gets context without direct device access

A web app running on Vidoxlabs servers cannot see a person's files, apps, or signed-in sessions, and should not pretend to. It gathers context only through routes the person turns on, each visible and revocable, cheapest first:

| Route | What it reaches | How it connects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Upload and drag-in | Files, screenshots, pasted text the person hands over | The browser; nothing else installed |
| Account connectors | Cloud data the person already keeps online (for example mail, drive, calendar, code hosting) | Standard OAuth grants with the narrowest scopes, loaded on demand through tool search (5.4, rung 2) |
| Browser extension | The page the person is looking at, selections, and tabs they share | Optional extension; reads only on the person's action or for sites they allow |
| The agent's own cloud browser | Public web research and sites the person signs the agent into once | A browser session that belongs to the agent, not to the person's own browser |
| Paired companion | Local files by reference, local apps, the clipboard, local models, and subscription sign-in programs that require a local runtime | The desktop app, or a small companion agent, paired to the web account by a one-time code. It opens an **outbound-only** connection, so no ports are opened on the person's network, and it enforces the same autonomy settings locally |

Device-only steps (a local file, a desktop app, a local model, a plan that must run on the person's own runtime) are handed to the companion. If none is paired, the agent says what it would need and offers the next-best route (upload, a connector), instead of guessing. Web pages and third-party chat sites are never driven from Vidoxlabs servers inside the person's own signed-in sessions.

Owners: `bloom` (pairing UI, route picker in setup), `drosera` (connector broker, companion tool faces), `capillary` (by-reference context with digests from every route), `seed` (session protocol between web app and companion), `aestivation` (holds for actions triggered by untrusted content), `trellis` (pairing and route probes).

Owners: `drosera` (access ladder, tool search, connector broker, OS action adapters), `bloom` (agent seat, live view, takeover, journal UI), `capillary` (by-reference context with digests), `myosotis` (what the agent may keep from what it saw), `aestivation` (action review, injection holds), `seed` (tool identity and action-class contract), `trellis` (probes that replay journals and check policies held).

---

## 6. Focus area 5: interfaces and platforms

### 6.1 Market share (StatCounter, October 2026, share of web page views, not installed base)

| Segment | Share | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Desktop worldwide | Windows 76.6%, macOS 15.7%, Linux 5.7%, ChromeOS 2.0% | [Dr. Windows summary of StatCounter](https://www.drwindows.de/news/browser-und-betriebssysteme-im-oktober-2026) |
| Mobile worldwide | Android 72.4%, iOS 27.6% (12-month average about 69% / 31%) | [Spreadcast summary of StatCounter](https://spreadcast.app/resources/android-vs-ios-market-share) |
| Mobile United States | iOS 52.0%, Android 48.0% (12-month average about 59% iOS) | same |
| All platforms worldwide | Android 44.7%, Windows 28.9%, iOS 17.5%, macOS 5.9%, Linux 2.2% | [Dr. Windows](https://www.drwindows.de/news/browser-und-betriebssysteme-im-oktober-2026) |

Reading: mobile is where people are; the desktop is where agents can do real work today; Windows dominates desktops; iOS leads in the United States; Android leads everywhere else.

### 6.2 Rollout order (decided 25 November 2026)

1. **Desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux) and a cloud-hosted web app, together.** One interface (`bloom`) in both. The desktop app runs agents on the person's own machine; the web app runs agents in the cloud and reaches the device through the routes in 5.5. Windows gets first-class attention because of its share; macOS because early adopters and developers are there; Linux because it costs little extra.
2. **Companion pairing and browser extension.** The context routes that make the web app useful without device access (5.5).
3. **Messaging channels.** Talk to your assistant from chat apps and email you already use, with the same question and autonomy settings. Low install friction.
4. **Mobile later (iOS and Android).** Chat, voice, the questions inbox, notifications, quick capture, and on-device triage with the phone's own small model. Mobile is harder to build well, so it follows the desktop and web apps.
5. **OS-native integrations.** Publish Vivarium actions through App Intents, AppFunctions, and Windows agent connectors.

Consumer chat sites (for example a vendor's own chat web app) cannot be configured from a hosted web app, and Vivarium does not try. Subscriptions connect only through official sign-in programs (3.2).

Owners: `bloom` (all surfaces), `seed` (one session protocol every surface speaks), `drosera` (OS-native action adapters), `trellis` (cross-platform probes).

---

## 7. Cross-cutting principles

- **Claims match evidence.** Every capability stays labelled `implemented`, `specified`, `planned`, or `observed`, as the systems already require.
- **One change, one repository.** The umbrella pins and explains; it never edits a system. Changes land as pull requests in the owning system.
- **Model-agnostic, device-agnostic, connector-light.** Prefer routes that need no new sign-in.
- **The person stays in charge.** Autonomy is chosen, visible, and revocable; credentials always ask.

## 8. Decisions and open questions

Decided by the owner on 25 November 2026:

| # | Question | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Where do the internal agents live? | Nowhere special: they are user-created agents, made through the same in-app setup as any user's, kept in the owner's own user data. No overlay, branch, or fork (2.5) |
| 2 | How do people pay for models at launch? | Existing subscriptions through official sign-in programs, their own API keys, and local models. No hosted plan or broker at launch; hosted credits later, maybe (3.4) |
| 3 | First surface? | Desktop app and cloud-hosted web app; mobile later (6.2) |
| 4 | Default autonomy? | None. Chosen in first-run setup, changeable later, with the setting linked from every question (2.3, 2.4a) |
| 5 | Codename or product name? | Product name: Vivarium. `bloom` is its user-interface system |
| 6 | Should the umbrella also pin `docs` and `videsign`? | No. `docs` stays product-neutral (it may serve future products) and already syncs every system's documentation; `videsign` is design canon. Link both |

Still open:

| # | Question | Options | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7 | Cloud seat for always-on agents: build or rent? | (a) rent cloud PCs; (b) self-host; (c) defer | (c) until the desktop app and web app ship |
| 8 | Subscription programs beyond ChatGPT? | Track each vendor's program; adopt only official ones | Adopt official programs only; never handle consumer-plan credentials outside the vendor's flow |
| 9 | Companion form | (a) the desktop app doubles as the companion; (b) a separate small companion agent; (c) both | (a) first, so there is one install; (b) later for people who want a minimal footprint |

## 9. Sources (read 25 November 2026)

- Feng, McDonald, Zhang, "Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents": https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12469
- OpenAI, Sign in with ChatGPT Terms: https://openai.com/policies/sign-in-with-chatgpt-terms/
- OpenAI Help, Using your ChatGPT plan in other apps: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001542-using-your-chatgpt-plan-in-other-apps-and-sites
- Anthropic, Claude Code legal and compliance: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance
- OpenAI API pricing (standard and batch): https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing
- Gemini API rate limits: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits
- OpenRouter limits: https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/limits
- Apple Foundation Models framework: https://developer.apple.com/foundation-models-framework/
- Android on-device inference: https://developer.android.com/blog/posts/build-intelligent-android-apps-on-device-inference
- HyDRA hybrid routing (arXiv): https://arxiv.org/html/2605.17106
- TrueFoundry routing benchmark: https://www.truefoundry.com/blog/engineering/llm-cost-routing-benchmark/
- Anthropic, advanced tool use: https://www.anthropic.com/research/advanced-tool-use
- Anthropic, code execution with tool servers: https://www.anthropic.com/research/code-execution-with-mcp
- Model Context Protocol, client best practices: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2025-11-25/develop/clients/client-best-practices
- Model Context Protocol, authorization: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization
- OSWorld-Verified leaderboard: https://www.llmboard.ai/benchmarks/osworld-verified-485
- Microsoft, Experimental agentic features: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/ai/ai-features/experimental-agentic-features
- Windows Experience Blog, Securing AI agents on Windows: https://blogs.windows.com/windowsexperience/2025/10/16/securing-ai-agents-on-windows/

sources/aestivation/README.md.text: Plans, verdicts, and the assembly gate # aestivation Plan proposal, deterministic validation, review verdicts, and the assembly gate. Aestivation is the admission and review member of the bloom agent family. Before work opens, it happens here: a plan is proposed, a deterministic rule pack validates it, reviewers record approve or revise verdicts, and a gate holds automatic assembly until the plan is both valid and approved. A revision verdict stops assembly; the reasons say what to change; the next plan is a new proposal. ## Status Version 0.5.0. The plan rule pack, verdict ledger, and assembly gate are `implemented` as a tested reference library. A durable ledger, live reviewers, and service interfaces remain `specified` or `planned`. ## Install ```bash npm install @vidoxlabs/aestivation ``` Requires Node >= 22.13. Zero runtime dependencies. ## Modules | Module | What it holds | Label | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `plan.mjs` | Plan proposals: objective plus ordered steps, the SHA-256 digest of each proposal's content, and the deterministic rule pack that validates stages, titles, and order. | `implemented` | | `verdict.mjs` | Verdict records (approve or revise) that may name the plan digest they reviewed, the append-only ledger, and the soundness check over every record. | `implemented` | | `intent.mjs` | Read-only intent assessments that name missing sources and ground personal recall in admitted memory references. Tool and memory-write lists stay under caller admission. | `implemented` | | `correction.mjs` | Corrections within existing scope after an exact-digest revise verdict, with new frozen proposals, a two-replan limit per in-process lineage, and a check that refuses superseded results. The judge cannot apply the patch. | `implemented` | | `gate.mjs` | The assembly gate: one function that checks the ledger, holds a review of a different plan version as stale, and composes validation and verdicts into permitted or held, with the reason. | `implemented` | ## The name Aestivation is the arrangement of petals in a bud before it opens. That is the entire doctrine: the work of arranging before the opening. Nothing assembles until the arrangement has been validated and reviewed. When it opens, it opens because the gate said so for stated reasons. ## The rule pack The baseline deterministic rules a plan must pass: 1. A plan has at least one step. 2. Every step names a known stage: `research`, `work`, `review`, `assemble`, or `verify`. 3. Every step has a non-empty title. 4. When review and assemble are both present, review precedes the first assemble. 5. When verify is present, it is the final step. The same plan validates the same way every time, and no review can wave it through. The split runs both ways: no rule pack approves a plan on a reviewer's behalf. Judgment and rules are separate lanes; the gate composes them. ## The family The family follows one design law: ordinary botanical words for public products. | Name | Province | | :--- | :--- | | [`seed`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed) | Harness foundation: runs, tools, providers | | [`capillary`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary) | Context retrieval and relations, provenance-first | | [`myosotis`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/myosotis) | Memory with consent and structural forget | | `aestivation` (this repo) | Plans, verdicts, and the gate before assembly | | [`drosera`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/drosera) | Tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks | | [`trellis`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/trellis) | Multi-point testing with dated evidence | | [`bloom`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) | The team workspace harness | | [`docs`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs) | Family documentation, synced from every public repository | ## Documentation - `AGENTS.md`: start here before editing. Stay in this repository's province. - `docs/charter.md`: mission, principles, non-goals. - `docs/architecture.md`: the bud and its four whorls. - `docs/contracts/`: the plan, verdict, and gate contracts. - `docs/interop.md`: how bloom runs the loop, and how seed carries its effects. ## Development ```bash npm test ``` Tests use the Node built-in runner. Adding a rule means adding the test that holds it. ## License MIT The Vidoxlabs name and mark are trademarks of Vidoxlabs LLC. They are not covered by this repository's MIT license.

sources/bloom/README.md.text: Workspace, CLI, and terminal UI # Bloom Give a head agent a brief and watch a team work through it in one group conversation. Specialists can research public sources, review the findings, and assemble a Markdown guide. Each contribution is a file on a shared desktop that you can open, attach to another task, or download. [Download the latest release](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom/releases/latest) · [View the phone layout](docs/previews/phone.png) ![Bloom’s scripted research team sharing its findings, review and guide in one workspace](docs/previews/workspace.png) ## Try it Download `bloom-VERSION.zip` from the [latest release](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom/releases/latest) and extract it, or clone this repository. Install Node.js 22.13 or newer and run this command from the project folder in a terminal on macOS, Linux, or Windows. The release ZIP already holds Bloom's one runtime dependency, seed; in a clone, run `npm install` first. ```sh npm run demo ``` Open the local address the demo prints, choose **Create a team** and give the head agent a name. Use **Add file** to paste some project notes, select **Try a sample task**, and send it. Open the assembler’s file in the group chat. The demo is scripted and requires no key. Its outputs and usage display identify it as a demonstration. Run `node bin/bloom.mjs eval --smoke` to check the built-in coding fixture offline and print its deterministic report. ## Connect a model endpoint Teams and coding sessions run on any service that speaks the chat-completions HTTP API (`POST {base}/chat/completions`). Bloom names no default service. The endpoint lives only in the private `config.json` in Bloom's data directory, described under **Terminal commands** below, and neither the web workspace nor the terminal takes it on the command line. ```sh npm start -- --workspace '' ``` The web workspace follows the terminal's rules: local providers only, the configured key setting, and the model profile saved by `bloom doctor --probe`. Team calls send the brief and admitted evidence to that endpoint. Without a provider, Bloom still opens the workspace, notes and files, and a team turn stops with a message pointing at `config.json`. Every provider runs behind [seed](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed)'s provider seam: Bloom checks the adapter when it starts and checks every reply against seed's record before the team reads it. A reply outside that record stops the turn. **Coding sessions** run the coding loop in the chosen folder when a provider is configured. The browser shows streamed text, a row for every model call and tool call, and an approval card before every write and every command. The scripted demo runtime shows the same view without a model. [docs/live-test.md](docs/live-test.md) is the runbook for a first live run in a throwaway sandbox. ## Terminal commands **Implemented.** After `npm install`, run `npm link` to install the `bloom` command from this checkout. Try the scripted runtime with `bloom chat --demo`, or run it once with `bloom run --headless --demo --json "Inspect the project"`. Headless runs reject requests by default. Use `--approve-policy allow-read` to allow read requests. A configured local model can run the existing team loop. In the terminal data directory, use a private `config.json` with `version: 1`, one entry under `providers` with `kind: "chat-completions"` and `baseURL` set to your OpenAI-compatible API base, and `models.aliases` containing an alias, backend model ID and workload. Set `models.default` to that alias or choose one with `--model`. Loopback is local by default. For a server on your private network, set `locality` to `local`. Enable `allowInsecureHttp` only if that server uses plain HTTP. Set `apiKeyEnv` to the name of an environment variable if the server requires a key. The team loop uses the desktop and saved specialists. `--team NAME --workspace PATH` records a team session's workspace. **Implemented:** `bloom chat --workspace PATH` without `--team` runs the coding loop in that folder: the model reads, searches, edits and runs `node`, `npm` or `git` there, and Bloom asks before every write and every command. A headless `bloom run --workspace PATH` never writes. Read the command gate and its residual risk in [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) before pointing it at a folder you care about. Terminal cloud providers need `--allow-cloud` inside a sandbox from `scripts/make-sandbox.mjs`; the web workspace stays local only. `bloom doctor` checks the local installation and endpoint rule without displaying the address. `bloom doctor --probe` also asks the configured provider what it supports, saves its model profile, and names the provider only by its config name and locality. Cloud providers need `--allow-cloud` on probe and chat. `bloom sessions list` lists session IDs. `bloom sessions export ID --jsonl` writes the stored events in order, and `bloom replay FILE --step` displays them one at a time. Use `--data-dir` to select the data directory, including when you read a demo session. `bloom memory --help` lists note commands. Forget requires `--confirm`. ## Work with a team - **Assign work.** Set the head agent’s **Jurisdiction** and describe the deliverable. Add a specialist under **Personas** before starting a new team with a configured model. The head assigns work to saved personas and team members. The scripted demo includes three example specialists. Select a recipient or type `@Reviewer: check the latest draft` for a direct assignment in the group. A review verdict of “revise” pauses assembly. Address the author with the requested changes and attach the review when continuing. - **Reuse specialists.** Use **Save as persona** on a roster member, or **+ New** under **Personas** in the left sidebar, to keep a specialist's name, **Jurisdiction**, voice, stage and optional model. Every head agent sees the library when it plans and can recruit a persona by name; the saved fields are used as they are, and the head only writes the assignment. **Add to team** puts a persona on the open team's roster for a direct `@Name:` message. Editing or deleting a persona leaves teams that already recruited it unchanged. - **Share evidence.** Paste up to three public HTTPS URLs in a brief or use **Add file** on the **Shared desktop** for a web page, GitHub repository README, or text. Bloom records the source and its digest. The head can select files from the shared catalog. The source reader retrieves public text over IPv4 and records excerpts. Specialists receive bounded excerpts and see which sources were shortened. - **Inspect a handoff.** Open a file in the conversation or inspector. Its detail includes the author, SHA-256, and input-file relationships. Each revision is a separate Markdown file. For an edit made in another application, import the changed text as a new source. - **Manage memory.** Use **Add note** under **Notes** to tell the team what to remember. Leave **Always use** checked for standing instructions, or turn it off for background facts that should reach a specialist only when they match the task. **Share with every team** makes a note available to all teams on this computer. Specialists can suggest facts to keep; they appear under **Suggested by agents** and are never used until you **Keep** them. **Activity** lists exactly which notes each specialist received. **Correct** replaces a note. **Forget** removes it. Either one invalidates cached recall, stops an active run, and withholds earlier outputs built from that note from future team prompts. Previous messages, exported files, provider logs and copies on the local disk have separate lifetimes. - **Ask another team.** When another team's **Jurisdiction** covers part of a brief, the head agent can ask it one question per task. Both conversations show the question and the answer. The other team answers from its jurisdiction, notes shared with every team, and its non-private posts and files, never its private notes. The asking team pays for the call. A busy team is skipped. **Stop** in the other team ends only the answer. - **Control usage.** Under **Model and limits**, the team form accepts a per-run **Model calls** limit and an optional **Token limit**. Bloom checks the token limit between calls. One call can cross it. Missing metering stops further calls when a token limit is active. Expand **Usage** under **Activity** for per-agent usage, provider-reported cache reads and writes, and cost when supplied. Local recall hits and provider token caching have separate counters. Model outputs and tool effects are never replayed as cache hits. - **Use the desktop.** One persistent `Desktop/` folder belongs to the local installation. Teams share ordinary files. Check a file and ask the team to change it: a specialist can revise it, rename it or file it into a folder. Each change is a new version, marked `v2`, `v3` and so on, and **Open** lists the other revisions. Team-note-derived files have room-scoped access through the harness. For a graphical Linux desktop over that same folder, install Docker with Compose, run `npm run desktop -- --demo` alongside the demo, and open the local address the command prints. For real profiles omit `--demo`. Stop it with `npm run desktop -- --demo --down`. Docker first downloads the desktop image. The desktop provides a persistent graphical environment for the operator. Team agents interact with its files through Bloom. [Webtop](https://docs.linuxserver.io/images/docker-webtop/) ## Storage and extension points Bloom serves the browser on loopback and stores SQLite history and desktop files under `~/.bloom` (`~/.bloom/demo` for the demo). Pass `--data-dir PATH` to select a different folder and pass the same argument to the optional desktop command. Existing ViBloom data directories are detected. Use one server per data directory. A running local account can access its files. Closing the browser leaves the local server working. Stopping the server interrupts active work. Agents start at [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). Stay in this repository's province. [Architecture and design sources](docs/architecture.md) explains the VI, OAI and LA roles, the portable memory implementation, design-token synchronization, and verification boundaries. ```sh npm test npm run test:network ``` ## License Bloom is available under the [MIT license](LICENSE). The bundled Geist fonts retain the [SIL Open Font License](public/fonts/Geist-OFL.txt). The Vidoxlabs name and mark are trademarks of Vidoxlabs LLC. They are not covered by this repository's MIT license.

sources/capillary/README.md.text: Context with its sources attached # Capillary Capillary is an open, local-first **context retrieval system** for agent workspaces. It records sources with their digests, retrieves **bounded, provenance-honest packets** of them, and keeps **typed relations** between the items it holds: the fine-channel work of lifting context up to the team that needs it, without letting prose smuggle in as fact. Agent surfaces like [Bloom](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) consume capillary exactly where retrieving (and organizing) their source and context matters: a team brief admits sources, and specialists receive bounded excerpts that say what they are, where they came from, and what was shortened. Harness foundations like [Seed](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed) admit capillary's retrieval tools to their runs and record each retrieval as an intent. **Status: `1.3.0`, retrieval contracts and library modules.** The retrieval seam, source recording, and relation contracts are implemented and covered by `npm test`. The backing stores (index, service) are specified, not shipped. Nothing in this repository opens a network listener or retrieves over the network today. ## What is here today (`implemented`) | Module | What it does | | --- | --- | | `src/provenance.mjs` | Records source digests, origins, evidence classes and confidence, and records why sources are unknown | | `src/packet.mjs` | Builds bounded context packets with **declared** truncation, budgeted admission, declared unknown sources, and relevance and recency kept as separate fields | | `src/epoch-guard.mjs` | Refuses a packet when the deletion epoch at the end of a read differs from the epoch at its start, or cannot be read | | `src/read.mjs` | Reads caller-supplied text under an estimated token budget and declares truncation in an untrusted envelope | | `src/search.mjs` | Searches caller-supplied records for literal matches and reports recency and snippet cuts in an untrusted envelope | | `src/conversation.mjs` | Shapes one conversation's thread, a recent list, a brief of the newest operator intent and verified outcome, and an envelope around the parent walk, all from caller-supplied records | | `src/relations.mjs` | Typed, append-only relations and bounded walks over supplied parent links | `npm install && npm test` verifies all of it. No runtime dependencies. ## Contracts - [Bounded retrieval](docs/contracts/retrieval.md): the packet, its budgets, declared shortening, declared omissions - [Provenance](docs/contracts/retrieval.md): digests and origin classes on every source ## How capillary fits the systems (`specified`) The botanic line, per [docs/systems.md](docs/systems.md): **seed** (the foundation a runtime grows from) → **capillary** (these channels, lifting context to it) → **myosotis** (governed memory: consent, keep, and forget) → **aestivation** (the bud's arrangement, admission and review before assembly) → **drosera** (the sundew's tentacles: tools, skills, hooks, cookbooks) → **bloom** (the opened team workspace), with the whole line growing against **trellis** (the testing lattice that keeps every member honest). Capillary owns retrieval and organization only. Remembering with consent is the memory fabric's job (forget is a promise there, not a default); deciding what gets admitted into runs and what assembles is the gate's job. [docs/interop.md](docs/interop.md) draws each seam. ## Documentation - [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): start here before editing. Stay in this repository's province. - [Charter](docs/charter.md): mission, principles, non-goals - [Architecture](docs/architecture.md): sources, index, packets, relations - [Contracts](docs/contracts/retrieval.md): bounded retrieval and provenance - [Relations contract](docs/contracts/relations.md): typed, append-only context relations - [Interop](docs/interop.md): Bloom, Seed, and the memory seam - [Systems](docs/systems.md): the botanic naming line ## License [MIT](LICENSE) The Vidoxlabs name and mark are trademarks of Vidoxlabs LLC. They are not covered by this repository's MIT license.

sources/drosera/README.md.text: Tools, skills, hooks, and cookbooks # drosera Tooling for agents: tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks. Drosera is the tooling member of the bloom agent family. It defines the four packaging forms an agent works with beyond its own context. Tool faces are neutral definitions of what can be called, following seed's tool-id grammar. Skills are packaged instructions that grow context without granting authority. Hooks are deterministic checks, fail closed, bound to run events. Cookbooks are recipes that compose published faces and skills, resolved at validation. ## The name Drosera is the sundew. A sundew works by extension: sticky tentacles that reach out from the plant and hold what they touch, each one honest about what it has caught. That is the doctrine here: tools reach, each face says what it grips (summary, effect class), and the extensions never become the organism. The harness is the organism; drosera is what it holds. ## Status Version 2.2.0. Pack formats, validation, reference resolution, the skill document reader, and the in-memory skill catalog are `implemented` in the reference library. A live registry, connector bindings, and server interfaces remain `specified` or `planned`. ## Install ```bash npm install @vidoxlabs/drosera ``` Requires Node >= 22.13. Zero runtime dependencies. ## Modules | Module | What it holds | Label | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `pack.mjs` | Tool faces under seed's neutral tool-id grammar, and the tool pack that collects them with unique IDs and domain listings. | `implemented` | | `skills.mjs` | Skill validation, lifecycle transitions, skill packs, and a catalog for promoted MIT skills. | `implemented` | | `skill-markdown.mjs` | Reads a skill document's text, which the caller already holds, into the record `skills.mjs` checks. It opens no file. | `implemented` | | `hooks.mjs` | Hook records: deterministic checks bound to run events, and the fail-closed hook pack. | `implemented` | | `cookbook.mjs` | Recipes composing faces and skills, with validation that every reference resolves. | `implemented` | ## The family The family follows one design law: ordinary botanical words for public products ([the law](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary/blob/main/docs/family.md)). | Name | Province | | :--- | :--- | | [`seed`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed) | Harness foundation: runs, tools, providers | | [`capillary`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary) | Context retrieval and relations, provenance-first | | [`myosotis`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/myosotis) | Memory with consent and structural forget | | [`aestivation`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/aestivation) | Plans, verdicts, and the gate before assembly | | `drosera` (this repo) | Tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks | | [`trellis`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/trellis) | Multi-point testing with dated evidence | | [`bloom`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) | The team workspace harness | | [`docs`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs) | Family documentation, synced from every public repository | ## Documentation - `AGENTS.md`: start here before editing. Stay in this repository's province. - `docs/charter.md`: mission, principles, non-goals. - `docs/architecture.md`: the tentacles and how they compose. - `docs/contracts/`: the tool, skill, hook, and cookbook contracts. - `docs/interop.md`: how each peer meets this fabric. ## Development ```bash npm test ``` Tests use the Node built-in runner. Adding a rule means adding the test that holds it. ## License MIT The Vidoxlabs name and mark are trademarks of Vidoxlabs LLC. They are not covered by this repository's MIT license.

sources/myosotis/README.md.text: Memory that keeps only what you allow # myosotis Governed memory for agents: consent to keep, structural forget. Myosotis is the memory member of the bloom agent family. It holds the contracts and reference modules for agent memory where two promises sit on the face of the thing: memory is only kept under proper consent, and a real forget is structural. A forget invalidates every projection built before it and withholds forgotten content from later reads. A stale projection fails closed; it never resurrects. ## Status Version 1.2.0. The record, consent, forget, bounded recall, and in-process continuity rules are `implemented` as a tested reference library. A durable store, projection adapters, and service interfaces remain `specified` or `planned`. ## Install ```bash npm install @vidoxlabs/myosotis ``` Requires Node >= 22.13. Zero runtime dependencies. ## Modules | Module | What it holds | Label | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `records.mjs` | Memory record shape and the closed set of memory classes: organizational, personal-consented, active-thread, unconfirmed. | `implemented` | | `consent.mjs` | Consent grants and revocations, ordered by an optional sequence so a later grant is re-consent, and the state that answers whether a scope currently has consent. | `implemented` | | `forget.mjs` | The memory store state machine: admission and supersede, the confirmed and keyed forget that tombstones a whole supersede chain, the epoch, and stamped projections of identifiers and digests that are refused once stale and rebuilt before they serve. | `implemented` | | `recall.mjs` | Bounded selection from caller-held records, with sensitivity checks and candidate, eligible, and selected counts. | `implemented` | | `continuity.mjs` | One active continuity per subject, held in the process. Lookup never opens one, attach refuses any id that is not this subject's active id without saying why, and isolate opens a new active id. | `implemented` | ## Why the classes stay distinguishable The four memory classes never collapse into one bucket: - **organizational**: knowledge that belongs to a scope, like a team's working notes. Kept without personal consent because it is not about a person. - **personal-consented** requires a live grant for its scope, an admissible sensitivity, and provenance of the principal's explicit confirmation. - **active-thread**: working context for the conversation happening now. Ephemeral by nature, never promoted to durable silently. - **unconfirmed**: an observation that has not been established. Stays marked. Never presented as known. Conflating them is the failure mode this fabric exists to prevent. ## Why forget is an epoch A forget that only deletes a row leaves every cached copy of that row alive. Myosotis models forget as an epoch bump: every projection (a cache, an index, a summary) carries the epoch it was built at, and any projection whose stamp no longer matches fails closed. Reading it is refused until it is rebuilt from the store. Bypass and rebuild, never resurrect. ## The family The family follows one design law: ordinary botanical words for public products. | Name | Province | | :--- | :--- | | [`seed`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed) | Harness foundation: runs, tools, providers | | [`capillary`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary) | Context retrieval and relations, provenance-first | | `myosotis` (this repo) | Memory with consent and structural forget | | [`aestivation`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/aestivation) | Plans, verdicts, and the gate before assembly | | [`drosera`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/drosera) | Tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks | | [`trellis`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/trellis) | Multi-point testing with dated evidence | | [`bloom`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) | The team workspace harness | | [`docs`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs) | Family documentation, synced from every public repository | ## Documentation - `AGENTS.md`: start here before editing. Stay in this repository's province. - `docs/charter.md`: mission, principles, non-goals. - `docs/architecture.md`: the parts and how they compose. - `docs/contracts/`: the record, consent, and forget contracts. - `docs/interop.md`: how bloom consumes memory, and where capillary ends and myosotis begins. ## Development ```bash npm test ``` Tests use the Node built-in runner. Adding a rule means adding the test that holds it. ## License MIT The Vidoxlabs name and mark are trademarks of Vidoxlabs LLC. They are not covered by this repository's MIT license.

sources/seed/README.md.text: Contracts and schemas for the runtime # Seed Seed is an open, local-first harness foundation for AI agents. It defines the contracts an agent runtime is built on: the run model, tool identity, and the provider adapter. Agent workspaces like [Bloom](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) can orchestrate model-backed workers, tools, and shared artifacts without depending on any single hosted service or third-party harness. **Status: `0.8.0`, specification and contract modules.** The contracts, grammar, and validators in this repository are implemented and covered by `npm test`. The runtime services on the roadmap are specified or planned, not shipped. Nothing in this repository opens a network listener, calls a hosted model, or touches your files today. ## Why Bloom proved the model-agnostic part: a notebook-shaped team workspace that treats any chat-completions-compatible service as one provider binding of several. The layer below the model is still rented: a third-party harness decides how tools are called, how runs are recovered, and how work proves itself. Seed takes that layer back as a small, open, inspectable foundation: - **One run model.** Work is an *objective* with *attempts*, recorded intents, and a verification receipt, not a loose prompt history. - **Neutral tool identity.** Tools are addressed by grammar, never by vendor, host, or product name, so adapters can be swapped without re-teaching agents. - **Provider-agnostic by contract.** Any inference service that can complete text can sit behind the same `generate` contract Bloom already speaks. ## What is here today (`implemented`) | Module | What it does | | --- | --- | | `src/tool-id.mjs` | Parse, format, and validate the neutral tool ID grammar; check registry entries, rollback postures, and cross-entry references | | `src/run-model.mjs` | Objective/attempt records, run statuses, legal transitions, and intent-time tool admission | | `src/resume.mjs` | Resume pending steps, report supplied failure classes, preview steps in a dry run, and manage in-process run leases | | `src/admission.mjs` | Fail-closed caller admission over a registry the caller holds | | `src/registry-documents.mjs` | Check agents and tools documents the caller already parsed: name a document not supplied, and report an agent that names an unknown tool | | `src/provider.mjs` | Validate provider adapters and normalize generation results | | `src/model-alias.mjs` | Resolve the alias a caller asks for to a backend model name from a table the caller holds, keeping the two names distinct and labeling deprecated aliases without swapping them | `npm install && npm test` verifies all of it. There are no runtime dependencies. ## Contracts (`specified`, `implemented` where modules cover them) - [Run model](docs/contracts/run-model.md): objectives, attempts, intents, receipts - [Tool identity](docs/contracts/tool-id.md): the neutral ID grammar and registry fields - [Provider adapter](docs/contracts/provider.md): the `generate` contract, compatible with Bloom's team provider ## How seed and Bloom fit (`specified`) Bloom already isolates its model layer behind one provider interface. Seed lands in three stages, each one usable by Bloom as it ships: 1. **Stage 1, library contracts.** Shared modules: tool IDs, run records, and provider validation (this release). 2. **Stage 2, inference endpoint.** A local service exposing an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions surface over any configured backend, which Bloom can consume today via its provider base URL. 3. **Stage 3, run engine and tool registry.** Durable objectives and attempts, an owner gate for effects that leave the run, and a tool registry adapters publish to. Details and worked examples: [docs/bloom-interop.md](docs/bloom-interop.md). ## Documentation - [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): start here before editing. Stay in this repository's province. - [Charter](docs/charter.md): mission, principles, non-goals - [Architecture](docs/architecture.md): planes, authority, and what seed refuses to own - [Lexicon](docs/lexicon.md): how public repositories stay in generalized terms - [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md): staged, status-labeled ## Design principles 1. Local-first. A clean checkout runs; nothing phones home. 2. One authority per fact. Runs own run state; memory owns memory; tools own effects. 3. Receipts over vibes. A run completes with a verification receipt, not a self-report. 4. Effects are gated. Side effects that leave a run pause for the owner. 5. No vendor names in tool identity. Grammar first; connectors carry the brand. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) The Vidoxlabs name and mark are trademarks of Vidoxlabs LLC. They are not covered by this repository's MIT license.

sources/trellis/README.md.text: Multi-point tests for the family # trellis Multi-point testing for the agent family: shape, behavior, consistency, operational. Trellis is the testing member of the bloom agent family. Every member repository keeps its own tests; trellis checks the family from the outside, from four points each: **shape** (the public surface is what it claims), **behavior** (the load-bearing invariants hold under direct calls), **consistency** (the peers agree where they claim to, one grammar, shared conventions), and **operational** (each test suite runs green when actually run). Verdicts are pass, fail, or unknown. A fail always outranks an unknown, an absent checkout is declared unknown, and health claims are dated runs kept as evidence, not standing truths. ## The name A trellis is the lattice a garden grows against. Climbing plants grip a lattice at many points, not one, and the lattice holds because every point it promises to hold is checked. The family is a garden of contract modules, and its health is a multi-point question, never a single green badge. ## Status Version 0.8.0. The probe, grid, and verdict engine is `implemented` as a tested reference library. Family health statements live in `docs/evidence/` as dated observed runs. The engine covers the family's module repositories. The harness and design canon keep their own checks. ## Install ```bash npm install @vidoxlabs/trellis ``` Requires Node >= 22.13. Zero runtime dependencies. ## Modules | Module | What it holds | Label | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `point.mjs` | The four test points and the probe record: deterministic checks, fail closed, dedicated to one point. | `implemented` | | `score.mjs` | Verdict math: pass, fail, unknown; fail outranks unknown, unknown outranks pass, and nothing is ever silently passed. | `implemented` | | `grid.mjs` | The multi-point grid: run probes against injected subjects and roll the results up per subject and per point. | `implemented` | | `probes.mjs` | The default probe lists for each family member and the cross-family consistency probes. A claim a member made after its first release is probed from the version that made it; an older checkout reads unknown. | `implemented` | The bundle runner, `scripts/family.mjs` (`npm run family`), wires the grid to the canonical family workspace: it loads each peer's modules, runs the default probes, runs each peer's own test suite for the operational point, and prints the dated report the evidence docs record. ## The family The family follows one design law: ordinary botanical words for public products ([the law](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary/blob/main/docs/family.md)). | Name | Province | | :--- | :--- | | [`seed`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed) | Harness foundation: runs, tools, providers | | [`capillary`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary) | Context retrieval and relations, provenance-first | | [`myosotis`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/myosotis) | Memory with consent and structural forget | | [`aestivation`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/aestivation) | Plans, verdicts, and the gate before assembly | | [`drosera`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/drosera) | Tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks | | `trellis` (this repo) | Multi-point testing with dated evidence | | [`bloom`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) | The team workspace harness | | [`docs`](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs) | Family documentation, synced from every public repository | The line grows against the trellis: the products are the plants; this is the lattice they are checked against. ## Documentation - `AGENTS.md`: start here before editing. Stay in this repository's province. - `docs/charter.md`: mission, principles, non-goals. - `docs/architecture.md`: probes, grid, verdicts; engine and bundle runner. - `docs/contracts/`: the probe and grid contracts. - `docs/interop.md`: what each peer is probed on, and the boundaries. - `docs/evidence/`: dated observed family runs, with their receipts. ## Development ```bash npm test # engine and probe mechanics, no siblings required npm run family # the bundle runner over the canonical workspace layout ``` Tests use the Node built-in runner. Adding a probe means adding the test that holds it. ## License MIT The Vidoxlabs name and mark are trademarks of Vidoxlabs LLC. They are not covered by this repository's MIT license.

sources/vivarium/README.md.text: # Vivarium Seven systems, one agent platform. Vivarium is a personal agent platform. A person raises an assistant with a character and a job, gives it memory they consent to keep, and works alongside it: it reads what they point it at, asks before it acts outside its bounds, and leaves a record of what it did. It runs on the person's own machine first, and every route it takes to a model, a file, or a service is one the person switched on. This repository is the umbrella, not the product. It pins the seven systems at exact commits, records what each one owns, and gives a code agent the context it needs to work in the family without guessing. No product code lives here: the code lives in the seven repositories, and this tree is the one snapshot that says which code that is. bloom is Vivarium's user interface; the other six systems are the parts behind it. ## The systems | System | Role | Layer | | --- | --- | --- | | [seed](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/seed) | Harness floor: run records, tool identity, provider adapters, the shared contracts | floor | | [capillary](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/capillary) | Context: bounded retrieval with sources attached, and relations | peer | | [myosotis](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/myosotis) | Memory: consent to keep, structural forget | peer | | [drosera](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/drosera) | Tools: tool faces, skills, hooks, cookbooks | peer | | [aestivation](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/aestivation) | Review and delegation: plans, verdicts, questions to the person, the assembly gate | peer | | [bloom](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/bloom) | User interface: the desktop and web app, first-run setup, the head agent; the only composer | composer | | [trellis](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/trellis) | Testing from outside the call path: shape, behavior, consistency, operational probes | outside | The floor holds the contracts. The four peers do not import each other; they meet at seed. bloom is the only composer: it is where a person raises an agent and where the parts are put together. trellis tests from outside the call path, so a failure in the tree is not a failure the tree can hide. ## System map ```mermaid flowchart BT bloom["bloom · interface"] capillary["capillary · context"] myosotis["myosotis · memory"] drosera["drosera · tools"] aestivation["aestivation · review"] trellis["trellis · probes"]:::outside seed["seed · harness floor"]:::floor bloom -->|imports drosera 7a396c0| drosera bloom -->|imports seed 0d158cd| seed bloom -.->|contracts| seed capillary -.->|contracts| seed myosotis -.->|contracts| seed drosera -.->|contracts| seed aestivation -.->|contracts| seed capillary -.->|"context to memory, planned"| myosotis trellis -.->|probes| bloom trellis -.->|probes| capillary trellis -.->|probes| myosotis trellis -.->|probes| drosera trellis -.->|probes| aestivation trellis -.->|probes| seed linkStyle 2,3,4,5,6,7 stroke-dasharray: 6 4 linkStyle 8,9,10,11,12,13 stroke-dasharray: 2 4 classDef floor stroke-width:3px classDef outside stroke-dasharray: 4 3 ``` Solid is an import today, labelled with the pinned short SHA. Run `git submodule update --init --recursive`. `npm run check` is offline and deterministic. It fails when a generated file drifts from the pins, when a submodule is not at its gitlink, when a relative link or a `systems/` path does not resolve, or when a public-safety rule trips. `npm test` runs the unit tests for the tool itself. ## How changes flow 1. **Change a system in its own repository.** A pull request there, its own tests, its own review. Nothing in this repository edits a submodule. 2. **The pin moves here.** Either the scheduled bump opens a pull request with the new pins and the regenerated manifest and map, or a person runs `npm run sync` and opens `chore(systems): bump `. Either way the pin is a commit that is on that system's `main`. 3. **Readers get the prose from the docs hub.** [docs](https://github.com/Vidoxlabs/docs) syncs every system's README and documentation, so this repository links to those pages instead of copying them. 4. **`docs` is linked, not pinned.** It is product-neutral and may serve more than one product, so it is not part of the snapshot.
